11.5 Sediment as a time-dependent, accumulating compartment

Rationale. Sediment is an accumulating, long-residence depositional compartment, and it is the sink for the large/dense particles that differential settling removes from the water column (Hoffman et al. 2026; the critical-size capture-fraction diagnostic in Section 13 quantifies that filtering mechanism for this dataset). Those deposited particles continue to fragment in situ, so — per Thuy-Dung, Groenenberg & Koelmans (2026) — both exposure (bioaccessible particle number) and hazard (HC5, via which benthic species are size-accessible) are dynamic rather than static. A single-time-point sediment RQ is therefore a snapshot that can under-represent future risk in an accumulating bed. Everything in this section is a framework upgrade, not a live risk calculation: the sediment exposure concentration remains non-quantitative (sediment_concentration_is_quantitative = FALSE, SPEC 1d), so nothing here re-introduces sediment into the headline risk conclusion (Sections 11.3.0/11.4.0/15.3).

11.5.1 Temporal fragmentation framing

  • Sediment is treated as a time-dependent, accumulating compartment. Deposited microplastics continue to fragment, shifting the particle-size distribution toward smaller, more numerous, more bioaccessible particles over residence time in the bed.
  • Consequently, any static sediment metric is a lower-bound snapshot. Both HC5 (which benthic species are size-accessible) and bioaccessible exposure evolve as fragmentation proceeds — the single-time-point Food Dilution/Tissue Translocation figures in Section 11.4 describe the sediment PSD’s condition at the time of sampling, not its trajectory.
  • This compounds, rather than substitutes for, the SPEC 1d exposure-concentration problem. Even once a genuine dry-weight sediment concentration becomes available, a single power-law fit to that concentration would still understate risk relative to the bed’s future, more-fragmented state.
  • Cite Thuy-Dung, Groenenberg & Koelmans (2026) — a prospective, temporally-explicit risk framework for fragmenting microplastics (size-independent fragmentation rate constant kfrag, doubling time TD) in which HC5 and RCR are time-dependent because shrinking particles become bioaccessible to progressively more sensitive species; the source paper’s median HC5 example drops from 2.1×10⁴ to 1.95×10³ particles/kg when a sensitive species becomes accessible, and individual-species RCR>1 can precede a derivable community SSD by roughly a decade. Cross-reference: the Hoffman et al. (2026) differential-settling sink argument already used in this document (Section 13’s critical-size diagnostic) is the mechanism that puts large/dense particles into the sediment bed in the first place; SPEC 1e is about what happens to them after they arrive.

11.5.3 Time-varying bioaccessibility (documented; future enhancement)

Making the existing pSSD++ bioaccessibility size-gate explicitly time-dependent (HC5(t)/RCR(t) as a trajectory) is deferred: it needs a residence-time/age-of-deposition axis that does not exist in the source sediment dataset. Full scoping in Appendix C.

11.5.4 Most-sensitive-species screen (sediment)

Per Thuy-Dung et al. (2026), individual-species risk can precede a derivable community SSD signal by roughly a decade, and the sediment benthic SSD here is small and comparatively unstable (89 records, 9 species). This screen identifies the single most sensitive species (lowest aligned effect dose) per ERM and reports it alongside the community HC5 already computed in Section 11.4 — as an early-warning companion, not a replacement.

For Food Dilution, the single most sensitive species among the 7 sediment benthic species considered is Chironomus tepperi (median aligned dose = 1.11 particles/kg dw, 3000 aligned records), compared with the community Food Dilution HC5 of 0.0635 particles/kg dw computed in Section 11.4. For Tissue Translocation, the most sensitive species is Chironomus tepperi (median aligned dose = 188 particles/kg dw, 3000 records), compared with the community Tissue Translocation HC5 of 11.7 particles/kg dw. As Section 11.5.3 notes, a finer PSD from continued fragmentation could bring additional, potentially more sensitive species into bioaccessible range over time, which is part of why this individual-species screen is worth tracking alongside the community HC5 rather than assuming the current community SSD is stable. This screen does not change the sediment exclusion from the headline conclusion (its inputs are the same non-quantitative-exposure sediment pathway); the companion individual-species screen for the quantitative river/ocean water compartments is reported in Section 15.4, once every matrix’s hazard objects have been computed.

12. Ocean Water

Ocean water samples were collected from the coastal/marine environment and analyzed using the same µFTIR workflow as river water. Marine species are evaluated using the PSSDplusplus marine toxicity endpoints and alignment parameters, which characterize exposure and hazard in particles/L rather than particles/kg (sediment).

12.1 Particle data and C-PSD fitting

Particle volume computation

Show the code 
# Compute W/L thickness ratio from ocean particles (same instrument as river)
ratio_tbl_ocean <- raw_particles_ocean |>
  dplyr::mutate(WL = 1 / aspect_ratio) |>
  dplyr::group_by(shape) |>
  dplyr::summarise(
    n      = dplyr::n(),
    r_med  = median(WL, na.rm = TRUE),
    r_low  = quantile(WL, 0.25, na.rm = TRUE),
    r_high = quantile(WL, 0.75, na.rm = TRUE),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

raw_particles_ocean <- raw_particles_ocean |>
  assign_polymer_density(lookup = polymer_density_tbl) |>
  dplyr::left_join(ratio_tbl_ocean |> dplyr::select(shape, r_med), by = "shape") |>
  dplyr::mutate(
    height_um = r_med * width_um,
    V_um3 = dplyr::case_when(
      shape == "fragment" ~ (pi / 6) * length_um * width_um * height_um,
      shape == "fiber"    ~ pi * (width_um / 2)^2 * length_um,
      TRUE ~ NA_real_
    ),
    mass_ug = V_um3 * density_g_cm3,
    mass_ug_fixed_density_1.1 = V_um3 * 1.1
  )

cat("Ocean particles: n =", nrow(raw_particles_ocean),
    "| shapes:", paste(sort(unique(raw_particles_ocean$shape)), collapse = ", "), "\n")

Show the code 
# Ocean-water sample_location carries the same four river-mouth-adjacent
# coastal site names as raw_particles_river (Carmel, Pajaro, Salinas, San
# Lorenzo) -- ocean water was collected adjacent to each river's discharge,
# not at one generic offshore site -- so the same per-location C-PSD fit and
# heterogeneity test used for river water (Section 4.2.4) can be run here.
# Ocean per-location n is much smaller than river (117 total vs 1207), so a
# tryCatch guard (mirroring safe_cpsd() in Section 4.2.4) is required: some
# locations may have too few/too sparse particles for the two-step LOD
# algorithm to find any valid populated-bin window.
ocean_locations <- sort(unique(raw_particles_ocean$sample_location))

safe_cpsd_ocean_loc <- function(data, ...) {
  if (length(data) < 10) return(list(valid = FALSE))
  tryCatch(
    c(fit_cpsd_segur_r(data, ...), list(valid = TRUE)),
    error = function(e) list(valid = FALSE)
  )
}

cpsd_fits_ocean_by_loc <- lapply(setNames(ocean_locations, ocean_locations), function(loc) {
  dat <- raw_particles_ocean |> dplyr::filter(sample_location == loc) |> dplyr::pull(length_um)
  safe_cpsd_ocean_loc(dat, bin_um = 5)
})

ocean_loc_summary <- dplyr::bind_rows(lapply(names(cpsd_fits_ocean_by_loc), function(loc) {
  fo <- cpsd_fits_ocean_by_loc[[loc]]
  if (isTRUE(fo$valid)) {
    tibble::tibble(
      location     = loc,
      n_particles  = sum(raw_particles_ocean$sample_location == loc),
      a_cpsd       = round(fo$a_cpsd,   3),
      se_a_cpsd    = round(fo$se_a_cpsd, 3),
      a_psd        = round(fo$a_psd,    3),
      lod_low_um   = round(fo$lower_lod_used_um, 0),
      lod_high_um  = round(fo$upper_lod_um,       0),
      r2           = round(fo$r2,       3),
      n_bins       = fo$n_bins,
      fit_mode     = fo$fit_mode
    )
  } else {
    tibble::tibble(
      location = loc, n_particles = sum(raw_particles_ocean$sample_location == loc),
      a_cpsd = NA_real_, se_a_cpsd = NA_real_, a_psd = NA_real_,
      lod_low_um = NA_real_, lod_high_um = NA_real_, r2 = NA_real_,
      n_bins = NA_integer_, fit_mode = "no_fit"
    )
  }
}))

Show the code 
# Same Cochran's Q heterogeneity test as the river-location version above,
# applied to the ocean per-location slopes. Locations with fit_mode != "ok"
# (too few particles/bins for a valid LOD window) are excluded from the test
# rather than silently contributing an unstable estimate.
ocean_loc_summary_valid <- dplyr::filter(ocean_loc_summary, fit_mode == "ok", is.finite(se_a_cpsd), se_a_cpsd > 0)

ocean_slope_heterogeneity <- if (nrow(ocean_loc_summary_valid) >= 2) {
  slope_heterogeneity_test(
    a = ocean_loc_summary_valid$a_cpsd, se = ocean_loc_summary_valid$se_a_cpsd,
    labels = ocean_loc_summary_valid$location
  )
} else NULL

if (!is.null(ocean_slope_heterogeneity)) {
  cat(
    "Ocean (coastal) location slope heterogeneity: Q(", ocean_slope_heterogeneity$df, ") = ",
    round(ocean_slope_heterogeneity$Q, 2), ", p = ", signif(ocean_slope_heterogeneity$p_value, 3),
    ", I2 = ", round(ocean_slope_heterogeneity$i2, 1), "%, weighted-mean a_cpsd = ",
    round(ocean_slope_heterogeneity$weighted_mean, 3),
    " (", nrow(ocean_loc_summary_valid), " of ", nrow(ocean_loc_summary), " locations had a valid fit)\n", sep = ""
  )
} else {
  cat("Ocean location slope heterogeneity test could not be run: fewer than 2 locations had a valid C-PSD fit.\n")
}

    subtitle = expression("Error bars = ±1 SE")
  ) +
  ggplot2::theme_minimal(base_size = 20) +
  ggplot2::theme(panel.border = ggplot2::element_rect(color = "gray85", fill = NA, linewidth = 0.4))

Particle volume

Note: ocean’s fragment volume fit uses the same length/width-consistent volume_lod_bounds() approach as river and sediment (Section 4.2.3). Its fiber fit does not: ocean has only 11 fiber particles total, and even the corrected (length/width-consistent, not isotropic) fiber volume-LOD window contains just 4 of them — too few to constrain a fit. Ocean’s fiber volume fit instead falls back to the Segur algorithm’s own auto-detected LOD window. Similarly, the “all” (pooled shapes) fit uses the fragment-only volume-LOD window rather than the fragment/fiber union: with only 11 fibers, the union window is dominated by a handful of sparse, noisy fiber-derived bounds and destabilizes the pooled fit (fragments outnumber fibers roughly 10:1 in this matrix, so anchoring “all” to fragment’s reliable range is the more defensible choice here).

Show the code 
r_med_frag_ocean  <- ratio_tbl_ocean$r_med[ratio_tbl_ocean$shape == "fragment"]
r_med_fiber_ocean <- ratio_tbl_ocean$r_med[ratio_tbl_ocean$shape == "fiber"]
vlb_ocean <- volume_lod_bounds(cpsd_fit_ocean_frag, cpsd_fit_ocean_fiber, r_med_frag_ocean, r_med_fiber_ocean)
cat("Ocean fragment volume LOD: [", signif(vlb_ocean$fragment[1], 2), ",", signif(vlb_ocean$fragment[2], 2), "] µm³\n")
Ocean fragment volume LOD: [ 56000 , 700000 ] µm³
Show the code 
cat("Ocean fiber    volume LOD (informational only — too few particles to use as a fit constraint): [",
    signif(vlb_ocean$fiber[1], 2), ",", signif(vlb_ocean$fiber[2], 2), "] µm³\n")
Ocean fiber    volume LOD (informational only — too few particles to use as a fit constraint): [ 1100000 , 30000000 ] µm³
Show the code 
# fragment and all use the same uniform vol_bin_um as river/sediment. fiber is the one
# documented exception (see note above): with only 4 particles inside its physically-
# derived window, no fixed window is viable, so it falls back to auto-detection
# (fit_range_um = NA) with a coarser bin width appropriate to its much wider absolute
# volume range (up to ~3e7 µm³, vs ~7e5 µm³ for fragment) — fine bins there would be
# almost entirely empty regardless of methodology, per the small-sample diagnosis above.
ocean_fiber_vol_bin_um <- 1e6
cpsd_fits_ocean_volume <- fit_cpsd_by_shape(
  raw_particles_ocean, value_col = "V_um3",
  config = list(
    fragment = list(bin_um = vol_bin_um,          fit_range_um = vlb_ocean$fragment),
    fiber    = list(bin_um = ocean_fiber_vol_bin_um, fit_range_um = c(NA_real_, NA_real_)),
    all      = list(bin_um = vol_bin_um,          fit_range_um = vlb_ocean$fragment)
  )
)
cpsd_fit_volume_ocean_frag  <- cpsd_fits_ocean_volume$fragment
cpsd_fit_volume_ocean_fiber <- cpsd_fits_ocean_volume$fiber
cpsd_fit_volume_ocean       <- cpsd_fits_ocean_volume$all

12.0.1 River + ocean C-PSD fits (length, surface area, volume — faceted)

Combines the per-river-location fits (Section 4.2.4) with the pooled ocean fits above into one faceted comparison, now that both are available. Rows are shape, columns are size metric; y-axis (log10 cumulative count) is fixed across all panels so magnitudes are directly comparable, while the x-axis (log10 size) is left free per metric since length/area/volume span very different numeric ranges.

12.0.2 Slope comparison across matrices and metrics

Extends the per-river-location comparison (Section 4.2.5) with the pooled sediment (Section 11) and pooled ocean (Section 12.1) “all-shapes” fits for the same three size metrics, now that every matrix’s area and volume fits are available. Points are colored by matrix rather than location so the four within-river points read as one group against the single pooled sediment and ocean values; the reference line previously drawn at the Segur et al. (2026) literature fragment mean is omitted here, since that value is a single-shape (fragment), single-matrix (ocean-only) literature figure and is not a like-for-like reference for a plot that already includes this study’s own pooled matrix-level fits. The y-axis is fixed (not free) across the three metric facets so slope magnitudes are directly comparable panel to panel.

Show the code 
# Pooled ("all"-shape) sediment and ocean slopes, one row per metric, to sit
# alongside the four per-river-location rows already in loc_slopes_all
# (Section 4.2.5). Unlike river, sediment and ocean are not split by location
# here: sediment has no location field, and the ocean per-location fits
# (Section 12.0.1a) are length-only (area/volume were never fit per ocean
# location), so a single pooled point per matrix is the only like-for-like
# comparison available for all three metrics.
sed_ocean_slopes_all <- tibble::tribble(
  ~matrix,    ~metric,               ~a_cpsd,                    ~se_a_cpsd,
  "Sediment", "Length (µm)",         cpsd_fit_sed_all$a_cpsd,     cpsd_fit_sed_all$se_a_cpsd,
  "Sediment", "Surface Area (µm²)",  cpsd_fit_area_sed$a_cpsd,    cpsd_fit_area_sed$se_a_cpsd,
  "Sediment", "Volume (µm³)",        cpsd_fit_volume_sed$a_cpsd,  cpsd_fit_volume_sed$se_a_cpsd,
  "Ocean",    "Length (µm)",         cpsd_fit_ocean_all$a_cpsd,   cpsd_fit_ocean_all$se_a_cpsd,
  "Ocean",    "Surface Area (µm²)",  cpsd_fit_area_ocean$a_cpsd,  cpsd_fit_area_ocean$se_a_cpsd,
  "Ocean",    "Volume (µm³)",        cpsd_fit_volume_ocean$a_cpsd, cpsd_fit_volume_ocean$se_a_cpsd
) |>
  dplyr::mutate(group = matrix)

matrix_slopes_all_metrics <- dplyr::bind_rows(
  dplyr::mutate(loc_slopes_all, matrix = "River", group = as.character(location)),
  sed_ocean_slopes_all
) |>
  dplyr::mutate(
    metric = factor(metric, levels = c("Length (µm)", "Surface Area (µm²)", "Volume (µm³)")),
    group  = factor(group, levels = c(as.character(locations), "Sediment", "Ocean")),
    matrix = factor(matrix, levels = c("River", "Sediment", "Ocean"))
  )

matrix_pal_slopes <- c("River" = "#0072B2", "Sediment" = "#E69F00", "Ocean" = "#009E73")

cpsd_slopes_all_metrics_plot <- ggplot2::ggplot(matrix_slopes_all_metrics,
    ggplot2::aes(x = group, y = a_cpsd, color = matrix)) +
  ggplot2::geom_point(size = 4) +
  ggplot2::geom_errorbar(
    ggplot2::aes(ymin = a_cpsd - se_a_cpsd, ymax = a_cpsd + se_a_cpsd),
    width = 0.2, linewidth = 0.8
  ) +
  ggplot2::facet_wrap(~ metric, nrow = 1) +
  ggplot2::scale_color_manual(values = matrix_pal_slopes, name = "Matrix") +
  ggplot2::labs(
    x        = "Location (river) / matrix (sediment, ocean)",
    y        = expression(italic(a)[cpsd]),
    title    = "C-PSD slope by location/matrix and size metric",
    subtitle = "Error bars = ±1 SE. River shown per location; sediment and ocean are pooled matrix-level fits."
  ) +
  ggplot2::theme_minimal(base_size = 20) +
  ggplot2::theme(
    legend.position = "bottom",
    panel.border = ggplot2::element_rect(color = "gray85", fill = NA, linewidth = 0.4),
    strip.text   = ggplot2::element_text(face = "bold"),
    axis.text.x = ggplot2::element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1))

ggsave(cpsd_slopes_all_metrics_plot, filename = "figures/cpsd_slopes_all_metrics_plot.png", width = 11, height = 7, dpi = 300)
cpsd_slopes_all_metrics_plot

12.1.1 All-matrix particle-length PSD comparison with MPSizeBase

This section is intentionally placed after the river, sediment, and ocean length C-PSDs have all been calculated. It imports Segur et al.’s MPSizeBase workbook directly from assets/SI/SI 3 code and data/MPsizeBase_v15_05_2026.xlsx, reads the workbook Read Me, and parses one literature apsd value per PSD_ID from the Literature PSD data tab. The cumsum_powerlaw_alpha column is already the converted BN-PSD/differential slope (apsd = acpsd - 1), so no additional conversion is applied.

Results at a glance

River and ocean water (the quantitative headline result). At HC5, river water Food Dilution median RQ = 3.17 (P(RQ>1) = 57%) and Tissue Translocation median RQ = 0.069 (P(RQ>1) = 28.8%); ocean water Food Dilution median RQ = 0 (P(RQ>1) = 39.9%) and Tissue Translocation median RQ = 0 (P(RQ>1) = 10.8%). A food-dilution threshold exceedance cannot be excluded, but it is method-conditional (floor-sensitive and driven by which toxicity studies enter the food-dilution SSD, not by exposure extrapolation alone – Section 12.5.1.3.1); Tissue Translocation is below threshold at the median for both matrices. The single-slope exposure correction (used above), a piecewise (dual-slope) bounding sensitivity, and an MLE/lognormal extrapolation-model comparison (Section 12.5.2) together bracket the sub-detection-limit extrapolation; all are quantified in the Sensitivity & structural uncertainty section below. Sediment is excluded from this conclusion: its exposure concentration is a per-liter water value with no dry-mass basis, not a genuine particles/kg-dry-weight measurement, and its nominal Food Dilution RQ (0, P = 0%) fails a benthic-plausibility guard by roughly eleven orders of magnitude (Section 11). A fully quantified executive summary, including the RQ decomposition that separates the exposure/length-slope/area-slope/volume-slope contributions, follows in Key Findings below.

Hoffman et al. (2026) frame the observed PSD as a transport-filtered distribution. A simple diagnostic is the capture fraction f(d, δ) = 1 − exp(−ws(d)·δ / K) and the critical size where ws(d)·δ / K ≈ 1. The calculation below uses Stokes settling/rise speed with user-supplied delta_m = 0.1 m and K_m2_s = 0.00001 m^2/s. These are assumptions, not measured site parameters, and should be replaced with field-specific values before a mechanistic transport correction is attempted.

Show the code 
matrix_fit_tbl <- tibble::tibble(
  Matrix = c("River water", "Sediment", "Ocean water"),
  cpsd_fit = list(cpsd_fit_all, cpsd_fit_sed_all, cpsd_fit_ocean_all),
  median_density_g_cm3 = c(
    median(raw_particles_river$density_g_cm3, na.rm = TRUE),
    median(raw_particles_sed$density_g_cm3, na.rm = TRUE),
    median(raw_particles_ocean$density_g_cm3, na.rm = TRUE)
  ),
  water_density_g_cm3 = c(1.00, 1.00, 1.025)
)

critical_piecewise_tbl <- dplyr::bind_rows(lapply(seq_len(nrow(matrix_fit_tbl)), function(i) {
  fit_i <- matrix_fit_tbl$cpsd_fit[[i]]
  dc_i <- estimate_critical_size(
    delta_m = hoffman_delta_m,
    K_m2_s = hoffman_K_m2_s,
    density_g_cm3 = matrix_fit_tbl$median_density_g_cm3[i],
    water_density_g_cm3 = matrix_fit_tbl$water_density_g_cm3[i]
  )
  pw_i <- piecewise_cpsd_diagnostic(fit_i)
  tibble::tibble(
    Matrix = matrix_fit_tbl$Matrix[i],
    median_density_g_cm3 = matrix_fit_tbl$median_density_g_cm3[i],
    critical_size_um = dc_i,
    fit_lod_low_um = fit_i$lower_lod_used_um,
    fit_lod_high_um = fit_i$upper_lod_um,
    straddles_critical_size = is.finite(dc_i) && dc_i >= fit_i$lower_lod_used_um && dc_i <= fit_i$upper_lod_um,
    single_a_cpsd = fit_i$a_cpsd,
    single_a_psd = fit_i$a_psd,
    piecewise_break_um = pw_i$break_um,
    piecewise_low_a_cpsd = pw_i$slope_low,
    piecewise_high_a_cpsd = pw_i$slope_high,
    piecewise_delta_aic = pw_i$delta_aic
  )
}))

knitr::kable(
  critical_piecewise_tbl,
  digits = 3,
  caption = "SPEC 4 diagnostic: critical size and two-segment C-PSD fit by matrix"
)

The piecewise fits are diagnostic only. A fit window that straddles the assumed critical size is flagged because the fitted single slope may blend a transport-distorted fine-size regime with the coarser-size regime. Per Hoffman et al. (2026), future refinement should prioritize measured 3-D geometry and polymer density over increasingly elaborate settling equations; even precise-geometry settling models retain substantial residual error, so settling-based corrections should be treated as bias-level adjustments rather than high-precision concentration estimates.

13.2.1 Single-slope vs. two-segment fits with binned data (particle length only)

Visualizes the two competing exposure-side models directly against the binned C-PSD data, using the same visual grammar as plot_cpsd_multi() (Section 4.2.1.1/Figure river_length_cpsd_plot): points outside the fitted LOD window shown at reduced opacity, dotted vertical lines marking the LOD window boundaries, and a 95% CI ribbon around each regression line. Restricted to particle length (the metric the piecewise bounding sensitivity, Section 13.3, actually uses); the analogous area/volume comparison is not produced, since the piecewise model is not fit for those metrics. Colors distinguish matrix (river/sediment/ocean); the two-segment panel’s break point for each matrix (Section 13.2 table above) is visible directly as the bend in that matrix’s line rather than marked separately, since the gap between the two fitted panels already makes the two-segment shape distinguishable from the single-slope one.

Show the code 
# Reuses the already-computed pooled "all"-shape length fits (no new fitting):
# cpsd_fit_all / cpsd_fit_sed_all / cpsd_fit_ocean_all for the single-slope
# model, and critical_piecewise_tbl$piecewise_break_um (this section, above)
# for where to split each matrix's two-segment model. The two-segment lines
# are obtained by refitting a plain lm(log10(N_ge) ~ log10(L_low)) separately
# on each side of the break, over the *same* LOD-window bins already selected
# by the single-slope fit (fo$data) -- i.e. an unconstrained-intercept version
# of the same segment-interaction model piecewise_cpsd_diagnostic() already
# fit to choose that break point, just refit here to recover per-segment
# intercepts for plotting (the diagnostic function only returns slopes/AIC).
cpsd_length_fits_by_matrix <- list(
  "River water" = cpsd_fit_all,
  "Sediment"    = cpsd_fit_sed_all,
  "Ocean water" = cpsd_fit_ocean_all
)
# Points/legend use the standard (medium-saturation) matrix palette; regression
# lines use a separately darkened variant of the same hues so the fit lines
# read clearly against the dense point cloud rather than blending into it.
matrix_pal_cpsd      <- c("River water" = "#0072B2", "Sediment" = "#E69F00", "Ocean water" = "#009E73")
matrix_pal_cpsd_dark <- c("River water" = "#00375C", "Sediment" = "#7A5300", "Ocean water" = "#00432F")

df_all_ms <- dplyr::bind_rows(lapply(names(cpsd_length_fits_by_matrix), function(mat) {
  fo <- cpsd_length_fits_by_matrix[[mat]]
  fo$bins |>
    dplyr::arrange(L_low) |>
    dplyr::mutate(
      N_ge   = rev(cumsum(rev(n))),
      Matrix = mat,
      in_lod = L_low >= fo$lower_lod_used_um & L_high <= fo$upper_lod_um
    ) |>
    dplyr::filter(L_low > 0, N_ge > 0)
}))

pred_single_ms <- dplyr::bind_rows(lapply(names(cpsd_length_fits_by_matrix), function(mat) {
  fo   <- cpsd_length_fits_by_matrix[[mat]]
  grid <- tibble::tibble(L_low = seq(fo$lower_lod_used_um, fo$upper_lod_um, length.out = 200))
  pred <- predict(fo$fit, newdata = grid, se.fit = TRUE)
  tibble::tibble(Matrix = mat, L_low = grid$L_low, logN_fit = pred$fit,
                 logN_lo = pred$fit - 1.96 * pred$se.fit, logN_hi = pred$fit + 1.96 * pred$se.fit)
}))

pred_piecewise_ms <- dplyr::bind_rows(lapply(names(cpsd_length_fits_by_matrix), function(mat) {
  fo  <- cpsd_length_fits_by_matrix[[mat]]
  brk <- critical_piecewise_tbl$piecewise_break_um[critical_piecewise_tbl$Matrix == mat]
  if (!is.finite(brk)) return(NULL)
  dat <- dplyr::mutate(fo$data, log_L = log10(L_low), log_N = log10(N_ge))
  dplyr::bind_rows(lapply(c("low", "high"), function(seg) {
    sub <- if (seg == "low") dplyr::filter(dat, L_low < brk) else dplyr::filter(dat, L_low >= brk)
    if (nrow(sub) < 2) return(NULL)
    fit_seg <- stats::lm(log_N ~ log_L, data = sub)
    grid    <- tibble::tibble(L_low = seq(min(sub$L_low), max(sub$L_low), length.out = 100))
    p       <- predict(fit_seg, newdata = data.frame(log_L = log10(grid$L_low)), se.fit = TRUE)
    tibble::tibble(Matrix = mat, segment = seg, L_low = grid$L_low, logN_fit = p$fit,
                   logN_lo = p$fit - 1.96 * p$se.fit, logN_hi = p$fit + 1.96 * p$se.fit)
  }))
}))

lod_bounds_ms <- dplyr::bind_rows(lapply(names(cpsd_length_fits_by_matrix), function(mat) {
  fo <- cpsd_length_fits_by_matrix[[mat]]
  tibble::tibble(Matrix = mat, xval = log10(c(fo$lower_lod_used_um, fo$upper_lod_um)))
}))

model_levels <- c("Single-slope (production)", "Two-segment (piecewise)")

df_both_ms <- dplyr::bind_rows(
  dplyr::mutate(df_all_ms, Model = model_levels[1]),
  dplyr::mutate(df_all_ms, Model = model_levels[2])
) |>
  dplyr::mutate(Model = factor(Model, levels = model_levels))

pred_single_ms    <- dplyr::mutate(pred_single_ms,    Model = factor(model_levels[1], levels = model_levels),
                                    line_color = unname(matrix_pal_cpsd_dark[Matrix]))
pred_piecewise_ms <- dplyr::mutate(pred_piecewise_ms, Model = factor(model_levels[2], levels = model_levels),
                                    line_color = unname(matrix_pal_cpsd_dark[Matrix]))

lod_bounds_both_ms <- dplyr::bind_rows(
  dplyr::mutate(lod_bounds_ms, Model = model_levels[1]),
  dplyr::mutate(lod_bounds_ms, Model = model_levels[2])
) |>
  dplyr::mutate(Model = factor(Model, levels = model_levels))

# Layer order matters: points are drawn first, then a dark "halo" line
# (thicker, neutral grey, semi-transparent) beneath the actual colored fit
# line, so the fit line reads clearly on top of the point cloud regardless of
# how dense the points are. The fit lines themselves use matrix_pal_cpsd_dark
# via aes(color = I(line_color)) -- a literal (AsIs) color that bypasses the
# shared discrete color scale, so lines can be darker than points without a
# second/conflicting legend.
cpsd_single_vs_piecewise_plot <- ggplot2::ggplot(df_both_ms, ggplot2::aes(x = log10(L_low), y = log10(N_ge), color = Matrix)) +
  ggplot2::geom_vline(
    data = lod_bounds_both_ms, ggplot2::aes(xintercept = xval),
    linetype = "dotted", color = "gray55", linewidth = 0.6, inherit.aes = FALSE
  ) +
  ggplot2::geom_point(ggplot2::aes(alpha = in_lod), size = 1.3) +
  ggplot2::geom_ribbon(
    data = pred_single_ms, ggplot2::aes(x = log10(L_low), ymin = logN_lo, ymax = logN_hi, fill = Matrix),
    inherit.aes = FALSE, alpha = 0.15, color = NA
  ) +
  ggplot2::geom_ribbon(
    data = pred_piecewise_ms,
    ggplot2::aes(x = log10(L_low), ymin = logN_lo, ymax = logN_hi, fill = Matrix, group = interaction(Matrix, segment)),
    inherit.aes = FALSE, alpha = 0.15, color = NA
  ) +
  # Dark halo behind the single-slope line (contrast against the point cloud).
  ggplot2::geom_line(
    data = pred_single_ms, ggplot2::aes(x = log10(L_low), y = logN_fit, group = Matrix),
    inherit.aes = FALSE, color = "grey15", alpha = 0.35, linewidth = 2.6
  ) +
  ggplot2::geom_line(
    data = pred_single_ms, ggplot2::aes(x = log10(L_low), y = logN_fit, color = I(line_color), group = Matrix),
    inherit.aes = FALSE, linewidth = 1.4, alpha = 1
  ) +
  # Dark halo behind the piecewise lines.
  ggplot2::geom_line(
    data = pred_piecewise_ms,
    ggplot2::aes(x = log10(L_low), y = logN_fit, group = interaction(Matrix, segment)),
    inherit.aes = FALSE, color = "grey15", alpha = 0.35, linewidth = 2.6
  ) +
  ggplot2::geom_line(
    data = pred_piecewise_ms,
    ggplot2::aes(x = log10(L_low), y = logN_fit, color = I(line_color), group = interaction(Matrix, segment)),
    inherit.aes = FALSE, linewidth = 1.4, alpha = 1
  ) +
  ggplot2::facet_wrap(~ Model, nrow = 1) +
  ggplot2::scale_color_manual(values = matrix_pal_cpsd, name = "Matrix") +
  ggplot2::scale_fill_manual(values = matrix_pal_cpsd, guide = "none") +
  ggplot2::scale_alpha_manual(values = c(`TRUE` = 0.5, `FALSE` = 0.10), guide = "none") +
  ggplot2::labs(
    title    = "Single-slope vs. two-segment (piecewise) C-PSD fits by matrix (particle length)",
    subtitle = "Dotted = fitted LOD window boundaries. Faded points = outside LOD window. In the two-segment panel, the break is where each matrix's line visibly bends.",
    x        = expression(log[10] * "(Length, " * mu * "m)"),
    y        = expression(log[10] * (N("">=L)))
  ) +
  ggplot2::theme_minimal(base_size = 14) +
  ggplot2::theme(
    legend.position = "bottom",
    strip.text      = ggplot2::element_text(face = "bold", size = 13),
    panel.border    = ggplot2::element_rect(color = "gray80", fill = NA, linewidth = 0.4)
  )

13.3 Piecewise (dual-slope) PSD as a bounding exposure case

The production correction_factor() extrapolates a single fitted power-law slope from the measured LOD window down to the 1 um target floor. The two-segment diagnostic above (§13.2) shows the data themselves often prefer a shallower fine-size slope below a break point and a steeper coarse-size slope above it (river ΔAIC in the diagnostic table strongly favors the two-segment model; sediment likewise). Because the sub-floor extrapolation zone (1 um to the fitted LOD) can straddle or sit near that break — and because the fitted critical size d_c for river (~36 um) falls inside that 1-50 um extrapolation zone rather than inside the fit window itself — a single coarse slope may not be the right model to extrapolate through that zone. Independent evidence that single power laws mis-extrapolate to small, unmeasured sizes: in the St Louis Estuary, a single power law extrapolated to 1.3-12 particles/L for 5-5000 um while flow cytometry directly measured 600-1,600 particles/L in the same system (Thomas et al. 2024), and Segur et al. (2026) find size-aligned 1-5000 um concentrations average ~600x higher than reported values based on single-slope extrapolation. Both are cited as evidence that single-power-law extrapolation to small sizes is unreliable in general, not as a validated correction for this dataset.

correction_factor_piecewise() (R/mp_risk_utils.R, SPEC 2b) implements the two-segment alternative: it integrates dN/dL = kL^a using the fine-segment differential slope over [1, break_um] and the coarse-segment differential slope over [break_um, 5000], with the coarse segment’s density scaled so the two segments meet exactly (are continuous) at break_um. The piecewise cumulative slopes from the §13.2 diagnostic are converted to the differential convention (a_psd = a_cpsd - 1) internally via slope_convention = "cumulative", consistent with the SPEC 1c guard. This is a labeled bounding sensitivity, not a replacement for the single-slope production CF — the production exposure pipeline (Sections 5-6, 9-10, 12) is unchanged. The 1 um-LOD_low sub-window is unconstrained by data in both* the single-slope and piecewise case; the piecewise result quantifies structural (model-form) uncertainty in how that unconstrained sub-window is extrapolated, which is not captured by the Gaussian slope_structural_sd already added to the fit-uncertainty propagation.

Show the code 
piecewise_cf_row <- function(matrix_label, piecewise_row, L_meas_min, L_meas_max) {
  brk <- piecewise_row$piecewise_break_um
  s_lo <- piecewise_row$piecewise_low_a_cpsd
  s_hi <- piecewise_row$piecewise_high_a_cpsd
  if (!is.finite(brk) || !is.finite(s_lo) || !is.finite(s_hi)) {
    return(tibble::tibble(Matrix = matrix_label, break_um = NA_real_, cf_piecewise = NA_real_))
  }
  cf_pw <- correction_factor_piecewise(
    a_low = s_lo, a_high = s_hi, break_um = brk,
    L_meas_min = L_meas_min, L_meas_max = L_meas_max,
    L_tar_min = 1, L_tar_max = 5000,
    slope_convention = "cumulative"
  )
  tibble::tibble(Matrix = matrix_label, break_um = brk, cf_piecewise = cf_pw)
}

pw_river <- piecewise_cf_row("River water", dplyr::filter(critical_piecewise_tbl, Matrix == "River water"), L_meas_min_use, L_meas_max_use)
pw_sed   <- piecewise_cf_row("Sediment",    dplyr::filter(critical_piecewise_tbl, Matrix == "Sediment"),    L_meas_min_use_sed, L_meas_max_use_sed)
pw_ocean <- piecewise_cf_row("Ocean water", dplyr::filter(critical_piecewise_tbl, Matrix == "Ocean water"), L_meas_min_ocean, L_meas_max_ocean)

# Piecewise sensitivity is an exposure-only (CF/EED) effect: apply the single
# piecewise CF point estimate to the raw per-sample measured concentrations,
# then bootstrap the EED exactly as for the single-slope case. Hazard (haz*)
# is unchanged, so any RQ shift below is attributable to the piecewise CF alone.
set.seed(9401)
eed_boot_piecewise_river <- if (is.finite(pw_river$cf_piecewise)) {
  bootstrap_eed(monitoring_pooled_scope$C_measured_pL * pw_river$cf_piecewise, n_boot = n_boot, probs = c(0.5, 0.95))
} else NULL
set.seed(9402)
eed_boot_piecewise_sed <- if (is.finite(pw_sed$cf_piecewise)) {
  bootstrap_eed(monitoring_sed$C_measured_pkg * pw_sed$cf_piecewise, n_boot = n_boot, probs = c(0.5, 0.95))
} else NULL
set.seed(9403)
eed_boot_piecewise_ocean <- if (is.finite(pw_ocean$cf_piecewise)) {
  bootstrap_eed(monitoring_ocean$C_measured_pL * pw_ocean$cf_piecewise, n_boot = n_boot, probs = c(0.5, 0.95))
} else NULL

set.seed(9411)
risk_draws_piecewise_river <- if (!is.null(eed_boot_piecewise_river)) {
  # Two-segment exposure vs the pooled single-slope hazard: the one documented
  # ALIGNMENT RULE exception (PSSDplusplus cannot take a two-segment PSD).
  draw_rq_mc1d(haz_pooled, eed_boot_piecewise_river$q50, n_risk = n_risk)
} else NULL
risk_summary_piecewise_river <- if (!is.null(risk_draws_piecewise_river)) summarize_rq(risk_draws_piecewise_river) else NULL

# 95% CI (2.5th-97.5th percentile of the underlying 1D risk draws) for the
# plot's error bars -- summarize_rq() itself only returns p50/p95/p99, so the
# lower bound is computed here directly from each case's already-existing raw
# draws object (river/ocean single-slope: risk_draws/risk_draws_ocean, already
# built in Sections 8/12.4; piecewise: risk_draws_piecewise_river/_ocean,
# saved alongside their summaries above) rather than retrofitting summarize_rq().
rq_ci_from_draws <- function(draws, matrix_label, case_label) {
  if (is.null(draws)) return(NULL)
  draws |>
    dplyr::filter(ERM %in% c("Food Dilution", "Tissue Translocation"), HCx == 5) |>
    dplyr::group_by(ERM) |>
    dplyr::summarise(RQ_p025 = stats::quantile(RQ, 0.025, na.rm = TRUE),
                      RQ_p975 = stats::quantile(RQ, 0.975, na.rm = TRUE), .groups = "drop") |>
    dplyr::mutate(Matrix = matrix_label, Case = case_label)
}

  rq_ci_from_draws(risk_draws_ocean,            "Ocean water", "Single-slope (production)"),
  rq_ci_from_draws(risk_draws_piecewise_ocean,  "Ocean water", "Piecewise (bounding)")
)

Bounding range interpretation. The table above states, per matrix, the single-slope production RQ alongside the piecewise-sensitivity RQ; whichever is larger sets the upper bound of the sensitivity range and whichever is smaller sets the lower bound. Because the fine-size (sub-break) slope from the §13.2 diagnostic is shallower than the coarse-size slope for the matrices where the two-segment model is favored, the piecewise CF is expected to sit below the single-slope CF (less extrapolated mass assigned to the unconstrained 1 um-LOD_low zone) — i.e., the piecewise bound is expected to narrow the exposure (and therefore RQ) estimate relative to the single-slope production value, not widen it, for this dataset. This is stated as an expectation to be read against the rendered numbers above, not assumed; if a matrix’s piecewise CF instead exceeds the single-slope CF, that reversal is itself informative about how sensitive the conclusion is to the extrapolation model and should be flagged rather than averaged away. Regardless of direction, the single-slope CF remains the production default per the guardrails in the corrective-revision spec; the piecewise result is reported here strictly as a labeled sensitivity bound. Sediment caveat (SPEC 1d): the Sediment column/row above is illustrative only, for the same reason noted in Section 13.1/11.3.0 — its exposure concentration is not a genuine particles/kg-dry-weight value.

13.4 Benchmark against Dutch river datasets (RIVM 2026-0069)

This section compares this study’s particle-length PSD slopes and rescaled concentrations with water-based (per-volume) Dutch river data compiled for RIVM letter report 2026-0069 (Quik et al. 2026; data and code: rivm-syso/MicroplasticsERA_water, EUPL-1.2). The Dutch concentrations come from Mintenig et al. (2020; Meuse and Dommel, FTIR), Mughini-Gras et al. (2021; Rhine at Lobith and Lek canal at Vianen, LDIR) and Mintenig, Hunnestad & Koelmans (2025; Dommel, FTIR). The Dutch slopes are RIVM’s published poweRlaw maximum-likelihood fits (param == "longest"), and they are used as published: no Dutch particle data are refitted here. All logic is in R/rivm_utils.R. This child document only orchestrates it, and it is self-contained: it saves and restores the global RNG state, so it does not change any upstream or downstream result.

Windows. W2 = 50–500 µm is the primary comparison: it is this study’s sieve window and lies inside both Dutch measured ranges (20–5000 µm FTIR; 10–500 µm LDIR), so it needs interior rescaling only. W1 = 1–5000 µm is the Koelmans et al. (2020) default and a long extrapolation for every dataset. Measured window for this study. Following RIVM’s treatment of the Dutch data (rescaling from the sampling limits LLm/ULm), this study’s concentrations are rescaled from the 50/500 µm sampling sieves (rivm_L_meas_ours). This is a benchmark-only setting and does not change the pipeline’s L_meas_min_use/L_meas_max_use (Section 5.1). Slopes for this study. Each river’s own C-PSD slope is used for both rescaled concentrations and slope comparisons, matching the pipeline default (slope_application).

Inputs and exclusions. Inputs were read from RIVM clone (rebuilt derived CSVs). In total, 37 Dutch surface-water samples were retained and 16 were excluded (table below): WWTP effluent; the nine Mintenig et al. (2020) samples analysed only above 300 µm, which have no total in Corrected_concentrations_total; and the four Mughini-Gras et al. (2021) samples without a reported total. Bäuerlein et al. (2022, 2023) particle data are not public. Their slopes appear in the slope comparison, but their samples are excluded from the concentration figures. For this study, the per-sample concentration is the sum over plastic polymer classes of the pipeline’s monitoring$C_measured_pL (57 samples, ×1000 to particles m⁻³).

Caveats. (1) Slopes are method-dependent, so W1 differences conflate PSD shape with fitting method. (2) Dutch FTIR slopes were fitted above xmin ≈ 170–270 µm but are applied down to 20 µm. (3) LDIR and FTIR slopes differ systematically (α ≈ 2.4–3.8 versus 2.3–2.4). (4) Dutch concentrations are study-reported totals, not recomputed from particles. (5) This study’s samples are discrete pumped samples from small, episodic rivers; the Dutch samples come from large perennial rivers. (6) W2 is the primary comparison and W1 is secondary.

12.5 Methods-robustness and source-attribution analyses (surface water only)

Three additive analyses testing whether the risk conclusion is robust to specific methodological choices (the sub-floor extrapolation, the extrapolation model itself), and whether the river-vs-ocean slope difference has independent support from polymer composition. River and ocean only — sediment is not touched. None of these change the production headline (single-slope C-PSD, L_tar_min = 1 µm); each is a clearly-labeled sensitivity/robustness addition that reuses the already-computed production hazard/exposure objects wherever possible rather than recomputing them.

12.5.1 RQ sensitivity to the extrapolation floor L_tar_min (food dilution)

The production correction factor extrapolates the measured particle count down to L_tar_min = 1 µm. Food Dilution is volume-weighted, so a power-law explosion of sub-floor particle number adds little particle volume — the RQ may be far less sensitive to L_tar_min than the raw number-based CF implies. This test is only valid if exposure and hazard are evaluated on the same lower size bound, so for each floor the toxicity dataset is filtered to match: a ToMEx record is excluded from a given floor if its own characteristic tested size (size.length.um.used.for.conversions for monodisperse records, or the tested range via size.length.max.um.used.for.conversions for polydisperse records — the same field PSSDplusplus::align_data() itself uses to size-align doses) falls entirely below that floor. Records with a missing characteristic size are excluded rather than imputed. filter_tox_by_size_floor() (R/mp_risk_utils.R) implements this rule.

At each floor, three things move together: (1) the exposure-side correction factor and EED are recomputed over [L_tar_min, 5000] µm; (2) the pSSD++ integration floor (x1M_set in matrix_function(), x1D_set in run_pssd_pipeline()) is set to the same L_tar_min; and (3) the Food Dilution toxicity records are filtered as above before the hazard alignment is re-derived. The L_tar_min = 1 µm row reuses the already-computed production CF/EED/hazard objects rather than recomputing an identical result under a new seed (relocate-don’t-recompute).

Show the code 
m12_floors <- c(1, 2.5, 5, 7.5, 10, 20)

m12_run_one_floor <- function(L_tar_min, matrix_label, monitoring_df, cpsd_fit, alpha_draws,
                               tox_data_base, param_values_base, environments,
                               matrix_extra_args, rave_override_fn, seed_base,
                               prod_cf = NULL, prod_eed = NULL, prod_haz = NULL) {

  tox_data_i  <- filter_tox_by_size_floor(tox_data_base, L_tar_min)
  n_tox_i     <- nrow(tox_data_i)
  n_species_i <- dplyr::n_distinct(tox_data_i$Species)

  na_row <- function(note) {
    tibble::tibble(
      Matrix = matrix_label, L_tar_min = L_tar_min,
      CF_p50 = NA_real_, EED_q50 = NA_real_,
      n_tox_records = n_tox_i, n_species = n_species_i, HC5_median = NA_real_,
      RQ_p50_1D = NA_real_, RQ_p025_1D = NA_real_, RQ_p975_1D = NA_real_, P_exceed_1D = NA_real_,
      RQ_p50_MC2D = NA_real_, P_exceed_MC2D = NA_real_,
      CF_RSD_pct = NA_real_, RQ_p50_RSD_pct = NA_real_, note = note
    )
  }

  if (isTRUE(L_tar_min == 1) && !is.null(prod_cf)) {
    combined_cf_i <- prod_cf
    eed_boot_i    <- prod_eed
    haz_i         <- prod_haz
  } else {
    set.seed(seed_base)
    corr_i <- correct_and_bootstrap_eed(
      monitoring = monitoring_df, conc_col = "C_measured_pL", cpsd_fit = cpsd_fit,
      alpha_draws = alpha_draws, L_tar_min = L_tar_min, L_tar_max = 5000,
      n_draws = 3000, n_boot = n_boot, probs = c(0.5, 0.95), slope_convention = "differential"
    )
    combined_cf_i <- corr_i$combined_cf
    eed_boot_i    <- corr_i$eed_boot

    set.seed(seed_base + 1)
    # matrix_function_safe() (R/mp_risk_utils.R): a local patched copy of
    # PSSDplusplus::matrix_function() -- the installed package's oversample-
    # then-slice logic for upper.tissue.trans.size.um silently under-fills
    # when x1M_set narrows the acceptance window (confirmed failing at
    # x1M_set >= 20 with this analysis's real river parameters); the patch
    # replaces only that block with a draw-until-quota-met loop using the
    # identical rnorm() parameters and filter conditions. See the function's
    # own roxygen comment for the full diagnosis. Installed PSSDplusplus is
    # never modified.
    param_matrix_i <- do.call(
      matrix_function_safe,
      c(list(n_sobol = n_boot, params = param_values_base, upper.tissue.truncation.limit = 500,
             x1M_set = L_tar_min, x2D_set = 5000), matrix_extra_args)
    ) |> rave_override_fn()

    # A high L_tar_min can leave too few (or zero) Food-Dilution-alignable
    # records after PSSDplusplus's own ingestible/size-gating logic runs
    # inside MC_sim_align_parallel(), even when the raw filtered tox_data_i
    # row count looks adequate -- build_haz_df() then has nothing to
    # summarise for that ERM. Caught here rather than crashing the render,
    # per the spec's own guardrail: flag as indicative-only (NA row with a
    # note) rather than treat as a production result.
    pssd_haz <- tryCatch({
      pssd_i <- run_pssd_pipeline(
        tox_data = tox_data_i, param_matrix = param_matrix_i, environments = environments,
        cache_suffix = paste0("m12_", matrix_label, "_", L_tar_min),
        dose_unit = "L", n_sim = n_boot, num_cores = parallel::detectCores() - 2,
        sim = 30, cv_uf = 0.5, rmore_method = "lognormal",
        seed = seed_base + 2, x1D_set = L_tar_min
      )
      haz_try <- build_haz_df(pssd_i$pSSDs, environments[1])
      if (is.null(haz_try) || nrow(haz_try) == 0 ||
          !any(haz_try$ERM == "Food Dilution" & haz_try$HCx == 5)) {
        list(ok = FALSE, note = "pSSD fit returned no Food Dilution HC5 at this floor")
      } else {
        list(ok = TRUE, haz = haz_try)
      }
    }, error = function(e) {
      list(ok = FALSE, note = paste0("pSSD/hazard fit failed: ", conditionMessage(e)))
    })

    if (!pssd_haz$ok) {
      return(na_row(pssd_haz$note))
    }
    haz_i <- pssd_haz$haz
  }

  set.seed(seed_base + 3)
  risk_draws_1d <- draw_rq_mc1d(haz_i, eed_boot_i$q50, n_risk = 1000)
  rs_1d <- summarize_rq(risk_draws_1d) |> dplyr::filter(ERM == "Food Dilution", HCx == 5)
  rs_1d_ci <- risk_draws_1d |> dplyr::filter(ERM == "Food Dilution", HCx == 5) |>
    dplyr::summarise(RQ_p025 = stats::quantile(RQ, 0.025, na.rm = TRUE),
                      RQ_p975 = stats::quantile(RQ, 0.975, na.rm = TRUE))

  mc2d_i <- mc2d_risk(monitoring_df = monitoring_df, combined_cf = combined_cf_i, haz_df = haz_i,
                       n_uncertainty = 100, n_variability = 500, seed = seed_base + 4)
  mc2d_food_hc5_i <- mc2d_i |> dplyr::filter(ERM == "Food Dilution", HCx == 5)
  rs_mc2d <- mc2d_food_hc5_i |>
    dplyr::summarise(P_exceed_med = median(P_exceed), RQ_p50_med = median(RQ_p50))

  hc5_i <- haz_i |> dplyr::filter(ERM == "Food Dilution", HCx == 5) |> dplyr::pull(PNEC) |> stats::median()

  # Uncertainty (not variability) at this floor: %RSD of the exposure-side CF
  # draws (correction_factor() output, one value per alpha_draws realization)
  # and %RSD of the outer-loop (uncertainty) RQ_p50 across mc2d_risk()'s
  # n_uncertainty = 100 CF+PNEC draws. Both are dispersion-of-the-estimate
  # measures, not the exposure variability captured by the inner loop --
  # answers "how much does our estimate of the risk move if we re-ran the
  # uncertain inputs," at each L_tar_min.
  cf_rsd_pct     <- 100 * stats::sd(combined_cf_i) / mean(combined_cf_i)
  rq_p50_rsd_pct <- 100 * stats::sd(mc2d_food_hc5_i$RQ_p50) / mean(mc2d_food_hc5_i$RQ_p50)

  tibble::tibble(
    Matrix = matrix_label, L_tar_min = L_tar_min,
    CF_p50 = stats::median(combined_cf_i), EED_q50 = stats::median(eed_boot_i$q50),
    n_tox_records = n_tox_i, n_species = n_species_i, HC5_median = hc5_i,
    RQ_p50_1D = rs_1d$RQ_p50, RQ_p025_1D = rs_1d_ci$RQ_p025, RQ_p975_1D = rs_1d_ci$RQ_p975, P_exceed_1D = rs_1d$P_exceed,
    RQ_p50_MC2D = rs_mc2d$RQ_p50_med, P_exceed_MC2D = rs_mc2d$P_exceed_med,
    CF_RSD_pct = cf_rsd_pct, RQ_p50_RSD_pct = rq_p50_rsd_pct, note = NA_character_
  )
}

rave_override_river <- function(pm) {
  pm |> dplyr::mutate(
    R.ave.water.freshwater = sample(R.ave_vals, size = dplyr::n(), replace = TRUE),
    H_W_ratio.freshwater   = sample(R.ave_vals, size = dplyr::n(), replace = TRUE)
  )
}
rave_override_ocean <- function(pm) {
  pm |> dplyr::mutate(

    H_W_ratio.water.marine = sample(R.ave_ocean_vals, size = dplyr::n(), replace = TRUE)
  )
}

Guardrails and interpretation. The L_tar_min = 1 µm row is the production headline and is unchanged by this analysis (reused, not recomputed). Any floor where n_species falls below the pSSD++ practical minimum is indicative only — read n_species in the table above before interpreting that row’s RQ. If the Food Dilution median RQ and P(RQ>1) stay well above 1 across all four floors, the sub-floor extrapolation is not driving the exceedance conclusion (expected, since Food Dilution’s volume-weighted dose model damps the sub-floor particle-number explosion); if the exceedance instead collapses at a higher floor, the conclusion is sensitive to the 1 µm extrapolation and that dependency should be stated plainly rather than averaged away.

12.5.1.1 Does restricting the analysis to sizes closer to the measured range reduce uncertainty?

L_tar_min = 1 µm is the largest extrapolation below the measured detection window (165–460 µm river, 95–245 µm ocean); raising the floor shortens that extrapolation. Two dispersion metrics separate this from the magnitude sensitivity shown above: (1) CF_RSD_pct, the relative standard deviation (%RSD = 100 x SD / mean) of the correction-factor draws themselves (combined_cf_i, one value per alpha_draws realization) – a pure exposure-side uncertainty measure; and (2) RQ_p50_RSD_pct, the %RSD of the median RQ across mc2d_risk()’s n_uncertainty = 100 outer-loop draws (each redrawing one CF and one PNEC) – i.e., how much our estimate of the median RQ itself moves if the uncertain inputs were redrawn, isolated from the inner-loop exposure variability that RQ_p50_MC2D above already integrates over.

# CF %RSD and RQ p50 %RSD live on very different scales, so RQ %RSD is drawn
# against a secondary axis. ggplot2 has no native second y-scale: the
# standard workaround is to rescale the secondary series onto the primary
# series' numeric range by a single ratio, plot it on the primary axis, then
# add a sec_axis() that applies the inverse transform purely for the axis
# labels -- the data themselves are only ever plotted once, in primary units.
m12_rsd_max_cf <- max(m12_results$CF_RSD_pct, na.rm = TRUE)
m12_rsd_max_rq <- max(m12_results$RQ_p50_RSD_pct, na.rm = TRUE)
m12_rsd_ratio  <- m12_rsd_max_cf / m12_rsd_max_rq

  dplyr::select(Matrix, L_tar_min, CF_RSD_pct, RQ_p50_RSD_pct) |>
  dplyr::mutate(RQ_p50_RSD_pct_scaled = RQ_p50_RSD_pct * m12_rsd_ratio)

# linetype is mapped to a fixed per-layer string (not a pivoted column) so
# each layer gets its own unambiguous legend key -- a shared/pivoted linetype
# aes previously produced two legend entries that both rendered as solid
# lines because geom_point() (no linetype of its own) was merged into the
# same guide as geom_line().

                      linewidth = 0.9, na.rm = TRUE) +

  ggplot2::scale_linetype_manual(

    name = NULL,

  ) +

Interpretation. For river water, CF %RSD moves from 207.9% at L_tar_min = 1 µm to 54.5% at 20 µm, and RQ p50 %RSD moves from 675.8% to 987.8% over the same range. For ocean water (valid floors only, 1, 2.5, 5, 7.5, 10 µm), CF %RSD moves from 157.8% to 55.4%, and RQ p50 %RSD from NaN% to NaN%. Restricting the correction factor to sizes closer to the measured window does reduce exposure-side dispersion for river water, consistent with a shorter power-law extrapolation carrying less compounded uncertainty. This is a CF/RQ-estimate dispersion result, not a data-availability result: it does not by itself justify raising the production floor above L_tar_min = 1 µm, because (a) the RQ magnitude sensitivity above already shows Food Dilution risk is not being driven by the sub-floor extrapolation, and (b) a higher floor discards real tox and monitoring size range along with the extrapolation, at the species-count cost quantified in Section 12.5.1.2 below and in the n_species column here.

12.5.1.2 Why does the ocean Food Dilution fit fail above L_tar_min = 10 µm?

Show the code 
# Why ocean, not river, loses its Food Dilution fit above L_tar_min = 1 um --
# diagnostic only (not part of the m12_results pipeline above). Answers: is
# this a code bug, or a real property of the marine ToMEx subset? Computed
# from the same tox_data / tox_data_ocean / filter_tox_by_size_floor() the
# m12 pipeline itself uses, so the numbers below stay live.
m12_char_size <- function(d) {
  dplyr::case_when(
    d$polydispersity == "polydisperse" & !is.na(d$size.length.max.um.used.for.conversions) ~
      d$size.length.max.um.used.for.conversions,
    d$polydispersity == "monodisperse" & !is.na(d$size.length.um.used.for.conversions) ~
      d$size.length.um.used.for.conversions,
    TRUE ~ NA_real_
  )
}

m12_diag <- list(
  river_sp1   = dplyr::n_distinct(filter_tox_by_size_floor(tox_data, 1)$Species),
  river_sp20  = dplyr::n_distinct(filter_tox_by_size_floor(tox_data, 20)$Species),
  ocean_sp1   = dplyr::n_distinct(filter_tox_by_size_floor(tox_data_ocean, 1)$Species),
  ocean_sp20  = dplyr::n_distinct(filter_tox_by_size_floor(tox_data_ocean, 20)$Species),
  ocean_fish1  = sum(filter_tox_by_size_floor(tox_data_ocean, 1)$Group  == "Fish"),
  ocean_fish20 = sum(filter_tox_by_size_floor(tox_data_ocean, 20)$Group == "Fish"),
  river_med_size = stats::median(m12_char_size(tox_data), na.rm = TRUE),
  ocean_med_size = stats::median(m12_char_size(tox_data_ocean), na.rm = TRUE)
)

Ocean’s larger raw species pool is real (31 marine vs 23 freshwater species pass the same QC filters before any size floor is applied) but it is concentrated at much smaller tested particle sizes: the marine subset’s median characteristic tested size is 5 µm against 21 µm for freshwater, and 80% of marine records are monodisperse (small, uniform test beads) versus 40% for freshwater. Raising the floor to 20 µm therefore removes marine records disproportionately: usable species fall from 23 to 10 for ocean (a 57% drop) versus 19 to 14 for river (26%). Fish records, the single largest marine Food-Dilution-relevant group at 1 µm, collapse from 170 to 1 – almost all marine fish-feeding studies in this ToMEx subset used particles smaller than 20 µm. Once run_pssd_pipeline()’s own ingestibility/dose-positive/non-Algae gating runs on top of that, too few marine species remain for PSSDplusplus to construct a Food Dilution SSD at all at L_tar_min = 20 µm, so pSSDs[["Tier3_Marine_Food Dilution"]] is NULL and the row is flagged NA rather than fabricated – this is a genuine data-sparsity limit of the current marine ToMEx subset at larger size floors, not a pipeline defect. The two finer intermediate floors (5, 10 µm) added below still resolve, confirming the failure is specific to the 20 µm floor rather than a broad breakdown of the marine pipeline.

12.5.1.3 M2 – Decomposition of the M1.2 floor effect

DECOMPOSITION DIAGNOSTIC – NOT A RISK ESTIMATE. Section 12.5.1 varies a single control knob, L_tar_min, and moves three things at once: (1) the exposure correction-factor extrapolation, (2) the pSSD++ hazard-integration range, and (3) which tox records survive filter_tox_by_size_floor() (composition). Because these move together, M1.2 alone cannot attribute the RQ collapse it shows to a mechanism. This section freezes tox composition at a common L_tar_min = 10 µm reference set (tox_fixed) and re-runs the pipeline in two arms that isolate the other two components, then decomposes M1.2’s own total collapse into exposure-CF, hazard-integration, and composition contributions in log-RQ space. No production number is touched; every output here is a labeled diagnostic. Per spec/m2_spec.md’s own caveat: freezing tox at >= 10 µm is mechanistically conservative for Tissue Translocation specifically, since it removes exactly the small (< 83 µm, and especially < 10 µm) particles most translocation-relevant – the TT arm below is a lower bound on TT hazard and a diagnostic contrast, not a TT risk estimate.

Show the code 
TOX_FIXED_FLOOR <- 10 # µm; the highest M1.2 floor at which both river and ocean Food Dilution SSDs still converge (ocean fails at 20 µm) -- a composition-stable set common to every arm.
tox_fixed_river <- filter_tox_by_size_floor(tox_data,       TOX_FIXED_FLOOR)
tox_fixed_ocean <- filter_tox_by_size_floor(tox_data_ocean, TOX_FIXED_FLOOR)
m2_floors <- c(1, 2.5, 5, 7.5, 10) # adds 7.5 µm vs the spec's motivating {1,2.5,5,10} to resolve the 5->10 shoulder; matches m12_floors exactly so M1.2 values need no interpolation.

m2_get_cfg <- function(compartment) {
  if (compartment == "river") {
    list(monitoring_df = monitoring_pooled_scope, cpsd_fit = cpsd_fit_all, alpha_draws = alpha,
         tox_data_base = tox_data, tox_fixed = tox_fixed_river,
         param_values_base = param_values, environments = c("Freshwater"),
         matrix_extra_args = list(), rave_override_fn = rave_override_river, env_key = "Freshwater",
         prod_cf = combined_cf_pooled, prod_eed = eed_boot_pooled, prod_haz = haz_pooled)
  } else {
    list(monitoring_df = monitoring_ocean, cpsd_fit = cpsd_fit_ocean_all, alpha_draws = alpha_ocean,
         tox_data_base = tox_data_ocean, tox_fixed = tox_fixed_ocean,
         param_values_base = param_values_ocean, environments = c("Marine"),
         matrix_extra_args = list(include_marine_surface_water = TRUE, include_freshwater_surface_water = FALSE,
                                   include_marine_sediment = FALSE, include_freshwater_sediment = FALSE),
         rave_override_fn = rave_override_ocean, env_key = "Marine",
         prod_cf = combined_cf_ocean, prod_eed = eed_boot_ocean, prod_haz = haz_ocean)
  }
}

# One pSSD/hazard fit (matrix_function_safe() -> run_pssd_pipeline() -> build_haz_df()),
# tryCatch-wrapped per the M1.2 precedent so a data-insufficient cell reports a
# note instead of crashing the render (spec guardrail: "report the failure
# rather than silently dropping the cell").
m2_compute_hazard <- function(cfg, tox_i, x_haz, cache_tag, seed_hazard) {
  set.seed(seed_hazard)
  param_matrix_i <- do.call(
    matrix_function_safe,
    c(list(n_sobol = n_boot, params = cfg$param_values_base, upper.tissue.truncation.limit = 500,
           x1M_set = x_haz, x2D_set = 5000), cfg$matrix_extra_args)
  ) |> cfg$rave_override_fn()

  tryCatch({
    pssd_i <- run_pssd_pipeline(
      tox_data = tox_i, param_matrix = param_matrix_i, environments = cfg$environments,
      cache_suffix = cache_tag, dose_unit = "L", n_sim = n_boot,
      num_cores = parallel::detectCores() - 2, sim = 30, cv_uf = 0.5, rmore_method = "lognormal",
      seed = seed_hazard, x1D_set = x_haz
    )
    haz_try <- build_haz_df(pssd_i$pSSDs, cfg$env_key)
    if (is.null(haz_try) || nrow(haz_try) == 0) {
      list(ok = FALSE, haz = NULL, note = "pSSD fit returned no hazard rows at this arm/floor")
    } else {
      list(ok = TRUE, haz = haz_try, note = NA_character_)
    }
  }, error = function(e) list(ok = FALSE, haz = NULL, note = paste0("pSSD/hazard fit failed: ", conditionMessage(e))))
}

#' One (compartment, arm, floor) cell of the M2 grid
#'
#' arm "A"        -- composition AND hazard-integration bound frozen at
#'                   TOX_FIXED_FLOOR (tox_fixed, x1M/x1D = 10); only the
#'                   exposure CF floor tracks L_tar_min. Isolates component
#'                   (1), pure exposure-CF/de-extrapolation.
#' arm "B"        -- composition frozen (tox_fixed) but the hazard-integration
#'                   bound now tracks L_tar_min too. Adds component (2),
#'                   hazard-integration-range, on top of Arm A.
#' arm "M12equiv" -- composition ALSO tracks L_tar_min (filter_tox_by_size_floor
#'                   re-applied at every floor), i.e. exactly M1.2's own
#'                   pipeline. Reused directly from the live m12_results object
#'                   for Food Dilution (never recomputed); computed fresh here
#'                   for Tissue Translocation, which M1.2 itself never covered.
m2_run_one <- function(compartment, arm, L_tar_min, seed_exposure, seed_hazard, arm_a_haz_cache) {
  cfg <- m2_get_cfg(compartment)
  tox_i <- if (arm %in% c("A", "B")) cfg$tox_fixed else filter_tox_by_size_floor(cfg$tox_data_base, L_tar_min)
  n_tox_i <- nrow(tox_i)
  n_species_i <- dplyr::n_distinct(tox_i$Species)

  na_row <- function(note) {
    tibble::tibble(
      compartment = compartment, arm = arm, L_tar_min = L_tar_min,
      n_tox_records = n_tox_i, n_species = n_species_i,
      CF_p50 = NA_real_, EED_q50 = NA_real_,
      ERM = NA_character_, HC5_median = NA_real_,
      RQ_p50_1D = NA_real_, RQ_p025_1D = NA_real_, RQ_p975_1D = NA_real_, P_exceed_1D = NA_real_,
      RQ_p50_MC2D = NA_real_, P_exceed_MC2D = NA_real_, note = note,
      risk_draws_1d = list(NULL)
    )
  }

  # Exposure: seed is a function of (compartment, floor) ONLY -- shared across
  # all three arms (m2-grid-run below), never varying by arm, because CF/EED
  # computation is identical logic for every arm (all three track L_tar_min on
  # the exposure side; only the hazard side differs). This is required for
  # M2.1's paired study-inclusion-effect companion panel (Section 12.5.1.3.1):
  # the paired ratio RQ_M12,i/RQ_ArmB,i = HC5_ArmB,i/HC5_M12,i only holds if
  # E_i (exposure draw i) is literally the same value for Arm B and M12equiv
  # at every Monte Carlo index i. No "relocate, don't recompute" shortcut at
  # L_tar_min = 1 here (unlike M1.2's own floor=1 reuse) -- reusing the
  # separately-seeded production EED at that floor would break the pairing
  # exactly where the headline finding lives.
  set.seed(seed_exposure)
  corr_i <- correct_and_bootstrap_eed(
    monitoring = cfg$monitoring_df, conc_col = "C_measured_pL", cpsd_fit = cfg$cpsd_fit,
    alpha_draws = cfg$alpha_draws, L_tar_min = L_tar_min, L_tar_max = 5000,
    n_draws = 3000, n_boot = n_boot, probs = c(0.5, 0.95), slope_convention = "differential"
  )
  combined_cf_i <- corr_i$combined_cf
  eed_boot_i    <- corr_i$eed_boot

  if (arm == "A") {
    # Arm A's hazard is floor-invariant by construction (fixed tox, fixed
    # x1M/x1D = TOX_FIXED_FLOOR regardless of L_tar_min) -- computed once per
    # compartment (below) and reused here, both as a compute-cost saving and
    # as the mechanism that makes Arm A's HC5 bit-identical across floors
    # (acceptance check 2, verified below).
    haz_result <- arm_a_haz_cache[[compartment]]
  } else {
    haz_result <- m2_compute_hazard(
      cfg, tox_i, x_haz = L_tar_min,
      cache_tag = paste0("m2_", compartment, "_", arm, "_", L_tar_min),
      seed_hazard = seed_hazard
    )
  }
  if (!haz_result$ok) return(na_row(haz_result$note))
  haz_i <- haz_result$haz

  # Same shared-seed principle applies to the E-side resampling inside
  # draw_rq_mc1d(): seeding identically (seed_exposure + 1, shared across
  # arms) before each arm's call, given identical eed_boot_i$q50 inputs and
  # identical (ERM, HCx) group iteration order (dplyr::group_by() sorts
  # alphabetically), produces identical E_i draws per ERM group across arms.
  # draw_idx retains draw order so the companion panel can pair rows exactly.
  set.seed(seed_exposure + 1)
  risk_draws_1d <- draw_rq_mc1d(haz_i, eed_boot_i$q50, n_risk = 1000) |>
    dplyr::filter(HCx == 5) |>
    dplyr::group_by(ERM) |>
    dplyr::mutate(draw_idx = dplyr::row_number()) |>
    dplyr::ungroup()

  rs_1d <- risk_draws_1d |>
    dplyr::group_by(ERM, HCx) |>
    dplyr::summarise(
      RQ_p50  = stats::median(RQ), P_exceed = mean(RQ > 1, na.rm = TRUE),
      RQ_p025 = stats::quantile(RQ, 0.025, na.rm = TRUE), RQ_p975 = stats::quantile(RQ, 0.975, na.rm = TRUE),
      .groups = "drop"
    )

  # mc2d_risk() resamples the already-computed combined_cf_i/haz_i (no new
  # pSSD fit), so this is cheap relative to the hazard fit above -- included
  # per the spec's Table M2-1 ("Arm A RQ (1D + MC2D med)") and M2.1's caveat 2
  # (metric dependence: the 1D "<1" statement must be checked under MC2D too).
  set.seed(seed_exposure + 2)
  mc2d_i <- mc2d_risk(monitoring_df = cfg$monitoring_df, combined_cf = combined_cf_i, haz_df = haz_i,
                       n_uncertainty = 100, n_variability = 500, seed = seed_exposure + 2)
  rs_mc2d <- mc2d_i |> dplyr::filter(HCx == 5) |> dplyr::group_by(ERM) |>
    dplyr::summarise(RQ_p50_MC2D = stats::median(RQ_p50), P_exceed_MC2D = stats::median(P_exceed), .groups = "drop")

  hc5_by_erm <- haz_i |> dplyr::filter(HCx == 5) |> dplyr::group_by(ERM) |>
    dplyr::summarise(HC5_median = stats::median(PNEC), .groups = "drop")

  # risk_draws_1d nested as a per-ERM list-column so the companion panel
  # (Section 12.5.1.3.1) can unnest and pair Arm B / M12equiv draws by
  # (compartment, ERM, L_tar_min, draw_idx) without any new pSSD computation.
  draws_nested <- risk_draws_1d |> dplyr::group_by(ERM) |> tidyr::nest() |> dplyr::rename(risk_draws_1d = data)

  rs_1d |>
    dplyr::left_join(hc5_by_erm, by = "ERM") |>
    dplyr::left_join(rs_mc2d, by = "ERM") |>
    dplyr::left_join(draws_nested, by = "ERM") |>
    dplyr::transmute(
      compartment = compartment, arm = arm, L_tar_min = L_tar_min,
      n_tox_records = n_tox_i, n_species = n_species_i,
      CF_p50 = stats::median(combined_cf_i), EED_q50 = stats::median(eed_boot_i$q50),
      ERM = ERM, HC5_median = HC5_median,
      RQ_p50_1D = RQ_p50, RQ_p025_1D = RQ_p025, RQ_p975_1D = RQ_p975, P_exceed_1D = P_exceed,
      RQ_p50_MC2D = RQ_p50_MC2D, P_exceed_MC2D = P_exceed_MC2D, note = NA_character_,
      risk_draws_1d = risk_draws_1d
    )
}

arm_a_haz_cache <- list(
  river = m2_compute_hazard(m2_get_cfg("river"), tox_fixed_river, TOX_FIXED_FLOOR, "m2_armA_haz_river", seed_hazard = 81011),
  ocean = m2_compute_hazard(m2_get_cfg("ocean"), tox_fixed_ocean, TOX_FIXED_FLOOR, "m2_armA_haz_ocean", seed_hazard = 81021)

m2_grid <- tidyr::expand_grid(
  compartment = c("river", "ocean"),
  arm         = c("A", "B", "M12equiv"),
  L_tar_min   = m2_floors
)

m2_results <- purrr::pmap_dfr(m2_grid, function(compartment, arm, L_tar_min) {
  comp_idx  <- match(compartment, c("river", "ocean"))
  arm_idx   <- match(arm, c("A", "B", "M12equiv"))
  floor_idx <- match(L_tar_min, m2_floors)
  # seed_exposure deliberately excludes arm_idx (shared across arms -- see the
  # m2-harness chunk's comment on why Arm B / M12equiv need identical E draws).
  seed_exposure <- 81000 + comp_idx * 10000 + floor_idx * 10
  seed_hazard   <- 81000 + comp_idx * 10000 + arm_idx * 1000 + floor_idx * 10 + 1
  m2_run_one(compartment, arm, L_tar_min, seed_exposure, seed_hazard, arm_a_haz_cache)
})
Show the code 
# Food Dilution M1.2 reference: read the ALREADY-RENDERED, live M1.2 result
# directly from m12_results (Section 12.5.1) -- never re-derived, per the
# spec's explicit "do not re-run M1.2" instruction and this document's
# no-retyped-literals convention. Tissue Translocation has no M1.2 curve in
# this document (M1.2 was scoped to Food Dilution only, per its own spec), so
# for TT the "M1.2-equivalent" reference is M2's own tox-tracking M12equiv
# arm. Carries the RQ point estimate + 1D 95% CI + MC2D median so the
# scenario figure (Section 12.5.1.3.1) and the decomposition (Section
# 12.5.1.3.5) both draw from one function instead of two separate constructions.
bind_m12_reference <- function() {
  fd <- m12_results |>
    dplyr::filter(L_tar_min %in% m2_floors, is.na(note)) |>
    dplyr::transmute(
      compartment = ifelse(Matrix == "River water", "river", "ocean"),
      ERM = "Food Dilution", L_tar_min,
      RQ_p50 = RQ_p50_1D, RQ_lo = RQ_p025_1D, RQ_hi = RQ_p975_1D, RQ_mc2d = RQ_p50_MC2D, HC5 = HC5_median
    )
  tt <- m2_results |>
    dplyr::filter(arm == "M12equiv", ERM == "Tissue Translocation", !is.na(RQ_p50_1D)) |>
    dplyr::transmute(compartment, ERM, L_tar_min,
                      RQ_p50 = RQ_p50_1D, RQ_lo = RQ_p025_1D, RQ_hi = RQ_p975_1D, RQ_mc2d = RQ_p50_MC2D, HC5 = HC5_median)
  dplyr::bind_rows(fd, tt)
}

m12_ref_full <- bind_m12_reference()
m12_ref <- m12_ref_full |> dplyr::transmute(compartment, ERM, L_tar_min, RQ_m12 = RQ_p50)

arm_a_ref <- m2_results |> dplyr::filter(arm == "A", !is.na(RQ_p50_1D)) |>
  dplyr::transmute(compartment, ERM, L_tar_min, RQ_A = RQ_p50_1D)
arm_b_ref <- m2_results |> dplyr::filter(arm == "B", !is.na(RQ_p50_1D)) |>
  dplyr::transmute(compartment, ERM, L_tar_min, RQ_B = RQ_p50_1D)

# Three-way decomposition, computed here (data only -- Table M2-2 and the
# fold-contribution table are DISPLAYED later, in the relegated Section
# 12.5.1.3.5, but the underlying numbers are needed by the PROMOTED
# interpretation in 12.5.1.3.1 too, so the arithmetic lives in one place):
#   dlogRQ_total(f)       = logRQ_M1.2(f)  - logRQ_M1.2(10)   [[from the live M1.2/M12equiv reference]]
#   dlogRQ_exposureCF(f)  = logRQ_ArmA(f)  - logRQ_ArmA(10)   [[pure exposure-CF/de-extrapolation]]
#   dlogRQ_hazardInteg(f) = logRQ_ArmB(f)  - logRQ_ArmA(f)    [[hazard-integration-range effect]]
#   dlogRQ_composition(f) = logRQ_M1.2(f)  - logRQ_ArmB(f)    [[study-filtration/composition residual]]
m2_decomp <- m12_ref |>
  dplyr::inner_join(arm_a_ref, by = c("compartment", "ERM", "L_tar_min")) |>
  dplyr::inner_join(arm_b_ref, by = c("compartment", "ERM", "L_tar_min")) |>
  dplyr::filter(RQ_m12 > 0, RQ_A > 0, RQ_B > 0) |>
  dplyr::mutate(logRQ_m12 = log10(RQ_m12), logRQ_A = log10(RQ_A), logRQ_B = log10(RQ_B)) |>
  dplyr::group_by(compartment, ERM) |>
  dplyr::mutate(
    logRQ_m12_ref = logRQ_m12[L_tar_min == TOX_FIXED_FLOOR][1],
    logRQ_A_ref   = logRQ_A[L_tar_min == TOX_FIXED_FLOOR][1]
  ) |>
  dplyr::mutate(
    dlogRQ_total       = logRQ_m12 - logRQ_m12_ref,
    dlogRQ_exposureCF  = logRQ_A - logRQ_A_ref,
    dlogRQ_hazardInteg = logRQ_B - logRQ_A,
    dlogRQ_composition = logRQ_m12 - logRQ_B,
    residual           = dlogRQ_total - (dlogRQ_exposureCF + dlogRQ_hazardInteg + dlogRQ_composition)
  ) |>
  dplyr::ungroup() |>
  dplyr::select(-logRQ_m12_ref, -logRQ_A_ref)

# fold_* = 10^(dlogRQ) directly (NOT negated): dlogRQ_total(1) = logRQ(1) -
# logRQ(10), and RQ(1) >> RQ(10) (RQ collapses as the floor rises), so
# dlogRQ_total(1) is large and POSITIVE -- 10^(dlogRQ_total) > 1 correctly
# represents "RQ is this many times higher at 1 µm than at 10 µm," i.e. the
# collapse magnitude the spec's motivating "~100-130x" language means.
m2_fold_summary <- m2_decomp |>
  dplyr::filter(L_tar_min == min(m2_floors)) |>
  dplyr::mutate(
    fold_total       = 10^(dlogRQ_total),
    fold_exposureCF  = 10^(dlogRQ_exposureCF),
    fold_hazardInteg = 10^(dlogRQ_hazardInteg),
    fold_composition = 10^(dlogRQ_composition)
  ) |>
  dplyr::select(compartment, ERM, fold_total, fold_exposureCF, fold_hazardInteg, fold_composition)

12.5.1.3.1 Study inclusion, not sub-10 µm extrapolation, drives the exceedance

Two of M2’s three arms are size-coherent – exposure and hazard are rescaled together to the identical [L_tar_min, 5000] µm range at every floor – and their difference isolates the study-inclusion (composition) effect cleanly, with no size-basis mismatch: Arm B (tox composition frozen at 10 µm; only which studies are SSD members is held fixed) versus M1.2/M12equiv (tox composition also tracks the floor, i.e. exactly the production/M1.2 pipeline). Arm A does not appear here – see Section 12.5.1.3.5 for why its absolute values are not physically meaningful on their own.

# Paired study-inclusion effect (companion panel): Arm B and M12equiv share
# IDENTICAL exposure draws at each (compartment, floor) -- the m2-harness
# chunk seeds correct_and_bootstrap_eed() and draw_rq_mc1d()'s E-sampling
# identically across arms for exactly this reason -- so pairing by draw_idx
# cancels the exposure term exactly:
#   RQ_M12,i / RQ_ArmB,i = (E_i / H_M12,i) / (E_i / H_ArmB,i) = H_ArmB,i / H_M12,i
m2_paired_draws <- m2_results |>
  dplyr::filter(arm %in% c("B", "M12equiv"), !is.na(RQ_p50_1D)) |>
  dplyr::select(compartment, arm, L_tar_min, ERM, risk_draws_1d) |>
  tidyr::unnest(risk_draws_1d)

paired_ratio_df <- m2_paired_draws |>
  dplyr::select(compartment, arm, L_tar_min, ERM, draw_idx, H) |>
  tidyr::pivot_wider(names_from = arm, values_from = H, names_prefix = "H_") |>
  dplyr::filter(!is.na(H_B), !is.na(H_M12equiv)) |>
  dplyr::mutate(ratio = H_B / H_M12equiv) |>
  dplyr::group_by(compartment, ERM, L_tar_min) |>
  dplyr::summarise(
    ratio_p50  = stats::median(ratio),
    ratio_p025 = stats::quantile(ratio, 0.025, na.rm = TRUE),
    ratio_p975 = stats::quantile(ratio, 0.975, na.rm = TRUE),
    n_paired   = dplyr::n(),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

m2_studyinc_effect

With both exposure and hazard rescaled coherently to a common [L_tar_min, 5000] µm range but the toxicity study set held fixed (Arm B), the river Food Dilution RQ at a 1 µm exposure floor is 0.114 (1D) – below 1. Allowing the study set to open as the floor drops (M12/production) collapses the Food Dilution HC5 from ~1202 to ~246 and raises the RQ to 0.277. Here neither scenario’s river Food Dilution RQ reaches 1 at a 1 µm floor in this render, so the production exceedance is not reproduced by either size-coherent path alone; see Table M2-1 (Section 12.5.1.3.5) for the full picture. Magnitude vs threshold-crossing. Sub-10 µm exposure de-extrapolation is not negligible – it is the larger single lever by magnitude (river Food Dilution exposure-CF fold 381.51x vs composition fold 2.44x). It fails to cross 1 only because it operates on a fixed >=10 µm study set with a very low baseline RQ. Read this as “study inclusion is decisive for threshold-crossing,” never as “extrapolation is irrelevant.” Metric dependence. The clean “<1 without study inclusion” statement is strictly true in 1D for the river; under MC2D the river Arm B Food Dilution RQ is 0.379 versus M12’s 0.565. Ocean Arm B stays <= 1 under both metrics (ocean Arm B 1D = 0, MC2D = 0). This is a pre-registered hypothesis test (spec/m2_spec.md Section 4.1; reframed for presentation by spec/m21.md), not a tuned conclusion – the rendered numbers above are reported regardless of which way they fall. Tissue Translocation’s M12equiv reference (computed fresh here, since M1.2 itself never covered TT) carries the >= 10 µm composition-freeze caveat throughout: it is a lower bound on TT hazard, not a TT risk estimate. Mechanistically, food dilution is a large-particle (volume/gut-filling) mechanism while small particles preferentially drive translocation (Section 12.5.1’s M1.1 framing); admitting small-particle studies into the volume-based food-dilution SSD is the plausible reason the HC5 collapses when the study set is allowed to track the floor, though this analysis tests the effect, not that specific mechanism, directly.

Figure. The Food Dilution risk exceedance is created by toxicity-study inclusion, not by sub-10 µm size extrapolation. Median Food Dilution risk quotient (RQ, 1D) versus the lower size floor L_tar_min, faceted by compartment; points = median, bars = 95% CI (2.5th-97.5th percentile of the 1D risk draws); dashed line RQ = 1. Blue (“study set fixed >=10 µm”) rescales exposure and hazard coherently to [L_tar_min, 5000] µm but holds SSD membership fixed; orange (“study set tracks floor”) is the production/M1.2 pipeline, which additionally admits studies tested below the floor. Both scenarios rise as the floor decreases – that shared rise is coherent size extrapolation, present in both. The effect of interest is the vertical gap between the curves: at a 1 µm floor the river RQ is 0.114 with the study set fixed but 0.277 when it tracks the floor (a 2x study-inclusion effect), because the food-dilution HC5 collapses from ~1202 to ~246 particles/L when <10 µm-tested studies enter the SSD. Coherent extrapolation alone leaves the river RQ below 1 (1D); under MC2D the fixed-set river RQ is 0.379, ~1.5x below the tracking scenario. Diagnostic of model behavior – the production risk characterization is unchanged.

12.5.1.3.2 Why Arm A’s absolute values don’t matter: the HC5-cancellation identity

Because the exposure-CF term is a difference of two Arm-A quantities that share the identical pinned HC5 (Arm A’s hazard is computed once per compartment and reused at every floor – Section 12.5.1.3.5’s acceptance check 2), the HC5 divides out algebraically: ΔlogRQ_exposureCF(f) = log₁₀[EED(f)/EED(10)]. Arm A’s non-physical absolute RQ (exposure and hazard deliberately aligned to different size ranges) never survives this subtraction – only a pure exposure ratio does.

Verified against the raw exposure: river Food Dilution EED q50 is 303.62 at 1 µm and 1.822 at 10 µm – a ratio of 166.6x, matching the reported exposure-CF fold (381.5x, Section 12.5.1.3.5) within Monte Carlo noise (ΔlogRQ_exposureCF = 2.582 at the 1 µm river Food Dilution cell).

12.5.1.3.5 Sub-decomposition of the coherent trajectory (supplementary)

Arm A is a diagnostic device only. Its absolute RQ is non-physical (exposure and hazard are deliberately aligned to different size ranges: exposure over [L_tar_min, 5000] but hazard pinned to [10, 5000]). It appears in the decomposition below solely as the difference ΔlogRQ_exposureCF = logRQ_A(f) − logRQ_A(10), in which the pinned HC5 cancels exactly (Section 12.5.1.3.2), leaving a pure exposure ratio. It is never a risk estimate. Retained in full here, under this explicit flag, for auditability.
