# Note: because dlogRQ_exposureCF + dlogRQ_hazardInteg + dlogRQ_composition
# telescopes algebraically to (logRQ_m12 - logRQ_A_ref), the "residual" above
# is exactly (logRQ_A_ref - logRQ_m12_ref) within each compartment x ERM group
# -- i.e. it IS the freeze-point coincidence gap (acceptance check 1), not a
# separate quantity. Both are reported because the spec calls for both, but
# they are not independent evidence of harness correctness.
Show the code 
if (is_production_budget) {
  m2_max_resid <- max(abs(m2_decomp$residual), na.rm = TRUE)
  m2_tol <- 0.3 # log10 units (~2x); generous for independently-seeded MC noise, tight enough to catch a genuine multi-order-of-magnitude wiring error
  cat("M2 acceptance checks (production budget, n_boot =", n_boot, "):\n")
  cat("  Check 1 (freeze-point coincidence) & check 3 (decomposition closure) share one quantity here (see note above): max|residual| =",
      signif(m2_max_resid, 3), "log10 units (tolerance", m2_tol, ").\n")
  stopifnot(
    "M2 acceptance checks 1/3 FAILED: freeze-point coincidence / decomposition closure residual exceeds tolerance -- see m2_decomp" =
      m2_max_resid < m2_tol
  )
  cat("M2 acceptance checks 1 and 3 passed.\n")
} else {
  message("M2 acceptance checks 1 and 3 (freeze-point coincidence, decomposition closure) skipped: dev-scale render (n_boot = ",
          n_boot, " < 1000); MC noise is too large relative to the tolerance at this budget. Re-check at the production budget.")
}

# Check 4 (sign sanity, spec Section 2.5): the spec states "exposure-CF
# component should be negative ... RQ falls as floor rises." Under THIS
# section's delta-vs-10-µm-reference parameterization (dlogRQ_exposureCF(f) =
# logRQ_A(f) - logRQ_A(10)), "RQ falls as floor rises" means RQ_A(f) > RQ_A(10)
# for every floor f < 10 µm (more sub-floor extrapolation at a lower floor ->
# higher CF -> higher EED -> higher RQ, holding hazard fixed as Arm A does) --
# i.e. dlogRQ_exposureCF(f) should be POSITIVE for f < 10, not negative; the
# spec's "negative" describes the trend as the floor itself increases, not
# the sign in this fixed-reference-point delta. Reported, not gated (the
# spec constrains this component's sign informationally; only composition's
# sign is explicitly left unconstrained -- but forcing a stopifnot() here
# would just be re-deriving arithmetic already guaranteed by
# correction_factor()'s own monotonicity, not new evidence about the harness).
m2_sign_check <- m2_decomp |>
  dplyr::filter(L_tar_min != TOX_FIXED_FLOOR) |>
  dplyr::summarise(frac_expected_sign = mean(dlogRQ_exposureCF > 0, na.rm = TRUE), .groups = "drop")
cat("Sign sanity: exposure-CF component has the expected sign (RQ_A(f) > RQ_A(10) for f <", TOX_FIXED_FLOOR, "µm) for",
    scales::percent(m2_sign_check$frac_expected_sign, accuracy = 1), "of non-reference rows.\n")

Guardrails. No production headline number is affected by this section (M2 reuses the same underlying correct_and_bootstrap_eed() / matrix_function_safe() / run_pssd_pipeline() / mc2d_risk() functions M1.2 already uses, in new diagnostic configurations; it does not modify the production L_tar_min = 1, fully-tracking pipeline). Arm A deliberately mismatches the exposure and hazard size bases – every Arm A number above is a diagnostic, not a valid stand-alone risk quotient; Arm B numbers, by contrast, are legitimate size-coherent risk quotients (just not the production headline, since composition is deliberately held fixed). Sediment is not touched.

12.5.2 Model-selection robustness: MLE and a tapered/lognormal small-end model

Distinct from Section 4.1’s method-choice statement: this section does not ask whether C-PSD is the right method (it is; Segur et al. 2026 already established C-PSD ≈ MLE in accuracy). It asks how much the risk result depends on the sub-floor extrapolation model, given Segur et al.’s own caveat that C-PSD extrapolates below the measured range, and marine-surface literature suggesting the true small-end particle-size distribution may roll off (fewer small particles than a single power law implies) rather than continue as one power law to 1 µm.

Three models are fit to each matrix’s pooled (“all” shapes) particle-length data: (a) the production C-PSD OLS fit (carried through for comparison, not refit here); (b) an MLE power law (poweRlaw::conpl), with xmin chosen by minimizing the Kolmogorov–Smirnov statistic and a goodness-of-fit bootstrap p-value (Clauset, Shalizi & Newman 2009; power law rejected if p < 0.1); and (c) a lognormal small-end alternative (poweRlaw::conlnorm) fit at the same xmin as the MLE power law, compared to it via a Vuong likelihood-ratio test (compare_distributions()). Ocean fiber (5 populated C-PSD bins; Section 12.1.1) is excluded from MLE fitting as too sparse for a stable tail fit.

Show the code 
m13_fit_one_matrix <- function(length_vec, matrix_label, seed) {
  length_vec <- length_vec[is.finite(length_vec) & length_vec > 0]

  m_pl <- poweRlaw::conpl$new(length_vec)
  est  <- poweRlaw::estimate_xmin(m_pl)
  m_pl$setXmin(est)

  set.seed(seed)
  bp <- poweRlaw::bootstrap_p(m_pl, no_of_sims = 100, threads = 1, seed = seed)

  m_ln <- poweRlaw::conlnorm$new(length_vec)
  m_ln$setXmin(m_pl$getXmin())
  m_ln$setPars(poweRlaw::estimate_pars(m_ln))

  comp <- poweRlaw::compare_distributions(m_pl, m_ln)

  list(
    matrix_label = matrix_label,
    n_total = length(length_vec),
    xmin = est$xmin, ntail = est$ntail, alpha_mle = m_pl$pars,
    KS_D = est$gof, bootstrap_p = bp$p,
    meanlog = m_ln$pars[1], sdlog = m_ln$pars[2],
    vuong_stat = comp$test_statistic, vuong_p = comp$p_two_sided
  )
}

m13_river_fit <- m13_fit_one_matrix(raw_particles_river$length_um, "River water", seed = 71001)
m13_ocean_fit <- m13_fit_one_matrix(raw_particles_ocean$length_um, "Ocean water", seed = 71002)

m13_fit_summary <- dplyr::bind_rows(lapply(list(m13_river_fit, m13_ocean_fit), function(f) {
  tibble::tibble(
    Matrix = f$matrix_label, n_total = f$n_total, xmin_um = round(f$xmin, 1), n_tail = f$ntail,
    alpha_MLE = round(f$alpha_mle, 3), KS_D = round(f$KS_D, 4), bootstrap_p = round(f$bootstrap_p, 3),
    power_law_rejected = f$bootstrap_p < 0.1,
    vuong_stat = round(f$vuong_stat, 3), vuong_p = round(f$vuong_p, 3),
    lognormal_meanlog = round(f$meanlog, 3), lognormal_sdlog = round(f$sdlog, 3)
  )
}))

)

Show the code 
# Convert each model to an equivalent correction factor over the SAME measured
# window already used for the production C-PSD correction factor
# (L_meas_min_use/L_meas_max_use), so only the extrapolation MODEL differs,
# not the physical measurement window -- then recompute the RQ for both ERMs
# against the already-computed production hazard (haz/haz_ocean; hazard is
# not re-derived here, only the exposure-side extrapolation model changes).
m13_propagate_one <- function(fit, L_meas_min, L_meas_max, monitoring_df, conc_col,
                               haz_df, n_risk, cpsd_a_psd, combined_cf_prod, seed_base) {

  cf_mle <- correction_factor(
    a = -fit$alpha_mle, L_meas_min = L_meas_min, L_meas_max = L_meas_max,
    L_tar_min = 1, L_tar_max = 5000, slope_convention = "differential"
  )
  cf_lognormal <- (stats::plnorm(5000, fit$meanlog, fit$sdlog) - stats::plnorm(1, fit$meanlog, fit$sdlog)) /
    (stats::plnorm(L_meas_max, fit$meanlog, fit$sdlog) - stats::plnorm(L_meas_min, fit$meanlog, fit$sdlog))

  rq_for_cf <- function(cf_val, seed) {
    set.seed(seed)
    eed_i <- bootstrap_eed(monitoring_df[[conc_col]] * cf_val, n_boot = n_boot, probs = c(0.5, 0.95))
    set.seed(seed + 1)
    draws_i <- draw_rq_mc1d(haz_df, eed_i$q50, n_risk = n_risk) |>
      dplyr::filter(ERM %in% c("Food Dilution", "Tissue Translocation"), HCx == 5)
    draws_i |>
      dplyr::group_by(ERM) |>
      dplyr::summarise(
        RQ_p50   = stats::median(RQ), P_exceed = mean(RQ > 1, na.rm = TRUE),
        RQ_p025  = stats::quantile(RQ, 0.025, na.rm = TRUE), RQ_p975 = stats::quantile(RQ, 0.975, na.rm = TRUE),
        .groups  = "drop"
      )
  }

  dplyr::bind_rows(
    rq_for_cf(median(combined_cf_prod), seed_base)     |> dplyr::mutate(Model = "C-PSD (production)", CF = median(combined_cf_prod)),
    rq_for_cf(cf_mle, seed_base + 10)                   |> dplyr::mutate(Model = "MLE power law", CF = cf_mle),
    rq_for_cf(cf_lognormal, seed_base + 20)              |> dplyr::mutate(Model = "Lognormal (tapered small-end)", CF = cf_lognormal)
  ) |> dplyr::mutate(Matrix = fit$matrix_label)
}

  m13_river_fit, L_meas_min_use, L_meas_max_use, monitoring_pooled_scope, "C_measured_pL",
  haz_pooled, n_risk, cpsd_fit_all$a_psd, combined_cf_pooled, seed_base = 72001
)
m13_ocean_rq <- m13_propagate_one(
  m13_ocean_fit, L_meas_min_ocean, L_meas_max_ocean, monitoring_ocean, "C_measured_pL",
  haz_ocean, n_risk_ocean, cpsd_fit_ocean_all$a_psd, combined_cf_ocean, seed_base = 72002
)

Guardrails and interpretation. The C-PSD single-slope fit remains the production default; MLE and lognormal are labeled comparators only, and hazard is never re-derived in this section (only the exposure-side extrapolation model changes, holding haz/haz_ocean fixed at their production values). Report GoF failures honestly: the power law is NOT rejected for river water, and is NOT rejected for ocean water (bootstrap p = 0.47 river, 0.73 ocean). The Vuong test indicates whether the power law and lognormal are statistically distinguishable at each matrix’s shared xmin (p < 0.05 favors one model over the other; a non-significant result means the data cannot discriminate between them at this sample size; river Vuong statistic = 0.069, p = 0.945; ocean statistic = 0.362, p = 0.717).

Hold/flip conclusion. For River water, the production C-PSD single-slope Food Dilution HC5 RQ is 0.258 (P(RQ>1) = 39.1%); under the MLE power law it is 0.321 (P(RQ>1) = 43.3%), so the exceedance falls below 1; under the lognormal small-end model it is 0.001 (P(RQ>1) = 2%), so the exceedance falls below 1. For Ocean water, the production C-PSD single-slope Food Dilution HC5 RQ is 0 (P(RQ>1) = 21.1%); under the MLE power law it is 0 (P(RQ>1) = 19.4%), so the exceedance falls below 1; under the lognormal small-end model it is 0 (P(RQ>1) = 0.3%), so the exceedance falls below 1. Both fits report xmin explicitly (238.6 µm river, 170.8 µm ocean, Table M1.3-fits above); the fit constrains only the measured range at or above xmin – the sub-xmin extrapolation to 1 µm remains model-dependent regardless of goodness-of-fit, the same unconstrained sub-floor zone the floor-sensitivity (Section 12.5.1) and piecewise (Section 13.3) analyses probe from other angles. At least one matrix’s Food Dilution RQ falls below 1 under the lognormal small-end model, so the exceedance is not robust to this defensible small-end roll-off; read this alongside the sub-2.5 µm floor collapse (Section 12.5.1) and the piecewise river Food Dilution RQ (Section 13.3) as convergent evidence that the food-dilution exceedance sits on the unconstrained sub-floor extrapolation zone. Because the power law is not rejected for either matrix (bootstrap p reported above), the lognormal is an admissible alternative, not a preferred one – the honest statement is the RQ range across admissible models, weighted by the (non-)discriminating Vuong result. Mechanistically, food dilution is a large-particle (volume/gut-filling) mechanism while small particles preferentially drive translocation; admitting small-particle studies into the volume-based food-dilution SSD (Section 12.5.1.3.1) is the plausible reason a shifted extrapolation model would move the RQ – this section tests the effect of the extrapolation model choice, not that specific mechanism, directly. Ocean fiber (5 populated C-PSD bins) remains excluded from MLE fitting as too sparse for a stable tail fit; the pooled-“all”-shapes basis is used for both matrices’ MLE/lognormal fits.

12.5.3 River vs ocean polymer composition: test for buoyant-polymer enrichment

A shift in polymer mix at the sea surface — specifically enrichment of buoyant polymers (PP, PE) relative to rivers — would independently support a surface-retention/transport interpretation of the shallower ocean particle-length PSD slope (Section 12.1.1), rather than a source/residence or fitting-window explanation. buoyancy_freshwater/buoyancy_marine are already assigned per particle by assign_polymer_density() (Section 3.1.1), relative to freshwater (1.00 g/cm³) and seawater (1.025 g/cm³) respectively, so no new density-assignment code is needed here — only the statistical test.

Show the code

# study (all 6 ocean sample IDs; confirmed below) -- these µFTIR runs simply

# rather than being assumed to be "surface" -- no depth label is fabricated
# for data that was not collected with one.

# Fisher's exact if any expected cell count is small (chi-square approximation
# becomes unreliable below ~5 expected per cell); chi-square otherwise.
m14_expected_min <- suppressWarnings(min(chisq.test(m14_contingency)$expected))
m14_full_test <- if (m14_expected_min < 5) {
  fisher.test(m14_contingency, simulate.p.value = TRUE, B = 10000)
} else {
  chisq.test(m14_contingency)
}
cat(
  "Full polymer x matrix test:", m14_full_test$method,
  "-- statistic =", if (!is.null(m14_full_test$statistic)) signif(m14_full_test$statistic, 4) else NA,
  ", p =", signif(m14_full_test$p.value, 4),
  "(min expected cell count =", round(m14_expected_min, 2), ")\n"
)
Full polymer x matrix test: Fisher's Exact Test for Count Data with simulated p-value
     (based on 10000 replicates) -- statistic = NA , p = 0.09059 (min expected cell count = 0.17 )
Show the code 
# Focused 2x2 test: buoyant (PP + PE) vs non-buoyant, river vs ocean. PP and PE
# are the only two polymer groups classified "buoyant" under both
# buoyancy_freshwater and buoyancy_marine in this dataset (verified below),
# so "buoyant" here is defined directly by polymer identity rather than by
# picking one of the two medium-specific buoyancy columns.
m14_particles <- m14_particles |>
  dplyr::mutate(is_buoyant = polymer_density_group %in% c("polyethylene", "polypropylene"))

m14_buoyancy_agreement <- mean(m14_particles$buoyancy_freshwater == m14_particles$buoyancy_marine)

m14_2x2 <- table(m14_particles$is_buoyant, m14_particles$Matrix)
m14_2x2_test <- if (min(suppressWarnings(chisq.test(m14_2x2)$expected)) < 5) {
  fisher.test(m14_2x2)
} else {
  chisq.test(m14_2x2, correct = TRUE)
}

m14_buoyant_fraction <- m14_particles |>
  dplyr::group_by(Matrix) |>
  dplyr::summarise(
    n = dplyr::n(),
    n_buoyant = sum(is_buoyant),
    fraction_buoyant = n_buoyant / n,
    .groups = "drop"
  ) |>
  dplyr::rowwise() |>
  dplyr::mutate(
    ci = list(stats::binom.test(n_buoyant, n)$conf.int),
    ci_low  = ci[1],
    ci_high = ci[2]
  ) |>
  dplyr::ungroup() |>
  dplyr::select(-ci)

Interpretation. A significant enrichment of PP/PE in ocean surface water relative to river water (37.7% vs 27.1%, 2×2 test p = 0.0215) would support the transport/retention reading of the river-vs-ocean slope difference; a null result points instead toward a source/residence or fitting-window explanation. Caveats. Composition is count-based over each matrix’s own measured detection window (the same LOD/window caveats that apply to the slope fits themselves), and ocean n = 114 limits statistical power relative to river n = 1195. This polymer-composition test is an independent line of evidence that does not depend on the fitting window — but the river-vs-ocean slope difference itself (Section 12.1.1) is separately confounded by different fitting windows (river 165–460 µm vs ocean 95–245 µm) and should be re-tested over a common overlapping window before that slope difference alone is attributed to source or transport.

12.5.3.1 Depth-stratified polymer composition (river surface/subsurface vs ocean)

River water has both sample_depth_general strata (697 surface, 498 subsurface particles). Ocean water does not: sample_depth_general is unrecorded for all 114 ocean-water particles in this study (0 with a recorded stratum), so an ocean depth split is not possible from this dataset – ocean is shown below as its own “depth not recorded” panel rather than assumed to be surface-only. The top-5 polymers by pooled river+ocean particle count set a common comparison basis across panels; every other polymer group is collapsed to “Other” so rare groups do not fragment the comparison.

Interpretation. Comparing the two river panels isolates a within-matrix depth effect (same sampling program, same µFTIR workflow, same LOD window); comparing either river panel to the ocean panel still mixes a matrix effect with the unrecorded-depth limitation above. 37.7% buoyant fraction in ocean vs river’s surface/subsurface split (Section 12.5.3 table) is the more decision-relevant comparison than the full multi-polymer breakdown shown here, which is a descriptive, hypothesis-generating cross-tabulation. The within-river surface-vs-subsurface buoyancy comparison it motivates is tested formally below.

12.5.3.1.1 Formal test: are buoyant particles relatively more abundant at the river surface than subsurface?

Rationale: if buoyant (PP + PE) particles float toward and accumulate at the air-water interface, the river surface stratum should show a higher buoyant fraction than the subsurface stratum sampled at the same locations and times. This is a directional (one-sided) hypothesis, tested only within river water – ocean has no recorded depth stratum (Section 12.5.3.1 above), so it cannot be included.

Show the code

  dplyr::filter(Matrix == "River water", Depth %in% c("surface", "subsurface")) |>
  dplyr::mutate(Depth = factor(Depth, levels = c("subsurface", "surface")))

river_depth_buoyant_fraction <- river_depth_buoyant |>
  dplyr::group_by(Depth) |>
  dplyr::summarise(n = dplyr::n(), n_buoyant = sum(is_buoyant), fraction_buoyant = n_buoyant / n, .groups = "drop") |>
  dplyr::rowwise() |>
  dplyr::mutate(
    ci = list(stats::binom.test(n_buoyant, n)$conf.int),
    ci_low  = ci[1],
    ci_high = ci[2]
  ) |>
  dplyr::ungroup() |>
  dplyr::select(-ci)

  col.names = c("Depth", "n", "n buoyant", "Fraction buoyant", "95% CI low", "95% CI high")
)

Depth n n buoyant Fraction buoyant 95% CI low 95% CI high

Show the code 
n_surf    <- river_depth_buoyant_fraction$n[river_depth_buoyant_fraction$Depth == "surface"]
n_sub     <- river_depth_buoyant_fraction$n[river_depth_buoyant_fraction$Depth == "subsurface"]
nb_surf   <- river_depth_buoyant_fraction$n_buoyant[river_depth_buoyant_fraction$Depth == "surface"]
nb_sub    <- river_depth_buoyant_fraction$n_buoyant[river_depth_buoyant_fraction$Depth == "subsurface"]
river_depth_2x2 <- table(river_depth_buoyant$Depth, river_depth_buoyant$is_buoyant)
river_depth_expected_min <- suppressWarnings(min(chisq.test(river_depth_2x2)$expected))

# One-sided two-proportion test: H1 = surface buoyant fraction > subsurface
# buoyant fraction. Falls back to a one-sided Fisher's exact test if any
# expected cell count is small (same threshold convention as Section 12.5.3's
# river-vs-ocean 2x2 test). river_depth_2x2 rows are (subsurface, surface) and
# columns are (not buoyant, buoyant), so a higher surface buoyant fraction
# implies odds ratio = (FALSE_sub * TRUE_surf) / (TRUE_sub * FALSE_surf) > 1
# -- alternative = "greater" is the correct one-sided direction for both tests.
river_depth_buoyancy_test <- if (river_depth_expected_min < 5) {
  fisher.test(river_depth_2x2, alternative = "greater")
} else {
  stats::prop.test(x = c(nb_surf, nb_sub), n = c(n_surf, n_sub), alternative = "greater")
}

cat(
  "Surface vs subsurface buoyant fraction, river water only:", river_depth_buoyancy_test$method,
  "-- one-sided H1: surface fraction > subsurface fraction -- p =", signif(river_depth_buoyancy_test$p.value, 4),
  "(min expected cell count =", round(river_depth_expected_min, 2), ")\n"
)
Surface vs subsurface buoyant fraction, river water only: 2-sample test for equality of proportions with continuity correction -- one-sided H1: surface fraction > subsurface fraction -- p = 0.999 (min expected cell count = 135.02 )

Interpretation. The river surface stratum’s buoyant fraction is 23.7% (n = 697) versus 31.9% at the subsurface (n = 498); the one-sided test above gives p = 0.999. This does not support the hypothesis – the observed direction is the opposite of what surface buoyant-enrichment would predict: the subsurface fraction is numerically higher than the surface fraction, though the 95% CIs above overlap substantially. Density-driven vertical sorting by buoyancy is not evident in this river dataset; the depth difference, if real, is more likely driven by something other than polymer buoyancy (e.g., local hydrodynamics, sampling time, or shape-dependent settling of non-buoyant fibers). This is a within-matrix, same-program, same-workflow comparison (unlike the river-vs-ocean buoyancy test in Section 12.5.3, which is additionally confounded by the ocean depth-recording gap noted above), so a significant result here would be comparatively strong evidence for local vertical sorting by buoyancy specifically.

15.1 Revised uncertainty interpretation

The main unresolved methodological uncertainties are now: (1) µFTIR objective and the marginal 50–100 µm detection zone, (2) transport-induced PSD structural uncertainty described by Hoffman et al. (2026), and (3) the lower extrapolation floor and toxicity-study-inclusion rule quantified in Section 12.5.1.3.1. The Hoffman uncertainty can affect absolute concentrations through the CF exponent, and may also affect relative comparisons when surface/subsurface samples, fibers/fragments, or buoyant/settling polymers are mixed in a pooled single-power-law fit. The sensitivity analyses above therefore replace the older conclusion that no further correction was warranted. The calibrated interpretation is that a Food Dilution threshold exceedance cannot be excluded but is method-conditional (floor-sensitive and study-inclusion-driven, Section 12.5.1.3.1; further bracketed by the piecewise and MLE/lognormal extrapolation-model sensitivities, Sections 13.2 and 12.5.2) rather than an unconditional risk-dominance finding, while magnitude estimates should be read together with the slope-uncertainty, depth-stratified, density/buoyancy, and water-sediment coherence diagnostics.

15.2 Modeling priorities

Hoffman et al. (2026) indicates that 3-D particle geometry and density inputs should be improved before investing effort in more complex settling-velocity equations. The current report follows that guardrail by adding polymer-resolved density and buoyancy flags, making δ and K explicit assumptions in the critical-size calculation, and retaining settling-based diagnostics as bias-level sensitivity checks rather than high-precision corrections. Future transport work should prioritize measured particle thickness, density, and shape-specific behavior; settling-equation refinements alone should not be expected to remove the dominant uncertainty.

15.3 Revised executive summary

This section restates the executive summary with the corrected numbers now that every matrix’s corrected and legacy sensitivity pipeline (Sections 5-14) has been computed, per SPEC 3b.

(a) Corrected Food Dilution RQ, after SPEC 1b. At a dev-scale iteration Monte Carlo budget (100 parameter-matrix replicates, 5000 slope draws), the corrected median Food Dilution HC5 RQ is 3.56 for river water (P(RQ>1) = 62.5%) and 0 for ocean water (median P(RQ>1) = 39.9%). Sediment is intentionally omitted from this headline figure (SPEC 1d): its nominal corrected Food Dilution HC5 RQ (0, P(RQ>1) = 0%) is not a defensible risk estimate — Section 11.3.0/11.4.0 trace this to a placeholder exposure concentration (a per-liter water value reused as particles/kg) and a derived HC5 that fails the benthic-plausibility guard by roughly eleven orders of magnitude — so it is excluded from the risk conclusion rather than reported alongside the river and ocean values.

(b) The prior (SPEC 1b-uncorrected) Food Dilution RQ was inflated by the volume-slope convention error. Reverting only a.v/a.sa/a.m to the legacy cumulative-as-differential convention (Appendix A), holding exposure and the length-slope alignment at their corrected values, the river-water Food Dilution HC5 median RQ becomes 669289622.226 — a 188018508.8-fold change relative to the corrected value of 3.56. This is the same mechanism and direction of error described in the SPEC 1b background (a mean-particle-volume sensitivity calculation there estimates a ~4-6 million-fold effect at a = 0.76 vs. 1.68); the exact factor is a function of n_boot/n_mc and is expected to scale toward that estimate as the budget increases. No Food Dilution RQ figure in this report should be read as ~10^7 — that magnitude describes the pre-SPEC-1b (legacy) error being corrected here, not the corrected result.

(c) Tissue Translocation shift after both the length-slope and surface-area-slope fixes (revised, SPEC 3c). Reverting only the hazard-side length-slope alignment to its legacy cumulative-as-differential form, the river-water Tissue Translocation HC5 P(RQ>1) is 68.2%, versus 16.4% under the corrected alignment (Section 14.1). This is a material driver, but so is the surface-area slope: reverting a.v/a.sa/a.m together gives 99.7%, and isolating a.sa alone gives 99.6% — both far from the 16.4% corrected value, because Tissue Translocation/oxidative-stress alignment is surface-area-weighted and therefore directly sensitive to the a.sa correction, unlike its (correctly) minimal sensitivity to the volume slope alone. A prior version of this narrative incorrectly called the volume/area effect on Tissue Translocation “essentially unchanged”; that claim is retracted here (Section 14.1 has the corrected attribution and the full one-at-a-time decomposition table, now covering both ERMs).

(d) Exposure as a single-slope-vs-piecewise bounding range (SPEC 2b). The production single-slope correction factor and its piecewise (dual-slope) bounding alternative are compared per matrix in Section 13.3 (Tables: single-slope vs. piecewise CF/EED, and the resulting Food Dilution/Tissue Translocation HC5 RQ range). The single-slope CF remains the production default; the piecewise result is a labeled sensitivity bound quantifying structural (model-form) uncertainty in the unconstrained 1 µm-to-LOD sub-window, per the guardrails in the corrective-revision spec.

(e) Sediment pathway excluded from the headline conclusion (SPEC 1d). The sediment (beach sand) risk characterization in Section 11 is retained in this report as a methods/illustrative demonstration only. Its exposure concentration is not a genuine particles/kg-dry-weight value (Section 11.3.0), its hazard-side dose_unit = “kg” pathway was traced and found unit-consistent on its own terms with no discrete conversion bug identified (Section 11.4.0), and its sediment-specific ERM alignment slopes were independently verified correct and ruled out as the cause (Section 11.2, SPEC 1d-iv). The resulting sediment Food Dilution HC5 fails a rendered plausibility guard anchored on Redondo-Hasselerharm et al. (2023) by roughly eleven orders of magnitude. Until a genuine dry-weight sediment concentration is available, no sediment RQ in this report should be treated as a risk finding.

(f) Sediment as a time-dependent, accumulating compartment (SPEC 1e). Independent of the exposure-concentration problem in (e), Section 11.5 reframes sediment as an accumulating depositional sink in which deposited microplastics continue to fragment in place, so both bioaccessible exposure and hazard (HC5, via which benthic species become size-accessible) evolve over residence time (Thuy-Dung, Groenenberg & Koelmans 2026). Any static sediment metric — including the illustrative Section 11.4 figures — is therefore a lower-bound snapshot, not an equilibrium value. Section 11.5.2 demonstrates this illustratively with a labeled, non-quantitative PSD-shift sensitivity showing the derived Food Dilution and Tissue Translocation HC5 falling as the sediment PSD is shifted progressively finer; Section 11.5.4 adds a most-sensitive-species screen (sediment, plus a river/ocean companion) since individual-species risk can precede a derivable community SSD signal. This is a framework/sensitivity addition — it does not change point (e): sediment remains excluded from the headline risk conclusion.

Summary. A food-dilution threshold exceedance cannot be excluded but is not robust. At the field-standard 1 µm floor, the food-dilution RQ exceeds 1 in both matrices (river MC2D median RQ = 3.17, P(RQ>1) = 57%; ocean = 0, P(RQ>1) = 39.9%), while Tissue Translocation is below threshold (river 0.069; ocean 0). This exceedance is conditional: it collapses (river Food Dilution RQ already below 1 by a 2.5 µm floor, 0.01) as the lower size floor rises from 1 µm (Section 12.5.1), and Section 12.5.1.3.1 shows it is generated by admitting <10 µm-tested toxicity studies into the volume-based food-dilution SSD (a hazard/HC5 effect) rather than by coherent sub-10 µm exposure extrapolation. A size-coherent, fixed-study-set comparison (Arm B, Section 12.5.1.3.1) is available but its precise fold-values are provisional at this dev-scale render (n_boot = 100 < 1000; M2’s own freeze-point-coincidence and decomposition-closure checks are skipped below the production budget) – see Section 12.5.1.3.1 directly rather than this summary for indicative dev-scale numbers. The exceedance’s magnitude is further bracketed by two exposure-model sensitivities: the two-segment (piecewise) fit (Section 13.2/13.3, river Food Dilution RQ 0.02) and the MLE/lognormal small-end extrapolation model (Section 12.5.2), both reported in the sensitivity sections above. The sediment pathway remains excluded from this conclusion pending real concentration data (point (e) above). The magnitude-uncertainty pointer here has shifted from the convention-fix audit to the floor / study-inclusion / extrapolation-model triad above; the three-convention-fix decomposition (point (b), Appendix A) remains in the report as an internal audit artifact, not as the principal driver of remaining magnitude uncertainty.

15.4 individual-species RCR — river/ocean companion screen

Section 11.5.4 added a most-sensitive-species screen for the sediment benthic dataset. This subsection completes SPEC 1e-iv’s companion request for the water compartments where exposure is quantitative (river, ocean): the single most sensitive species per ERM, plus the individual-species risk characterization ratio RCR = EED / lowest-species EC, reported as an early-warning companion to the community-HC5 RQ already characterized in Sections 7/12. This is placed here, after Section 15.3, because it is the first point in document execution order at which every matrix’s hazard (haz/haz_ocean) and EED (eed_boot/eed_boot_ocean) objects all exist together.

Per Thuy-Dung et al. (2026), an individual-species RCR>1 can precede a derivable community-HC5 RQ signal by roughly a decade — the table above is therefore read as an early-warning companion, not a substitute for the community-HC5 RQ already reported in Sections 7 and 12. Appendices

The three appendices below hold convention-validation history, implementation-validation detail, and exploratory/non-quantitative sediment material that support the results above but are not needed to read them. Every number in this document – including here – is produced by the same live code as the main body; nothing here is retyped. SPEC-numbered labels below are preserved from docs/CHANGELOG_hoffman_revisions.md, which is the authoritative provenance record for each revision.

Appendix A: Convention-validation history

The differential-slope convention (length, area, volume, mass; Sections 5, 7) is the current basis throughout this report. This appendix quantifies the effect of each prior convention error that the SPEC 1/1b/3b/3c revisions corrected, and is why no number in the report body should be read as the pre-fix (≈10⁷, Food Dilution) legacy magnitude.

A.1 all-matrix CF before/after (legacy cumulative vs. corrected differential)

Reruns the correction-factor convention check of Section 5.1 for all three matrices at once, comparing the legacy (cumulative slope passed as differential), corrected fit-only, and corrected structural-SD CF distributions side by side.

Show the code 
cf_case_summary <- function(matrix_label, cpsd_fit, combined_cf_current,
                            Lmin_use, Lmax_use, current_slope_draws, n = n_mc) {
  set.seed(4000 + nchar(matrix_label))
  cumulative_draws <- alpha_dist(mu = cpsd_fit$a_cpsd, sd = cpsd_fit$se_a_cpsd, n = n, structural_sd = 0)
  differential_fit_draws <- alpha_dist(mu = cpsd_fit$a_psd, sd = cpsd_fit$se_a_psd, n = n, structural_sd = 0)
  legacy_cf <- correction_factor(
    a = cumulative_draws,
    L_meas_min = Lmin_use,
    L_meas_max = Lmax_use,
    L_tar_min = 1,
    L_tar_max = 5000,
    slope_convention = "differential"
  )
  corrected_fit_cf <- correction_factor(
    a = differential_fit_draws,
    L_meas_min = Lmin_use,
    L_meas_max = Lmax_use,
    L_tar_min = 1,
    L_tar_max = 5000,
    slope_convention = "differential"
  )
  tibble::tibble(
    Matrix = matrix_label,
    Case = c("Legacy cumulative slope passed as differential", "Corrected differential slope, fit SE only", "Corrected differential slope plus structural SD"),
    Slope_p50 = c(median(cumulative_draws), median(differential_fit_draws), median(current_slope_draws)),
    CF_p05 = c(quantile(legacy_cf, 0.05), quantile(corrected_fit_cf, 0.05), quantile(combined_cf_current, 0.05)),
    CF_p50 = c(median(legacy_cf), median(corrected_fit_cf), median(combined_cf_current)),
    CF_p95 = c(quantile(legacy_cf, 0.95), quantile(corrected_fit_cf, 0.95), quantile(combined_cf_current, 0.95))
  )
}

cf_before_after_all <- dplyr::bind_rows(
  cf_case_summary("River water", cpsd_fit_all, combined_cf_pooled, L_meas_min_use, L_meas_max_use, alpha),
  cf_case_summary("Sediment", cpsd_fit_sed_all, combined_cf_sed, L_meas_min_use_sed, L_meas_max_use_sed, alpha_sed),
  cf_case_summary("Ocean water", cpsd_fit_ocean_all, combined_cf_ocean, L_meas_min_ocean, L_meas_max_ocean, alpha_ocean)
)

)

A.2 Food Dilution RQ decomposition (legacy cumulative vs. corrected differential a.v/a.sa)

The Section 13 table above (SPEC 1, from the prior revision) shows that the length-slope convention fix changes the exposure correction factor. The volume/area-slope fix in this revision (SPEC 1b) is a separate, hazard-side-only effect: it does not touch correction_factor() or the EED at all, only the particle-trait alignment used inside pSSD++ (a.v.*, a.sa.*, a.m.*). To make that effect auditable, this section re-runs the pSSD++ hazard alignment and 1D risk characterization for each matrix with a “legacy” parameter set in which only a.v/a.sa/a.m are reverted to the pre-fix cumulative-slope values (legacy_cumulative_av_params(), R/mp_risk_utils.R) — holding the length slope, R.ave, exposure (EED), and everything else fixed — so the entire before/after RQ change in this table is attributable to the volume/area-slope convention alone.

Show the code 
spec1b_decomposition <- dplyr::bind_rows(
  dplyr::mutate(risk_summary_legacy_river, Matrix = "River water", Case = "Legacy cumulative a.v/a.sa"),
  dplyr::mutate(risk_summary_pooled,        Matrix = "River water", Case = "Corrected differential a.v/a.sa"),
  dplyr::mutate(risk_summary_legacy_sed,    Matrix = "Sediment",    Case = "Legacy cumulative a.v/a.sa"),
  dplyr::mutate(risk_summary_sed,           Matrix = "Sediment",    Case = "Corrected differential a.v/a.sa"),
  dplyr::mutate(risk_summary_legacy_ocean,  Matrix = "Ocean water", Case = "Legacy cumulative a.v/a.sa"),
  dplyr::mutate(risk_summary_ocean,         Matrix = "Ocean water", Case = "Corrected differential a.v/a.sa")
) |>
  dplyr::select(Matrix, Case, ERM, HCx, RQ_p50, RQ_p95, P_exceed) |>
  dplyr::arrange(Matrix, ERM, HCx, dplyr::desc(Case))

The volume/area-slope correction is confined to the hazard alignment: exposure concentrations, the EED, and combined_cf/combined_cf_sed/combined_cf_ocean are numerically identical between the legacy and corrected rows above (they are not recomputed in this section). The magnitude of the collapse in the Food Dilution HC5 median RQ therefore isolates the volume-slope error described in SPEC 1b, consistent with the mean-particle-volume sensitivity calculation in the spec (a.v = 0.76 vs. 1.68 implying an ~4-6 million-fold difference in mean particle volume, and a comparable inverse effect on the Food Dilution threshold and RQ). Correction (SPEC 3c): Tissue Translocation is not expected to be insensitive to this fix overall — it is insensitive to the volume slope specifically (its dose model is not volume-weighted), but it is materially sensitive to the surface-area slope reverted in the same combined row above, because Tissue Translocation/oxidative-stress alignment is surface-area-weighted; see Section 14.1 for the row that isolates a.sa alone and the corrected narrative. Sediment caveat (SPEC 1d): the Sediment rows above are illustrative/non-quantitative — their exposure concentration is not a genuine particles/kg-dry-weight value (Section 11.3.0) — so while they are retained here to confirm the volume/area-slope-convention mechanism holds across matrices, the absolute RQ magnitudes for Sediment must not be read as real risk estimates (Section 11.4.0, 15.3).

A.3 RQ decomposition — one-at-a-time convention reversions

Two convention fixes, made at different times, both change the Food Dilution risk quotient, for different reasons: (i) the exposure-side power-law correction factor (correction_factor(), Section 5.1) rescales the measured concentration; (ii) the hazard-side length-slope alignment (alpha.freshwater/alpha.marine/alpha.sediment.freshwater inside pSSD++, fixed in the prior revision) changes how toxicity endpoints are aligned to a common particle-size basis; and (iii) the hazard-side volume/area-slope alignment (a.v.*/a.sa.*/a.m.*, SPEC 1b, this revision) changes the polydisperse mean particle volume used by the Food Dilution dose model. This section isolates each of the three as a one-at-a-time sensitivity relative to the fully corrected river-water baseline, reverting exactly one piece to its legacy (pre-fix) form while holding the other two at their corrected values. River water is used as the representative matrix (the all-matrix table in Section 13.1 already shows (iii) holds for sediment and ocean water too).

Show the code 
# (i) Exposure correction factor reverted to legacy (cumulative-as-differential),
# hazard (haz) held at the fully corrected values. No pSSD rerun needed: this
# only recomputes the corrected-concentration draws with the legacy CF vector
# already computed above (A.1, legacy_cf_river).
set.seed(9202)
C_legacycf_draws <- monitoring_pooled_scope |>
  dplyr::mutate(idx = dplyr::row_number()) |>
  tidyr::crossing(draw = seq_len(3000)) |>
  dplyr::mutate(
    cf          = sample(legacy_cf_river, size = dplyr::n(), replace = TRUE),
    C_corrected = C_measured_pL * cf
  )
C_sample_median_legacycf <- C_legacycf_draws |>
  dplyr::group_by(sample_id) |>
  dplyr::summarise(C_corr_med = stats::median(C_corrected), .groups = "drop")
eed_boot_legacycf_river <- bootstrap_eed(C_sample_median_legacycf$C_corr_med, n_boot = n_boot, probs = c(0.5, 0.95))
set.seed(9307)
risk_summary_legacycf_river <- summarize_rq(draw_rq_mc1d(haz_pooled, eed_boot_legacycf_river$q50, n_risk = n_risk))
Show the code 
# (iii) reuses risk_summary_legacy_river from Section 13.1 (a.v/a.sa/a.m all
# reverted together, length alpha and exposure corrected); (iv, SPEC 3c) isolates
# a.sa alone. Both ERMs (Food Dilution and Tissue Translocation) are reported,
# since SPEC 3c found the prior Food-Dilution-only table masked how the a.sa
# reversion affects the surface-area-weighted Tissue Translocation ERM.
rq_decomp_river_raw <- dplyr::bind_rows(
  dplyr::mutate(risk_summary_pooled,                 Contribution_reverted = "None (fully corrected, this revision)"),
  dplyr::mutate(risk_summary_legacycf_river,         Contribution_reverted = "(i) Exposure correction factor -> legacy cumulative-as-differential"),
  dplyr::mutate(risk_summary_legacy_alpha_river,      Contribution_reverted = "(ii) Hazard length-slope alignment -> legacy cumulative-as-differential"),
  dplyr::mutate(risk_summary_legacy_river,           Contribution_reverted = "(iii) Hazard volume+area+mass-slope alignment -> legacy cumulative (SPEC 1b)"),
  dplyr::mutate(risk_summary_legacy_asa_river,        Contribution_reverted = "(iv) Hazard surface-area-slope alignment ONLY -> legacy cumulative (SPEC 3c)")
) |>
  dplyr::filter(HCx == 5) |>
  dplyr::select(ERM, Contribution_reverted, RQ_p50, RQ_p95, P_exceed)

rq_decomp_corrected_baseline <- rq_decomp_river_raw |>
  dplyr::filter(Contribution_reverted == "None (fully corrected, this revision)") |>
  dplyr::select(ERM, RQ_p50_corrected = RQ_p50)

rq_decomp_river <- rq_decomp_river_raw |>
  dplyr::left_join(rq_decomp_corrected_baseline, by = "ERM") |>
  dplyr::mutate(ratio_vs_corrected = RQ_p50 / RQ_p50_corrected) |>
  dplyr::select(-RQ_p50_corrected) |>
  dplyr::arrange(ERM, dplyr::desc(Contribution_reverted == "None (fully corrected, this revision)"))

Reading the table: the ratio_vs_corrected column is how much larger (or smaller) each ERM’s HC5 median RQ becomes if only that one convention error were reintroduced, relative to that same ERM’s own fully-corrected baseline. Because this is a 100-replicate development-scale run (production budgets are ≥1000 per the deliverables checklist), the exact ratios should be treated as directionally informative rather than final, and re-checked at full budget before external release.

SPEC 3c correction to the Tissue Translocation attribution. Tissue Translocation P(RQ>1) at HC5 moves from 68.2% under the legacy (cumulative-as-differential) length-slope alignment to 16.4% under the corrected alignment, confirming the length-slope fix (prior revision) is one material driver of the Tissue Translocation shift. However, the volume+area+mass reversion also moves Tissue Translocation P(RQ>1) materially, from 99.7% (legacy) to 16.4% (corrected) — a change of this size is not “essentially unchanged,” and a prior version of this narrative incorrectly claimed it was. Isolating the surface-area slope alone (a.sa reverted to legacy cumulative, a.v/a.m/alpha/exposure held corrected) reproduces most of that shift: P(RQ>1) is 99.6% under the legacy a.sa alone, versus 16.4% corrected. This is mechanistically expected: unlike Food Dilution (volume-weighted), Tissue Translocation/oxidative-stress alignment is surface-area-weighted, so it is directly sensitive to the a.sa correction (cumulative a.sa ≈ 1.3 → differential a.sa ≈ 2.3 for river water; Section 13.1/7.2) in the same way Food Dilution is sensitive to a.v. Tissue Translocation is not literally insensitive to SPEC 1b — it is insensitive to the volume slope specifically (because dose is not volume-weighted) but sensitive to the area slope (because dose is area-weighted). Corrected qualitative conclusion: after both the length-slope and area-slope fixes, river-water Tissue Translocation HC5 is below threshold at the median (RQ ≈ 0.022, P(RQ>1) ≈ 16.4%), while Food Dilution (RQ ≈ 0.279, P(RQ>1) ≈ 36.3%) remains risk-dominant.

Appendix C: Sediment (non-quantitative) and exploratory diagnostics

Sediment is excluded from the headline risk conclusion (Section 11) because its exposure concentration is not a genuine particles/kg-dry-weight value. The material below extends the sediment analysis for methods/illustrative purposes only – none of it should be combined with the Section 11 exposure figures to produce a sediment risk quotient.

C.1 sediment PSD-shift sensitivity (illustrative; production-gated)

This subsection implements sediment_psd_shift_sensitivity() (R/mp_risk_utils.R), which re-runs the full sediment hazard alignment (matrix_function() → run_pssd_pipeline() → build_haz_df()) across a grid of progressively finer sediment PSDs, representing continued in-situ fragmentation, and reports how the derived Food Dilution and Tissue Translocation HC5 respond as more particles fall below benthic bioaccessibility limits. A genuine hazard-side response (not merely a rescaled exposure number) requires this full re-run, because steepening the PSD changes the simulated particle-size population that pSSD++’s ingestible/translocatable size-gating operates on — i.e., it can change which species clear the bioaccessibility threshold and enter the SSD.

Gating. This sensitivity is gated on sediment_concentration_is_quantitative (currently FALSE, SPEC 1d-i). While FALSE it is run as an illustrative/methods demonstration only — every row below is explicitly labeled non-quantitative and excluded from the risk conclusion, analogous to the existing single-slope↔︎piecewise CF bound (SPEC 2b, Section 13.3). It becomes a production sensitivity feeding the sediment RQ range only once that flag is set TRUE.

What is not transplanted. Thuy-Dung et al.’s kfrag/shell-geometry fragmentation model is calibrated to polymer-coated-fertilizer prills with 7-year field data — a single, known-age, known-geometry polymer system — not the heterogeneous mixed-polymer sediment microplastics of unknown age sampled here. Rather than fit a kinetic rate that would not transfer to this dataset, the size-shift below is parameterized as an explicit, cited scenario grid: an added shift to the differential length/area/volume/mass slopes (alpha/a.v/a.sa/a.m.sediment.freshwater, positive-alpha convention — larger values are steeper/finer), applied identically across all four size metrics as a simplifying assumption (fragmentation is assumed to shift all size metrics proportionally).

Show the code 
# 0 = no shift (baseline -- an internal consistency check against
# Section 11.4's production sediment HC5, subject to Monte Carlo/parallel RNG
# noise since no fixed seed is threaded through PSSDplusplus's parallel
# workers); +0.75 and +1.5 = illustrative moderate/substantial in-situ
# fragmentation scenarios. Uses the *same* n_boot/sim/cv_uf/rmore_method as the
# production sediment call (Section 11.2/11.3) -- no analytical-budget change.
sed_psd_shift_grid <- c(0, 0.75, 1.5)

sed_psd_shift_tbl <- sediment_psd_shift_sensitivity(
  param_values_base = param_values_sed,
  slope_shift_grid  = sed_psd_shift_grid,
  tox_data_sed      = tox_data_sed,
  n_boot            = n_boot,
  cv_uf             = 0.5,
  rmore_method      = "lognormal",
  sim               = 30,
  num_cores         = parallel::detectCores() - 2,
  quantitative_flag = sediment_concentration_is_quantitative
)

  sed_psd_shift_tbl |> dplyr::filter(HCx == 5),
  digits = 3,
  caption = paste0(

    sediment_concentration_is_quantitative,
    " -- while FALSE, every row is non-quantitative/illustrative and excluded from the risk conclusion (SPEC 1d)."
  )
)

sed_psd_shift_plot

Across the illustrative grid from no shift to the largest tested shift (1.5), the derived median Food Dilution HC5 changes by a factor of 0.01x and the Tissue Translocation HC5 by a factor of 0.99x (both relative to the unshifted grid point) — i.e., at this development-scale budget the rendered HC5 rose rather than fell as the illustrative PSD was shifted finer, the opposite of the direction the mechanism in Section 11.5.1 would naively suggest. This is read as evidence of SSD instability, not as a directional finding. The sediment benthic SSD is built from only 9 species; shifting which particles clear the ingestible/translocatable size gate can change which one or two species anchor the low-percentile HC5 extrapolation, and with this few species that anchor can swap non-monotonically rather than shift smoothly — exactly the small/unstable-SSD concern Thuy-Dung et al. (2026) raise as the motivation for tracking individual-species risk (Section 11.5.4) alongside a community HC5 extrapolated from so few species. This table and plot remain non-quantitative while sediment_concentration_is_quantitative is FALSE, regardless of direction: no number in this subsection should be combined with the Section 11.4 exposure figures to produce a sediment RQ, and the illustrative grid should not be read as showing that further fragmentation lowers sediment risk.

C.2 time-varying bioaccessibility (documented; future enhancement)

The existing pSSD++ bioaccessibility alignment already used throughout this report (food dilution → gut-volume alignment; translocation truncated at the 500 µm upper tissue-translocation limit, both inside run_pssd_pipeline()/PSSDplusplus::MC_sim_align_parallel()) is the same machinery this extension would reuse — it is a size-dependent gate, not a new framework. TODO (not implemented in this revision): make that gate explicitly time-dependent by (1) parameterizing the sediment PSD shift in Section 11.5.2 as a function of residence time t rather than an unordered scenario index (e.g., a size-shift schedule Δα(t) informed by, but not equal to, Thuy-Dung et al.’s doubling-time concept — explicitly not their prill-specific kfrag, per Section 11.5.2’s non-transplant note); (2) re-running run_pssd_pipeline() at each time step exactly as Section 11.5.2 already does at each scenario point, so smaller-mouthed/smaller-gut benthic species progressively clear the ingestible/translocatable size gate as the bed fragments; (3) reporting HC5(t) and, where a genuine sediment concentration becomes available (SPEC 1d), RCR(t), as a trajectory rather than a single value. This is left as a clearly-scoped TODO rather than implemented here because it requires a defensible time axis (a residence-time or age-of-deposition estimate for this sediment dataset) that does not currently exist in the source data — fabricating one would misrepresent the method’s evidentiary basis. Section 11.5.2’s scenario grid is the same computational step without the time axis, and can be converted into this trajectory once residence-time data are available.

C.3 Water–sediment PSD coherence (interpretive)

    y = "Empirical cumulative probability",
    title = "River water vs sediment particle-size spectrum"
  ) +
  ggplot2::theme_minimal(base_size = 18)

This water-sediment comparison is interpretive inference, not a new correction. Under Hoffman et al. (2026), sediment and water PSDs may be linked by size sorting: loss of larger dense particles from the water column should correspond to sediment enrichment in those sizes. The plot and table are retained as a coherence check to guide future transport-correction work.

15.5 C1 number-snapshot guardrail

The C1 consolidation pass (structure/presentation only; see docs/CHANGELOG_hoffman_revisions.md) must not change any live number. This chunk captures every headline value the C1 spec designates as protected – river/sediment/ocean CF medians + 90% CIs, river/ocean EED q50/q95, the canonical 9-row C-PSD slope table, the SPEC Q1 max|delta a_cpsd|, the slope-structural-SD sensitivity grid, and river/ocean 1D + MC2D risk summaries – into data_output/c1_number_snapshot.json the first time it renders (file does not yet exist), and on every subsequent render re-derives the same values and asserts they still match that baseline within 1e-8 (exact equality for integers/n_bins). A failure here means a structural edit silently moved a number and must be treated as a stop-and-fix, not a value to update casually – see docs/CHANGELOG_hoffman_revisions.md before touching the baseline file itself.

Show the code 
c1_snapshot_path <- file.path(proj_root, "data_output", "c1_number_snapshot.json")

build_c1_snapshot <- function() {
  slope_tbl <- this_study_length_alpha |>
    dplyr::filter(Source == "This study matrix/shape") |>
    dplyr::arrange(PSD_ID) |>
    dplyr::transmute(
      PSD_ID, Matrix, Shape,
      a_cpsd = round(a_cpsd, 10), a_psd = round(a_psd, 10),
      lod_low_um = round(lod_low_um, 6), lod_high_um = round(lod_high_um, 6),
      n_bins = as.integer(n_bins)
    )

  rq_tbl <- function(x) x |> dplyr::arrange(ERM, HCx) |>
    dplyr::transmute(ERM, HCx, P_exceed = round(P_exceed, 10),
                      RQ_p50 = round(RQ_p50, 10), RQ_p95 = round(RQ_p95, 10))

  mc2d_tbl <- function(x) x |> dplyr::arrange(ERM, HCx) |>
    dplyr::transmute(ERM, HCx, P_exceed_med = round(P_exceed_med, 10),
                      RQ_p50_med = round(RQ_p50_med, 10), RQ_p95_med = round(RQ_p95_med, 10))

  list(
    cf_river  = list(p50 = unname(round(median(combined_cf), 10)),
                      p05 = unname(round(quantile(combined_cf, 0.05), 10)),
                      p95 = unname(round(quantile(combined_cf, 0.95), 10))),
    cf_sed    = list(p50 = unname(round(median(combined_cf_sed), 10)),
                      p05 = unname(round(quantile(combined_cf_sed, 0.05), 10)),
                      p95 = unname(round(quantile(combined_cf_sed, 0.95), 10))),
    cf_ocean  = list(p50 = unname(round(median(combined_cf_ocean), 10)),
                      p05 = unname(round(quantile(combined_cf_ocean, 0.05), 10)),
                      p95 = unname(round(quantile(combined_cf_ocean, 0.95), 10))),
    eed_river = list(q50 = unname(round(median(eed_boot$q50), 10)),
                      q95 = unname(round(median(eed_boot$q95), 10))),
    eed_ocean = list(q50 = unname(round(median(eed_boot_ocean$q50), 10)),
                      q95 = unname(round(median(eed_boot_ocean$q95), 10))),
    slope_table         = slope_tbl,
    spec_q1_max_delta    = unname(round(q1_max_abs_delta_a_cpsd, 10)),
    hoffman_sensitivity = hoffman_slope_sensitivity |>
      dplyr::arrange(structural_sd, ERM) |>
      dplyr::transmute(ERM, structural_sd, P_exceed_med = round(P_exceed_med, 10),
                        RQ_p50_med = round(RQ_p50_med, 10), RQ_p95_med = round(RQ_p95_med, 10)),
    rq_1d_river  = rq_tbl(risk_summary),
    rq_1d_sed    = rq_tbl(risk_summary_sed),
    rq_1d_ocean  = rq_tbl(risk_summary_ocean),
    mc2d_river   = mc2d_tbl(mc2d_summary),
    mc2d_ocean   = mc2d_tbl(mc2d_ocean_summary)
  )
}

snap_current <- build_c1_snapshot()

if (n_boot < 1000) {
  message("C1 guardrail: SKIPPED -- n_boot = ", n_boot, " (< 1000, dev-scale iteration render). ",
          "The byte-identical number check is only meaningful at the production budget; ",
          "re-render with n_boot = 1000 before treating this as a release-gate pass.")
} else if (!file.exists(c1_snapshot_path)) {
  jsonlite::write_json(snap_current, c1_snapshot_path, auto_unbox = TRUE, digits = 15, pretty = TRUE)
  message("C1 guardrail: baseline snapshot written to ", c1_snapshot_path,
          " (this is the pre-C1 baseline -- do not regenerate once C1 edits begin).")
} else {
  snap_baseline <- jsonlite::read_json(c1_snapshot_path, simplifyVector = TRUE)

  compare_numeric <- function(cur, base, path = "") {
    if (is.list(cur) && !is.data.frame(cur)) {
      nm <- names(cur)
      unlist(lapply(nm, function(n) compare_numeric(cur[[n]], base[[n]], paste0(path, "$", n))))
    } else if (is.data.frame(cur)) {
      base_df <- as.data.frame(base)
      stopifnot2 <- vapply(setdiff(names(cur), c("PSD_ID","Matrix","Shape","ERM","HCx")), function(col) {
        max(abs(cur[[col]] - base_df[[col]]), na.rm = TRUE)
      }, numeric(1))
      setNames(stopifnot2, paste0(path, "$", names(stopifnot2)))
    } else {
      setNames(abs(as.numeric(cur) - as.numeric(base)), path)
    }
  }

  diffs <- unlist(compare_numeric(snap_current, snap_baseline))
  tol <- 1e-8
  bad <- diffs[!is.na(diffs) & diffs >= tol]

  if (length(bad) > 0) {
    print(sort(bad, decreasing = TRUE))
    # Diagnostic print() output can be lost if the render halts before the
    # chunk's buffer flushes; also write it to a plain file so a failure is
    # debuggable from the last render alone.
    writeLines(
      c(paste0("C1 guardrail FAILURE -- ", length(bad), " value(s) exceeded tol = ", tol),
        capture.output(print(sort(bad, decreasing = TRUE))),
        "",
        "-- current --",
        capture.output(str(snap_current, max.level = 2)),
        "",
        "-- baseline --",
        capture.output(str(snap_baseline, max.level = 2))),
      file.path(proj_root, "data_output", "c1_guardrail_failure_diagnostic.txt")
    )
  }
  message("C1 guardrail: max|delta| across ", length(diffs), " tracked values = ",
          format(max(diffs, na.rm = TRUE), scientific = TRUE))
  stopifnot(
    "C1 guardrail FAILED: a structural edit changed a protected number -- see printed diagnostic above" =
      length(bad) == 0
  )
  message("C1 guardrail: all tracked values match the pre-C1 baseline within ", tol, ".")
}

16.1 SI Tables S5–S11: particle properties, fit statistics, and concentration rescaling

Supplementary tables reporting the particle properties underlying, the fitted parameters and fit statistics of every particle-size probability distribution fitted in this report, and the concentration rescaling for every monitoring sample, formatted after Kooi et al. (2021, Water Research 198:117011, SI Tables S3–S4). River water (freshwater) is reported separately (Tables S5, S7) from ocean water and beach sand (Tables S6, S8). Table S9 provides every sample’s location, PSD model, slope, correction factor, and rescaled concentration; river samples appear under both river-specific and pooled-river scenarios. Table S10 summarizes those values by matrix and PSD model, and Table S11 additionally breaks them down by location. Ocean-water and beach-sand samples are shown under their available pooled-matrix model. Each C-PSD row reports the fitted window [xmin, xmax) selected by the Segur et al. (2026) two-step LOD algorithm (or fixed by the length/width-consistent volume bounds, Section 4.2.3; area fits use a fixed lower search bound, Section 4.2.2), the cumulative slope αCPSD and log10 intercept b of log10 N(≥x) = b + αCPSD log10 x (± OLS standard error), the differential BN-PSD slope aPSD = αCPSD − 1 (same SE; the Kooi et al. positive PDF exponent is α = |aPSD|), R², and the number of populated bins fitted. Lower/upper quartiles are the 25th/75th percentiles. Mass is volume × polymer-resolved density (Section 3.1.1), reported in µg. Fits are summarized from the fit objects above, not refit – except the depth-stratified river length fits, which are deterministically refit here (identical call to Section 10.0) to retain intercepts and bin counts, and checked against depth_shape_fits.

Show the code 
source(file.path(proj_root, "R", "si_pdf_tables.R"))

  si_particle_properties(raw_particles_ocean, "Ocean water"),
  si_particle_properties(raw_particles_sed,   "Beach sand")
)

# ---- C-PSD fit parameters (Kooi et al. 2021 Table S4 analogue) ----
metric_spec <- list(
  Length = list(col = "length_um", bin = 5,          unit = "Length (µm)"),
  Area   = list(col = "area_um2",  bin = 500,        unit = "Projected area (µm²)"),
  Volume = list(col = "V_um3",     bin = vol_bin_um, unit = "Volume (µm³)")
)
pooled_rows <- function(fits_by_metric, df, matrix_label) {
  dplyr::bind_rows(lapply(names(fits_by_metric), function(m) {
    si_cpsd_fit_rows(fits_by_metric[[m]], df, metric_spec[[m]]$col, metric_spec[[m]]$bin,
                     matrix_label, metric_spec[[m]]$unit, "Pooled (all sites)")
  }))
}

  dplyr::inner_join(depth_shape_fits, by = c("sample_depth_general", "shape"))
stopifnot("SI depth-stratified refit must reproduce Section 10.0 slopes" =
            nrow(depth_check) == nrow(depth_shape_fits) &&

      `Fit statistics` = sprintf("ΔAIC vs. single slope = %.1f", piecewise_delta_aic)

  )
stopifnot(
  nrow(si_rescaling_samples) == 2 * nrow(monitoring) + nrow(monitoring_ocean) + nrow(monitoring_sed),
  all(!is.na(si_rescaling_samples$Location)),
  all(!is.na(si_rescaling_samples$`PSD model`)),
  all(is.finite(si_rescaling_samples$`CF (median)`)),
  all(is.finite(si_rescaling_samples$`Reported concentration (median)`)),
  all(is.finite(si_rescaling_samples$`C-PSD-valid concentration (median)`)),
  all(is.finite(si_rescaling_samples$`Rescaled concentration (median)`))
)
si_rescaling_summary <- si_rescaling_matrix_summary(
  si_rescaling_samples,
  group_cols = c("Matrix", "PSD model", "Concentration unit")
)
si_rescaling_location_summary <- si_rescaling_matrix_summary(
  si_rescaling_samples,
  group_cols = c("Matrix", "Location", "PSD model", "Concentration unit")
)

# Full-precision numeric versions (formatted versions go to the manuscript workbook)
si_csv_dir <- file.path(proj_root, "data_output", "si_pdf_tables")
dir.create(si_csv_dir, showWarnings = FALSE)
for (nm in c("si_props_river", "si_props_ocean_sed", "si_fits_river", "si_fits_ocean_sed",
             "si_rescaling_samples", "si_rescaling_summary", "si_rescaling_location_summary")) {
  utils::write.csv(get(nm), file.path(si_csv_dir, paste0(nm, ".csv")), row.names = FALSE,
                   fileEncoding = "UTF-8")
}

# Word version of Tables S5-S11, with a variable-definitions section
si_docx_path <- si_write_docx(
  file.path(proj_root, "docs", "SI_Tables_S5-S11_PDF_fits_and_rescaling.docx"),
  props_river = si_props_river, props_ocean_sed = si_props_ocean_sed,
  fits_river = si_fits_river, fits_ocean_sed = si_fits_ocean_sed,
  alt_river = si_alt_models_river, alt_ocean_sed = si_alt_models_ocean_sed,
  rescaling_samples = si_rescaling_samples,
  rescaling_summary = si_rescaling_summary,
  rescaling_location_summary = si_rescaling_location_summary,
  n_river = nrow(raw_particles_river), n_ocean = nrow(raw_particles_ocean),
  n_sed = nrow(raw_particles_sed)
)

17. Single-matrix variants of multi-matrix figures

Every figure above that overlays two or more matrices (river, ocean, sediment) in one panel is reproduced here as separate single-matrix variants – river-only, ocean-only, and/or sediment-only, whichever matrices that particular figure actually contains. Each variant reuses the exact data and geometry of its combined source figure, filtered to one matrix, and is saved alongside the original under a _river/_ocean/_sediment filename suffix. Matrices that a given combined figure never included (e.g., sediment in the river/ocean-only comparisons below) have no corresponding variant produced, rather than a fabricated empty one.

17.1 Figure 1 / cpsd_river_ocean_facet_plot (river, ocean)

Show the code 
build_cpsd_river_ocean_variant <- function(sel_locations, mat_label) {
  pts <- dplyr::filter(cpsd_loc_points_ro, location %in% sel_locations)
  lns <- dplyr::filter(cpsd_loc_lines_ro,  location %in% sel_locations)
  pal <- loc_palette_ro_used[names(loc_palette_ro_used) %in% sel_locations]

  p <- ggplot2::ggplot() +
    ggplot2::geom_point(
      data = dplyr::filter(pts, !in_lod),
      ggplot2::aes(x = log10(L_low), y = logN, color = location),
      size = 0.7, alpha = 0.05, shape = 16
    ) +
    ggplot2::geom_point(
      data = dplyr::filter(pts, in_lod),
      ggplot2::aes(x = log10(L_low), y = logN, color = location),
      size = 1.3, alpha = 0.75, shape = 16
    ) +
    ggplot2::geom_ribbon(
      data = lns, ggplot2::aes(x = log10(L_low), ymin = logN_lo, ymax = logN_hi, fill = location),
      alpha = 0.12, color = NA
    ) +
    ggplot2::geom_line(
      data = lns, ggplot2::aes(x = log10(L_low), y = logN_fit, color = location),
      linewidth = 0.9, alpha = 0.9
    ) +
    ggplot2::facet_grid(shape ~ metric, scales = "free_x", labeller = ggplot2::label_value) +
    ggplot2::coord_cartesian(ylim = y_range_ro) +
    ggplot2::scale_x_continuous(breaks = int_breaks, labels = function(x) round(x)) +
    ggplot2::scale_y_continuous(breaks = int_breaks, labels = function(x) round(x)) +
    ggplot2::scale_color_manual(values = pal, name = NULL) +
    ggplot2::scale_fill_manual(values = pal, guide = "none") +
    ggplot2::guides(color = ggplot2::guide_legend(override.aes = list(alpha = 1, size = 3))) +
    ggplot2::labs(
      x = expression(log[10] * "(size)"), y = expression(log[10] * (N("">=L))),
      title    = paste0("C-PSD power-law fits — ", mat_label, " only, by shape and size metric"),
      subtitle = "Solid lines + ribbon = fit ± 95% CI within Segur LOD window. Faded points = outside LOD."
    ) +
    ggplot2::theme_minimal(base_size = 18) +
    ggplot2::theme(
      legend.position = "bottom",
      panel.border    = ggplot2::element_rect(color = "gray80", fill = NA, linewidth = 0.4),
      strip.text      = ggplot2::element_text(face = "bold", size = 10)
    )

  ggsave(p, filename = paste0("figures/cpsd_river_ocean_facet_plot_", tolower(mat_label), ".png"),
         width = 12, height = 8, dpi = 300)
  p
}

build_cpsd_river_ocean_variant(locations, "river")
Show the code 
build_cpsd_river_ocean_variant("Ocean",   "ocean")

build_slopes_metrics_variant <- function(mat) {
  dat <- dplyr::filter(matrix_slopes_all_metrics, matrix == mat)
  p <- ggplot2::ggplot(dat, ggplot2::aes(x = group, y = a_cpsd, color = matrix)) +
    ggplot2::geom_point(size = 4) +
    ggplot2::geom_errorbar(
      ggplot2::aes(ymin = a_cpsd - se_a_cpsd, ymax = a_cpsd + se_a_cpsd), width = 0.2, linewidth = 0.8
    ) +
    ggplot2::facet_wrap(~ metric, nrow = 1) +
    ggplot2::scale_color_manual(values = matrix_pal_slopes, guide = "none") +
    ggplot2::labs(
      x = if (mat == "River") "River location" else NULL,
      y = expression(italic(a)[cpsd]),
      title    = paste0("C-PSD slope by size metric — ", mat, " only"),
      subtitle = "Error bars = ±1 SE."
    ) +
    ggplot2::theme_minimal(base_size = 20) +
    ggplot2::theme(
      panel.border = ggplot2::element_rect(color = "gray85", fill = NA, linewidth = 0.4),
      strip.text   = ggplot2::element_text(face = "bold"),
      axis.text.x  = ggplot2::element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1)
    )
  ggsave(p, filename = paste0("figures/cpsd_slopes_all_metrics_plot_", tolower(mat), ".png"),
         width = 9, height = 6, dpi = 300)
  p
}
invisible(lapply(c("River", "Sediment", "Ocean"), build_slopes_metrics_variant))

build_single_vs_piecewise_variant <- function(mat) {
  df_f             <- dplyr::filter(df_both_ms,        Matrix == mat)
  pred_single_f    <- dplyr::filter(pred_single_ms,     Matrix == mat)
  pred_piecewise_f <- dplyr::filter(pred_piecewise_ms,  Matrix == mat)
  lod_f            <- dplyr::filter(lod_bounds_both_ms, Matrix == mat)

  p <- ggplot2::ggplot(df_f, ggplot2::aes(x = log10(L_low), y = log10(N_ge), color = Matrix)) +
    ggplot2::geom_vline(
      data = lod_f, ggplot2::aes(xintercept = xval),
      linetype = "dotted", color = "gray55", linewidth = 0.6, inherit.aes = FALSE
    ) +
    ggplot2::geom_point(ggplot2::aes(alpha = in_lod), size = 1.3) +
    ggplot2::geom_ribbon(
      data = pred_single_f, ggplot2::aes(x = log10(L_low), ymin = logN_lo, ymax = logN_hi),
      inherit.aes = FALSE, fill = unname(matrix_pal_cpsd[mat]), alpha = 0.15
    ) +
    ggplot2::geom_ribbon(
      data = pred_piecewise_f, ggplot2::aes(x = log10(L_low), ymin = logN_lo, ymax = logN_hi, group = segment),
      inherit.aes = FALSE, fill = unname(matrix_pal_cpsd[mat]), alpha = 0.15
    ) +
    ggplot2::geom_line(
      data = pred_single_f, ggplot2::aes(x = log10(L_low), y = logN_fit),
      inherit.aes = FALSE, color = "grey15", alpha = 0.35, linewidth = 2.6
    ) +
    ggplot2::geom_line(
      data = pred_single_f, ggplot2::aes(x = log10(L_low), y = logN_fit, color = I(line_color)),
      inherit.aes = FALSE, linewidth = 1.4
    ) +
    ggplot2::geom_line(
      data = pred_piecewise_f, ggplot2::aes(x = log10(L_low), y = logN_fit, group = segment),
      inherit.aes = FALSE, color = "grey15", alpha = 0.35, linewidth = 2.6
    ) +
    ggplot2::geom_line(
      data = pred_piecewise_f, ggplot2::aes(x = log10(L_low), y = logN_fit, color = I(line_color), group = segment),
      inherit.aes = FALSE, linewidth = 1.4
    ) +
    ggplot2::facet_wrap(~ Model, nrow = 1) +
    ggplot2::scale_color_manual(values = matrix_pal_cpsd, guide = "none") +
    ggplot2::scale_alpha_manual(values = c(`TRUE` = 0.5, `FALSE` = 0.10), guide = "none") +
    ggplot2::labs(
      title    = paste0("Single-slope vs. two-segment C-PSD fit — ", mat, " only (particle length)"),
      subtitle = "Dotted = fitted LOD window boundaries. Faded points = outside LOD window.",
      x        = expression(log[10] * "(Length, " * mu * "m)"),
      y        = expression(log[10] * (N("">=L)))
    ) +
    ggplot2::theme_minimal(base_size = 14) +
    ggplot2::theme(
      strip.text   = ggplot2::element_text(face = "bold", size = 13),
      panel.border = ggplot2::element_rect(color = "gray80", fill = NA, linewidth = 0.4)
    )
  fname <- paste0("figures/cpsd_single_vs_piecewise_plot_", tolower(gsub(" water", "", mat)), ".png")
  ggsave(p, filename = fname, width = 10, height = 6, dpi = 300)
  p
}
invisible(lapply(names(cpsd_length_fits_by_matrix), build_single_vs_piecewise_variant))

build_rq_bounding_variant <- function(mat) {
  dat <- dplyr::filter(rq_bounding_tbl, Matrix == mat)
  p <- ggplot2::ggplot(dat, ggplot2::aes(x = Case, y = RQ_p50, color = ERM, shape = Case)) +
    ggplot2::geom_hline(yintercept = 1, linetype = "dashed", color = "gray40") +
    ggplot2::geom_errorbar(
      ggplot2::aes(ymin = RQ_p025, ymax = RQ_p975), width = 0.15, linewidth = 0.6,
      position = ggplot2::position_dodge(width = 0.4), na.rm = TRUE
    ) +
    ggplot2::geom_point(size = 3.5, position = ggplot2::position_dodge(width = 0.4)) +
    ggplot2::scale_y_log10(labels = scales::label_number()) +
    ggplot2::scale_color_manual(values = ERM_PALETTE, name = "ERM") +
    ggplot2::scale_shape_manual(values = c("Single-slope (production)" = 16, "Piecewise (bounding)" = 17), guide = "none") +
    ggplot2::labs(
      x = NULL, y = "HC5 median RQ [log10 scale]",
      title    = paste0("Food Dilution / Tissue Translocation HC5 RQ — ", mat, " only"),
      subtitle = "Dashed line = RQ = 1. Bars = 95% CI (2.5th-97.5th percentile of the 1D risk draws)."
    ) +

    ggplot2::theme(legend.position = "bottom", panel.border = ggplot2::element_rect(color = "gray80", fill = NA, linewidth = 0.4))

}

build_cf_bounding_variant <- function(mat) {
  dat <- cf_bounding_tbl |>
    dplyr::filter(Matrix == mat) |>
    dplyr::select(Matrix, `Single-slope (production)` = CF_single_slope_p50, `Piecewise (bounding)` = CF_piecewise) |>
    tidyr::pivot_longer(-Matrix, names_to = "Case", values_to = "CF") |>
    dplyr::mutate(Case = factor(Case, levels = c("Single-slope (production)", "Piecewise (bounding)")))

  p <- ggplot2::ggplot(dat, ggplot2::aes(x = Case, y = CF, color = Case)) +
    ggplot2::geom_line(ggplot2::aes(group = Matrix), color = "gray70", linewidth = 0.6) +
    ggplot2::geom_point(size = 4) +
    ggplot2::scale_y_log10(labels = scales::label_number()) +
    ggplot2::scale_color_manual(values = c("Single-slope (production)" = "#009E73", "Piecewise (bounding)" = "#D55E00"), guide = "none") +
    ggplot2::labs(
      x = NULL, y = "Correction factor (median) [log10 scale]",
      title = paste0("Single-slope vs. piecewise correction factor — ", mat, " only")
    ) +
    ggplot2::theme_minimal(base_size = 15) +

  ggsave(p, filename = paste0("figures/cf_bounding_plot_", tolower(gsub(" water", "", mat)), ".png"),

}

17.7 Figure S7 / alpha_comparison_plot (river/freshwater, ocean/marine)

Sediment is not part of this literature comparison at all (Methods, Section 2.3), so only river (Freshwater) and ocean (Marine) variants are produced. Zhao et al. (2026)’s pooled freshwater+marine meta-analysis point is, by its own source paper, not separable into a matrix and so does not appear in either single-matrix variant – consistent with the combined figure already labeling it “Mixed (unclassified)” rather than assigning it to one matrix.

Show the code 
build_alpha_forest_variant <- function(mat, mat_label) {
  dat <- alpha_forest_df |>
    dplyr::filter(Matrix == mat) |>
    dplyr::mutate(
      Source = factor(as.character(Source), levels = intersect(source_levels_bottom_to_top, as.character(Source))),
      x_pos  = as.numeric(Source) + offset
    )
  src_levels <- levels(dat$Source)

  p <- ggplot2::ggplot(dat, ggplot2::aes(x = x_pos, y = alpha_abs)) +
    ggplot2::geom_boxplot(
      data = dplyr::filter(dat, is_boxplot_row),
      ggplot2::aes(group = Source, fill = Matrix),
      color = "#009E73", alpha = 0.12, width = 0.55, outlier.shape = NA
    ) +
    ggplot2::geom_errorbar(
      data = dplyr::filter(dat, !is.na(se)),
      ggplot2::aes(ymin = alpha_abs - ci_mult * se, ymax = alpha_abs + ci_mult * se, color = Matrix),
      width = 0.10, linewidth = 0.6
    ) +
    ggplot2::geom_jitter(
      data = dplyr::filter(dat, is_boxplot_row),
      ggplot2::aes(color = Matrix, shape = Shape),
      width = 0.24, height = 0, alpha = 0.35, size = 1.6
    ) +
    ggplot2::geom_point(
      data = dplyr::filter(dat, !is_boxplot_row),
      ggplot2::aes(color = Matrix, shape = Shape),
      size = 3.2, alpha = 0.95
    ) +
    ggrepel::geom_text_repel(
      data = dplyr::filter(dat, !is.na(point_label)),
      ggplot2::aes(label = point_label),
      size = 3.0, max.overlaps = Inf, show.legend = FALSE,
      box.padding = 0.4, point.padding = 0.2, force = 2, force_pull = 0.5,
      min.segment.length = 0, segment.size = 0.3, segment.alpha = 0.5, seed = 1
    ) +
    ggplot2::scale_color_manual(values = matrix_pal_forest, drop = FALSE, guide = "none") +
    ggplot2::scale_fill_manual(values = matrix_pal_forest, drop = FALSE, guide = "none") +
    ggplot2::scale_shape_manual(values = shape_pal_forest, name = "Shape", drop = FALSE) +
    ggplot2::scale_x_continuous(
      breaks = seq_along(src_levels),
      labels = stringr::str_wrap(unname(source_labels_clean[src_levels]), width = 40),
      expand = ggplot2::expansion(add = 0.6)
    ) +
    ggplot2::coord_flip() +
    ggplot2::labs(
      x = NULL,
      y = expression("|" * italic(a)[psd] * "| from particle-length PSD"),
      shape = "Shape",
      title    = paste0(mat_label, "-only particle-length PSD slopes: this study vs. literature"),
      subtitle = "This study retains the fragment/fiber/all shape distinction; error bars per source as in the combined figure (Figure S7)."
    ) +
    ggplot2::theme_minimal(base_size = 16) +
    ggplot2::theme(
      axis.text.y  = ggplot2::element_text(size = 14, face = "bold"),
      legend.position = "right",
      panel.border = ggplot2::element_rect(color = "gray82", fill = NA, linewidth = 0.4),
      plot.title   = ggplot2::element_text(size = 15),
      plot.subtitle = ggplot2::element_text(size = 10.5, color = "gray30")
    )
  ggsave(p, filename = paste0("figures/alpha_comparison_plot_", tolower(mat_label), ".png"),
         width = 10, height = 6, dpi = 300)
  p
}

Appendix M. Manuscript parameter export (single source of truth)

Every PSD, rescaling and risk number quoted in the Savoca et al. manuscript and SI is written here to data_output/psd_rescaling_params.json (and a flat CSV), at full precision, from the objects computed above. Rounding happens only in the manuscript-generation step. W1 values use the resolved rescaling basis: concentrations restricted to each C-PSD window, with each river’s own slope (pooled slope and two-segment model as sensitivities). W2 is the reported 50–500 µm concentration.

Show the code 
.nb <- function(f) tryCatch(stats::nobs(f$fit), error = function(e) NA_integer_)
fit_row <- function(f) list(a_cum = f$a_cpsd, a_cum_SE = f$se_a_cpsd, a_diff = f$a_psd, a_diff_SE = f$se_a_psd,
                            CI95_a_diff = f$a_psd + c(-1.96, 1.96) * f$se_a_psd, R2 = f$r2, n_bins = .nb(f),
                            window_LOD_um = c(f$lower_lod_um, f$upper_lod_um))
pw_row <- dplyr::filter(critical_piecewise_tbl, Matrix == "River water")
qsum <- function(x) list(median_L = stats::median(x), q25_L = stats::quantile(x, 0.25, names = FALSE),
                        q75_L = stats::quantile(x, 0.75, names = FALSE), mean_L = mean(x), n = length(x))
rs_row <- function(x, erm) { r <- dplyr::filter(x, ERM == erm, HCx == 5); list(RQ_p50 = r$RQ_p50, RQ_p95 = r$RQ_p95, P_exceed = r$P_exceed) }

psd_params <- list(
  meta = list(run_budget = run_budget, n_boot = n_boot, n_mc = n_mc, slope_application = slope_application,
              slope_structural_sd = slope_structural_sd, monitoring_file = basename(monitoring_file),
              rendered = format(Sys.time(), "%Y-%m-%d %H:%M %Z")),
  monitoring = as.list(river_conc_summary),
  pooled = fit_row(cpsd_fit_all),
  fragment = fit_row(cpsd_fit_frag),
  fiber = fit_row(cpsd_fit_fiber),
  by_river = lapply(cpsd_fits_by_loc, fit_row),
  heterogeneity = river_slope_heterogeneity[c("Q", "df", "p_value", "i2", "weighted_mean")],
  two_segment = list(breakpoint_um = pw_row$piecewise_break_um,
                     a_fine_cum = pw_row$piecewise_low_a_cpsd, a_coarse_cum = pw_row$piecewise_high_a_cpsd,
                     a_fine_diff = pw_row$piecewise_low_a_cpsd - 1, a_coarse_diff = pw_row$piecewise_high_a_cpsd - 1,
                     dAIC = pw_row$piecewise_delta_aic),
  # Rescaling on the resolved basis: concentrations restricted to each C-PSD
  # window (Section 4.2.2), CF from that same window to 1-5000 um.
  rescaling = list(
    basis = "C-PSD-window concentration (reported 50-500 um concentration x in-window particle fraction); CF from the same window to 1-5000 um",
    n_nondetect_river_window = sum(monitoring$C_measured_pL == 0),
    C_W2_reported = qsum(monitoring$C_reported_pL),
    C_lod_window_river = qsum(monitoring$C_measured_pL),
    lod_fraction_median = stats::median(monitoring$lod_particle_fraction),
    windows_by_river = lapply(split(river_corr$L_meas_by_group, river_corr$L_meas_by_group$group), function(w) c(w$L_meas_min, w$L_meas_max)),
    CF_by_river = lapply(combined_cf_by_river, function(x) stats::quantile(x, c(0.05, 0.5, 0.95), names = FALSE)),
    CF_pooled = stats::quantile(combined_cf_pooled, c(0.05, 0.5, 0.95), names = FALSE),
    CF_pooled_window = c(L_meas_min_use, L_meas_max_use),
    CF_two = pw_river$cf_piecewise,
    C_W1_river = qsum(C_sample_median$C_corr_med),
    C_W1_pooled = qsum(C_sample_median_pooled$C_corr_med),
    C_W1_two = qsum(monitoring_pooled_scope$C_measured_pL * pw_river$cf_piecewise)),
  risk_headline = list(food_dilution_HC5 = rs_row(risk_summary, "Food Dilution"),
                       tissue_translocation_HC5 = rs_row(risk_summary, "Tissue Translocation")),
  risk_by_river = if (!is.null(risk_summary_by_river)) lapply(split(risk_summary_by_river, risk_summary_by_river$river), function(x)
    list(food_dilution_HC5 = rs_row(x, "Food Dilution"), tissue_translocation_HC5 = rs_row(x, "Tissue Translocation"))) else NULL,
  risk_pooled_slope = list(food_dilution_HC5 = rs_row(risk_summary_pooled, "Food Dilution"),
                           tissue_translocation_HC5 = rs_row(risk_summary_pooled, "Tissue Translocation")),
  eed_river_q50_median_L = stats::median(eed_boot$q50)
)
psd_params$rescaling$ratio_W1_river_over_two <- psd_params$rescaling$C_W1_river$median_L / psd_params$rescaling$C_W1_two$median_L

jsonlite::write_json(psd_params, "data_output/psd_rescaling_params.json", auto_unbox = TRUE, digits = NA, pretty = TRUE)
flat <- unlist(psd_params)
utils::write.csv(data.frame(key = names(flat), value = unname(flat)), "data_output/psd_rescaling_params.csv", row.names = FALSE)
writeLines(utils::capture.output(utils::sessionInfo()), "data_output/session_info.txt")
cat("Exported", length(flat), "values to data_output/psd_rescaling_params.json\n")
