# 10. Sensitivity analysis
**Sensitivity analysis** to identify dominant uncertainty contributors (e.g., alpha, plastic proportion, analytical recovery).

## 10.0 Hoffman et al. (2026) transport and slope-structure diagnostics

Hoffman et al. (2026) show that vertical transport can make a sampled PSD deviate from a single power law, with apparent slopes differing from the underlying PSD by about two exponent units across a critical size. The following diagnostics are model-based sensitivities. They do not replace the production CF, but they show how much the Food Dilution and Tissue Translocation risk summaries move when the slope uncertainty is widened beyond OLS fit error and when surface/subsurface samples are analyzed separately.

```{r hoffman-slope-uncertainty-sensitivity, cache=TRUE, cache.extra=list(n_boot, raw_data_cache_key)}
summarize_mc2d_hc5 <- function(x) {
  x |>
    dplyr::filter(HCx == 5) |>
    dplyr::group_by(ERM, HCx) |>
    dplyr::summarise(
      P_exceed_med = median(P_exceed),
      RQ_p50_med = median(RQ_p50),
      RQ_p95_med = median(RQ_p95),
      .groups = "drop"
    )
}

slope_sd_grid <- c(0, slope_structural_sd, 0.5, 1.0)
# Pooled-slope sensitivity. ALIGNMENT RULE: the hazard is re-derived at every
# structural SD from the SAME widened slope draws used to rescale the exposure
# (plus the pooled area/volume fits and aspect ratio), so exposure and hazard
# always share one particle-population description.
hoffman_slope_sensitivity <- dplyr::bind_rows(lapply(slope_sd_grid, function(sd_i) {
  alpha_i <- withr::with_seed(1000 + as.integer(sd_i * 1000), alpha_dist(
    mu = cpsd_fit_all$a_psd, sd = cpsd_fit_all$se_a_psd, n = 3000, structural_sd = sd_i))
  cf_i <- correction_factor(
    a = alpha_i, L_meas_min = L_meas_min_use, L_meas_max = L_meas_max_use,
    L_tar_min = 1, L_tar_max = 5000, slope_convention = "differential")
  haz_i <- aligned_freshwater_hazard(
    tox_data = tox_data, alpha_draws = alpha_i, aspect_ratio_vec = raw_particles_river$aspect_ratio,
    fit_volume = cpsd_fit_volume, fit_area = cpsd_fit_area, n = n_boot,
    seed = 5300 + as.integer(sd_i * 1000), psd_key = paste0("river:pooled:sd", sd_i))$haz
  mc_i <- mc2d_risk(
    monitoring_df = monitoring_pooled_scope,
    combined_cf = cf_i,
    haz_df = haz_i,
    n_uncertainty = 100,
    n_variability = 500,
    seed = 2000 + as.integer(sd_i * 1000)
  )
  summarize_mc2d_hc5(mc_i) |>
    dplyr::mutate(
      structural_sd = sd_i,
      CF_p50 = median(cf_i),
      CF_p95 = quantile(cf_i, 0.95),
      HC5_median = vapply(ERM, function(e) stats::median(haz_i$PNEC[haz_i$ERM == e & haz_i$HCx == 5]), numeric(1))
    )
}))

knitr::kable(
  hoffman_slope_sensitivity,
  digits = 3,
  caption = "SPEC 2 sensitivity: river HC5 risk response to widened differential-slope structural uncertainty"
)
```

The `structural_sd = 0` row isolates the corrected differential-slope convention with fit uncertainty only. Wider rows are assumptions motivated by Hoffman et al. (2026) and the RIVM (2025) precedent for deliberately broad slope priors; they are sampled in the MC2D outer uncertainty loop through the CF, not in the inner exposure-variability loop. This sensitivity uses the pooled slope on both sides. Following the alignment rule, the hazard (HC5) is re-derived at each structural SD from the same widened slope draws as the exposure, so the rows show the joint effect of slope uncertainty on exposure and hazard.

```{r hoffman-depth-stratified-sensitivity, cache=TRUE, cache.extra=list(n_boot, raw_data_cache_key)}
depth_levels <- levels(monitoring$sample_depth_general)

depth_shape_fits <- dplyr::bind_rows(lapply(depth_levels, function(depth_i) {
  dplyr::bind_rows(lapply(c("fragment", "fiber", "all"), function(shape_i) {
    dat_i <- raw_particles_river |> dplyr::filter(sample_depth_general == depth_i)
    if (shape_i != "all") dat_i <- dat_i |> dplyr::filter(shape == shape_i)
    vals <- dat_i |> dplyr::pull(length_um)
    fit_i <- fit_cpsd_segur_r(vals, bin_um = 5)
    tibble::tibble(
      sample_depth_general = depth_i,
      shape = shape_i,
      n_particles = length(vals),
      a_cpsd = fit_i$a_cpsd,
      a_psd = fit_i$a_psd,
      se_a_psd = fit_i$se_a_psd,
      lod_low_um = fit_i$lower_lod_used_um,
      lod_high_um = fit_i$upper_lod_um,
      r2 = fit_i$r2
    )
  }))
}))

depth_slope_plot <- depth_shape_fits |>
  ggplot2::ggplot(ggplot2::aes(x = sample_depth_general, y = a_psd, color = shape)) +
  ggplot2::geom_point(size = 3, position = ggplot2::position_dodge(width = 0.35)) +
  ggplot2::geom_errorbar(
    ggplot2::aes(ymin = a_psd - se_a_psd, ymax = a_psd + se_a_psd),
    width = 0.15,
    position = ggplot2::position_dodge(width = 0.35)
  ) +
  ggplot2::labs(
    x = "Sampling depth stratum",
    y = expression(italic(a)[psd]),
    title = "River C-PSD slope by sampling depth and shape"
  ) +
  ggplot2::theme_minimal(base_size = 18)

ggsave(depth_slope_plot, filename = "figures/hoffman_depth_slope_plot.png", width = 9, height = 6, dpi = 300)
depth_slope_plot

depth_sensitivity <- dplyr::bind_rows(lapply(depth_levels, function(depth_i) {
  fit_row <- depth_shape_fits |>
    dplyr::filter(sample_depth_general == depth_i, shape == "all") |>
    dplyr::slice(1)
  fit_i <- fit_cpsd_segur_r(
    raw_particles_river |>
      dplyr::filter(sample_depth_general == depth_i) |>
      dplyr::pull(length_um),
    bin_um = 5
  )
  alpha_i <- withr::with_seed(3100 + match(depth_i, depth_levels), alpha_dist(
    mu = fit_i$a_psd,
    sd = fit_i$se_a_psd,
    n = 3000,
    structural_sd = slope_structural_sd
  ))
  # ALIGNMENT RULE: hazard aligned to this depth stratum's own particles
  # (length draws above, plus its own area/volume fits and aspect ratio).
  part_i <- raw_particles_river |> dplyr::filter(sample_depth_general == depth_i)
  haz_i <- aligned_freshwater_hazard(
    tox_data = tox_data, alpha_draws = alpha_i, aspect_ratio_vec = part_i$aspect_ratio,
    fit_volume = fit_cpsd_segur_r(part_i$V_um3, bin_um = vol_bin_um, fit_range_um = vlb_river$all),
    fit_area = fit_cpsd_segur_r(part_i$area_um2, bin_um = 500, fit_range_um = c(2000, 500000)),
    n = n_boot, seed = 5400 + 10 * match(depth_i, depth_levels), psd_key = paste0("river:depth:", depth_i))$haz
  mon_i <- lod_scope_monitoring_concentrations(
    monitoring = monitoring |> dplyr::filter(sample_depth_general == depth_i) |>
      dplyr::select(-dplyr::any_of(c("reported_lower_um", "reported_upper_um", "lod_lower_um", "lod_upper_um", "n_particles_reported_window", "n_particles_lod_window", "lod_particle_fraction"))),
    raw_particles = part_i, reported_conc_col = "C_reported_pL",
    output_conc_col = "C_measured_pL", cpsd_fit = fit_i)
  corr_i <- correct_and_bootstrap_eed(
    monitoring = mon_i,
    conc_col = "C_measured_pL",
    cpsd_fit = fit_i,
    alpha_draws = alpha_i,
    L_tar_min = 1,
    L_tar_max = 5000,
    n_draws = 1000,
    n_boot = n_boot,
    probs = c(0.5, 0.95),
    slope_convention = "differential"
  )
  mc_i <- mc2d_risk(
    monitoring_df = corr_i$monitoring,
    combined_cf = corr_i$combined_cf,
    haz_df = haz_i,
    n_uncertainty = 100,
    n_variability = 500,
    seed = 3000 + match(depth_i, depth_levels)
  )
  summarize_mc2d_hc5(mc_i) |>
    dplyr::mutate(
      sample_depth_general = depth_i,
      n_monitoring = nrow(mon_i),
      a_psd = fit_i$a_psd,
      CF_p50 = median(corr_i$combined_cf),
      EED_q50_p50 = median(corr_i$eed_boot$q50),
      EED_q95_p50 = median(corr_i$eed_boot$q95)
    )
}))

knitr::kable(
  depth_sensitivity,
  digits = 3,
  caption = "SPEC 3 river depth-stratified sensitivity for corrected EED and HC5 risk"
)
```

Surface and subsurface strata are both large enough to fit C-PSD slopes and bootstrap monitoring observations. The headline assessment remains pooled because this is a screening ERA and the transport correction is not yet mechanistic; the stratified rows are retained as a sensitivity that can identify whether boundary-enriched samples materially alter EED or RQ.

## 10.0.1 By-river risk characterization (not pooled)

With `slope_application = "river"` (the default), the headline river assessment (Sections 5-9) already rescales each river's samples with its own slope and divides by that river's own aligned hazard, so this section is the per-river view of the headline result. It runs the full workflow for each river independently: C-PSD fit, the identical differential-slope draws (`alpha_by_river`), correction factor, EED bootstrap, and Food Dilution/Tissue Translocation risk. Each river uses its own aligned hazard (`haz_by_river`, Section 7.5), never the pooled hazard, per the alignment rule.

```{r river-stratified-risk, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE, cache=TRUE, cache.extra=list(n_boot, n_mc, raw_data_cache_key)}
river_hc5_risk <- dplyr::bind_rows(lapply(locations, function(loc) {
  fit_i     <- cpsd_fits_by_loc[[loc]]
  seed_base <- 41000 + match(loc, locations) * 10

  # ALIGNMENT RULE: the same slope draws that built this river's hazard.
  alpha_i <- alpha_by_river[[loc]]

  mon_i <- monitoring |> dplyr::filter(river == loc)

  set.seed(seed_base + 1)
  corr_i <- correct_and_bootstrap_eed(
    monitoring = mon_i, conc_col = "C_measured_pL", cpsd_fit = fit_i, alpha_draws = alpha_i,
    L_tar_min = 1, L_tar_max = 5000, n_draws = 3000, n_boot = n_boot,
    probs = c(0.5, 0.95), slope_convention = "differential"
  )

  set.seed(seed_base + 2)
  risk_draws_i <- draw_rq_aligned(
    haz_by_group = stats::setNames(list(haz_by_river[[loc]]), loc),
    exposure_by_group = stats::setNames(list(with_psd_key(corr_i$eed_boot$q50, paste0("river:", loc))), loc),
    n_risk = 1000) |>
    dplyr::filter(HCx == 5)

  risk_draws_i |>
    dplyr::group_by(ERM, HCx) |>
    dplyr::summarise(
      RQ_p5    = stats::quantile(RQ, 0.05, na.rm = TRUE),
      RQ_p50   = stats::quantile(RQ, 0.50, na.rm = TRUE),
      RQ_p95   = stats::quantile(RQ, 0.95, na.rm = TRUE),
      P_exceed = mean(RQ > 1, na.rm = TRUE),
      .groups  = "drop"
    ) |>
    dplyr::mutate(
      river        = loc,
      n_monitoring = nrow(mon_i),
      n_particles  = sum(raw_particles_river$sample_location == loc),
      a_psd        = fit_i$a_psd,
      CF_p50       = stats::median(corr_i$combined_cf)
    )
}))

knitr::kable(
  river_hc5_risk |>
    dplyr::select(river, ERM, n_particles, n_monitoring, a_psd, CF_p50, RQ_p5, RQ_p50, RQ_p95, P_exceed),
  digits = 3,
  caption = "By-river (not pooled) Food Dilution / Tissue Translocation HC5 risk quotient, p5/p50/p95 across the 1D Monte Carlo risk draws."
)
```

**Interpretation.** All four rivers have adequate independent support for this analysis (`r paste(river_hc5_risk$n_particles[match(locations, river_hc5_risk$river)], collapse=", ")` particles and `r paste(river_hc5_risk$n_monitoring[match(locations, river_hc5_risk$river)], collapse=", ")` monitoring replicates for Carmel/Pajaro/Salinas/San Lorenzo respectively), so no river is flagged as data-insufficient here (contrast Section 12.5.1.2's marine floor-sensitivity case, where the underlying tox data itself became too sparse). The pooled headline result (Section 5) remains the primary conclusion for this screening assessment; this by-river breakdown is a sensitivity showing whether any single location drives that pooled result, or whether the Food Dilution vs. Tissue Translocation risk ranking is consistent across all four independently.

## 10.1 Morris global sensitivity analysis (future work)

A Morris elementary-effects screen (global sensitivity ranking of RQ uncertainty drivers) is deferred to a dedicated compute pass: it repeatedly rebuilds small pSSD++ hazard models and, at a budget large enough to produce a stable ranking, is too slow for a routine report render. It did not run in this render.


## 10.2 µFTIR objective: critical assessment of the detection floor and its intersection with the LOD/CF workflow

### Instrument configuration

The µFTIR analysis used an objective equivalent to ~4× magnification with **25 µm pixel size**. At this pixel resolution, the practical nominal minimum detectable particle size (requiring ≥ 2 pixels across the shortest dimension) is approximately **50 µm**. The reported 50–500 µm interval is retained only to normalize each sample's particle concentration; the production exposure and CF denominator use the C-PSD-valid window selected from the particle data for that river.

### Why the Wang et al. (2026) ×33 scaling factor does not apply here

Wang et al. (2026) found that a 4× µFTIR objective (20 µm pixel) detects only 3 ± 3% of particles relative to a 25× reference (2 µm pixel). At face value this suggests a ×33 upward scaling should be applied to our concentrations. **This is incorrect for the following reasons:**

**1. The 97% "missed" particles lie almost entirely below our measurement floor.**

The 25× objective in Wang et al. detects particles as small as ~4 µm. The 4× objective detects only those ≥ ~40–50 µm. The difference (97% of total particle count) is dominated by particles in the 4–50 µm size class. Our workflow uses the C-PSD-valid lower bound, rather than the nominal 50 µm reporting limit, and extrapolates from that measured window down to 1 µm. The Wang et al. sub-window particles are therefore the population that `correction_factor()` reconstructs via power-law integration.

**2. Within the measured range (50–500 µm), the 4×/25 µm system is effective.**

At 25 µm pixel size:

| Particle size | Pixels across | Detection status |
|---|---|---|
| 50 µm | 2 px | Marginal (meets minimum) |
| 100 µm | 4 px | Reliable |
| 200 µm | 8 px | Well-resolved |
| 500 µm | 20 px | Fully resolved |

For particles at or above 100 µm — which covers the entire Segur LOD fitting window (fragments: `r round(cpsd_fit_frag$lower_lod_used_um)`–`r round(cpsd_fit_frag$upper_lod_um)` µm; all shapes: `r round(cpsd_fit_all$lower_lod_used_um)`–`r round(cpsd_fit_all$upper_lod_um)` µm) — detection is reliable with this pixel size. The ×33 correction factor was derived from total particle counts including the sub-50 µm population; it does not represent within-range inefficiency.

**3. The Segur LOD algorithm implicitly handles the marginal 50–100 µm zone.**

The Segur LOD search specifically identifies the size window where the C-PSD is most linear ($R^2 \geq 0.90$). The 50–100 µm region, where detection by the 4×/25 µm system may be incomplete, would manifest as a deviation from power-law behavior at the lower end of the binned distribution — and would therefore be *excluded* from the fitting window. Indeed, the fitted lower LODs (`r round(cpsd_fit_frag$lower_lod_used_um)` µm for fragments, `r round(cpsd_fit_all$lower_lod_used_um)` µm pooled) are well above 50 µm, confirming that the algorithm already pushed the lower bound into the reliable detection zone.

**4. Applying ×33 on top of the existing CF would double-count.**

The current CF has a median of `r round(median(combined_cf), 1)`× (90% CI: `r round(quantile(combined_cf, 0.05), 1)`–`r round(quantile(combined_cf, 0.95), 1)`×). This already accounts for the unmeasured sub-50 µm population via power-law extrapolation. Multiplying `C_corrected` by an additional 33× would apply a second, conflicting correction to the same particle pool, producing a total inflation factor of ~`r round(median(combined_cf) * 33, 0)`× — far in excess of any defensible estimate.

### Residual uncertainty: the nominal 50–100 µm marginal zone

The one genuine uncertainty from the 4×/25 µm configuration is **incomplete counting in the 50–100 µm particle size class**. Particles in this range occupy 2–4 pixels and may be undercounted relative to a higher-magnification system. The C-PSD fit-window selection addresses this directly in the production workflow: concentrations and correction-factor denominators are restricted to the fitted valid window. The following nominal-window calculation is retained only as an instrument-context diagnostic, not as a production exposure scenario.

```{r lmeas-sensitivity, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
# Compare CF and risk outcomes under two L_meas_min assumptions:
# 50 µm (current, includes marginal zone) vs 100 µm (excludes marginal zone — conservative floor)
lmeas_scenarios <- list(
  "L_meas_min = 50 µm (current)" = list(L_lo = 50,  L_hi = 500),
  "L_meas_min = 100 µm (conservative)" = list(L_lo = 100, L_hi = 500)
)

lmeas_cf_summary <- dplyr::bind_rows(lapply(names(lmeas_scenarios), function(scen) {
  s   <- lmeas_scenarios[[scen]]
  cf_s <- correction_factor(
    a           = alpha,                  # differential a_psd draws (n_mc)
    L_meas_min  = s$L_lo,
    L_meas_max  = s$L_hi,
    L_tar_min   = 1,
    L_tar_max   = 5000,
    slope_convention = "differential"
  )
  data.frame(
    scenario = scen,
    CF_p05   = round(quantile(cf_s, 0.05),  1),
    CF_med   = round(median(cf_s),           1),
    CF_p95   = round(quantile(cf_s, 0.95),  1)
  )
}))

knitr::kable(lmeas_cf_summary,
  caption = paste0(
    "Correction factor (50–500 µm → 1–5000 µm) under alternative lower detection limits. ",
    "Using differential a_psd = ", round(cpsd_fit_all$a_psd, 3), " (all shapes, Segur LOD). ",
    "n_mc = ", n_mc, " Monte Carlo draws."
  ),
  col.names = c("Scenario", "CF 5th pct", "CF median", "CF 95th pct")
)
```

```{r lmeas-inline, include=FALSE}
cf_50  <- lmeas_cf_summary$CF_med[lmeas_cf_summary$scenario == "L_meas_min = 50 µm (current)"]
cf_100 <- lmeas_cf_summary$CF_med[lmeas_cf_summary$scenario == "L_meas_min = 100 µm (conservative)"]
```

Raising the *nominal* lower bound from 50 to 100 µm increases the diagnostic median CF from `r cf_50`× to `r cf_100`× because more particles are treated as extrapolated. This calculation does not change the production result: the production workflow uses the C-PSD-selected LOD window and recomputes each sample's input concentration within that same window.

**Summary.** No additional objective-based correction factor is applied to `C_measured_pL`. The workflow accounts for detection reliability by rebuilding each sample concentration within its C-PSD-selected window and then applying the power-law CF from that same window to the 1 µm target. The Wang et al. (2026) ×33 factor would be appropriate only if converting a 4× total particle count to an equivalent 25× total count *without* this size-resolved reconstruction and power-law extrapolation.

# 11. Sediment — Beach Sand

## 11.1 Derive power-law values from raw sediment particle data

```{r}
# import sediment particle data (beach sand as sediment proxy)
raw_particles_sed <- raw_particles |> 
  dplyr::filter(sample_type == "beach sand") |>
  assign_polymer_density(lookup = polymer_density_tbl)

# ---- Thickness (height) factor from sediment data ----
ratio_tbl_sed <- raw_particles_sed |>
  mutate(
    WL = 1 / aspect_ratio,
    width_eff_um = case_when(
      shape == "fragment" & !is.na(area_um2) & !is.na(length_um) & length_um > 0 &
        !is.na(circularity) & circularity < 0.7 ~ area_um2 / length_um,
      TRUE ~ width_um
    )
  ) |> 
  group_by(shape) |>
  summarise(
    n = n(),
    r_med  = median(WL, na.rm = TRUE),
    r_low  = quantile(WL, 0.25, na.rm = TRUE),
    r_high = quantile(WL, 0.75, na.rm = TRUE),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

# ---- Volumes ----
raw_particles_sed <- raw_particles_sed |>
  left_join(ratio_tbl_sed |> dplyr::select(shape, r_med), by = "shape") |>  
  mutate(
    height_um = r_med * width_um,
    V_um3 = case_when(
      shape == "fragment" ~ (pi / 6) * length_um * width_um * height_um,
      shape == "fiber"    ~ pi * (width_um / 2)^2 * length_um,
      TRUE ~ NA_real_
    ),
    mass_ug = V_um3 * density_g_cm3,
    mass_ug_fixed_density_1.1 = V_um3 * 1.1
  )
```

### Particle length
```{r cpsd-fits-sed-length, cache=TRUE, cache.extra=raw_data_cache_key}
cpsd_fits_sed_length <- fit_cpsd_by_shape(
  raw_particles_sed, value_col = "length_um",
  config = list(
    fragment = list(bin_um = 5, fit_range_um = c(NA_real_, NA_real_)),
    fiber    = list(bin_um = 5, fit_range_um = c(NA_real_, NA_real_)),
    all      = list(bin_um = 5, fit_range_um = c(NA_real_, NA_real_))
  )
)
cpsd_fit_sed_frag  <- cpsd_fits_sed_length$fragment
cpsd_fit_sed_fiber <- cpsd_fits_sed_length$fiber
cpsd_fit_sed_all   <- cpsd_fits_sed_length$all

set.seed(8002)
alpha_sed <- alpha_dist(
  mu = cpsd_fit_sed_all$a_psd,
  sd = cpsd_fit_sed_all$se_a_psd,
  n = 20000,
  structural_sd = slope_structural_sd
)

alpha_sed_mu <- mean(alpha_sed)
alpha_sed_se <- sd(alpha_sed)
```

### Particle volume


## 11.3 Sediment monitoring concentrations and EED

### 11.3.0 Sediment concentration provenance audit

Before treating any sediment concentration as a genuine particles/kg-dry-weight value, this subsection verifies where it actually comes from. The check below is rendered so the finding is auditable rather than asserted.

```{r spec1d-sediment-provenance-audit}
part_dets_summ_raw <- monitoring_raw

cat("Columns available in data_input/Part_dets_summ_final.rds:\n")
print(names(part_dets_summ_raw))

raw_sed_check <- part_dets_summ_raw |>
  dplyr::filter(sample_type == "beach sand", material_simple == "plastic", sample_or_blank == "sample")

# extrap_conc_PPL is reconstructed here as extrap_count / divisor to check whether
# it is a per-liter (water/processing-volume) concentration -- the same quantity
# used, under the identical column name and identical construction, for river
# water (where extrap_conc_PPL is the reported normalization before Section 5
# reconstructs C_measured_pL over the C-PSD-valid interval) and ocean water
# (Section 12).
implied_divisor_sed <- round(raw_sed_check$extrap_count / raw_sed_check$extrap_conc_PPL, 3)
cat("\nSediment ('beach sand') rows: n =", nrow(raw_sed_check),
    "| implied denominator of extrap_conc_PPL (extrap_count / extrap_conc_PPL), summary:\n")
print(summary(implied_divisor_sed))
cat("(a single fixed value here -- independent of which sediment sample/date/location --",
    "is the signature of a per-liter processing/pumped-volume normalization, not a",
    "per-kg dry-sediment-mass normalization, since no two real sediment samples share",
    "an identical dry mass)\n")

has_mass_or_density_col <- any(grepl("mass|weight|density|dry|bulk", names(part_dets_summ_raw), ignore.case = TRUE))
cat("\nAny sample dry-weight / wet-weight / bulk-density column present in the source data:",
    has_mass_or_density_col, "\n")
```

**Finding (SPEC 1d-i).** `extrap_conc_PPL` — the only concentration column in `data_input/Part_dets_summ.rds` — is constructed identically for every `sample_type` (river water, ocean water, and beach sand/sediment): `extrap_count` divided by a single fixed volume-like denominator, with no sediment sample dry-mass, wet-mass, or bulk-density column present anywhere in the source data to convert it to particles/kg dry weight. Concretely, `monitoring_sed$C_measured_pkg` was set to this same per-liter-type column (`extrap_conc_PPL`) with a `# placeholder` comment, i.e., a per-liter water/processing-volume value was carried through the sediment pipeline and reported as if it were particles/kg sediment. No genuine particles/kg-dry-weight sediment concentration exists in the data available to this analysis (verified above; `Opt_micro_all_cut.rds`, a separate large-microplastics dataset, similarly records beach-sand samples on a `Volume_Pumped_L` basis, not a dry-sediment-mass basis). Per SPEC 1d-i, the sediment concentration pathway is therefore flagged **non-quantitative/illustrative** rather than corrected in place (there is nothing to convert it *to*), and is excluded from the headline risk characterization (Sections 14-15) -- see the flag and downstream caveats below.

```{r spec1d-sediment-quantitative-flag}
# set to TRUE only once a genuine particles/kg-dry-weight sediment
# concentration (from a real sediment sample mass) is available; the sediment
# EED/RQ machinery below is retained for illustrative/methods purposes (e.g. to
# confirm the slope-convention fix direction in Section 13.1) but must not be
# read as a real risk estimate while this flag is FALSE.
sediment_concentration_is_quantitative <- FALSE
```

```{r}
monitoring_sed <- monitoring_raw |>
  filter(
    sample_type == "beach sand",
    material_simple == "plastic",
    sample_or_blank == "sample"
  ) |>
  mutate(
    date_raw = str_extract(Client_ID_MSSupdate, "\\d{8}"),
    date = ymd(date_raw),
    sample_id = Client_ID_MSSupdate,
    # SPEC 1d-i: NOT a genuine particles/kg sediment concentration -- this is the
    # same per-liter water/processing-volume column used for river and ocean water
    # (see spec1d-sediment-provenance-audit above). Retained only so the EED/RQ
    # pipeline below can serve as an illustrative/methods demonstration; see
    # `sediment_concentration_is_quantitative` (FALSE) and the Section 11.4/14/15
    # caveats before reading any downstream sediment RQ as a real risk estimate.
    C_reported_pkg = extrap_conc_PPL,
    C_measured_pkg = C_reported_pkg,
    Lmin_reported_um = 50,
    Lmax_reported_um = 500,
    Lmin_measured_um = Lmin_reported_um,
    Lmax_measured_um = Lmax_reported_um
  ) |>
  # One row per sample (sum over polymer classes); see the river monitoring chunk.
  collapse_to_sample_totals(sum_cols = c("count", "extrap_count", "extrap_conc_PPL", "C_reported_pkg", "C_measured_pkg"))

monitoring_sed <- lod_scope_monitoring_concentrations(
  monitoring = monitoring_sed,
  raw_particles = raw_particles_sed,
  reported_conc_col = "C_reported_pkg",
  output_conc_col = "C_measured_pkg",
  cpsd_fit = cpsd_fit_sed_all
)

set.seed(9102)
sed_corr <- correct_and_bootstrap_eed(
  monitoring  = monitoring_sed,
  conc_col    = "C_measured_pkg",
  cpsd_fit    = cpsd_fit_sed_all,
  alpha_draws = alpha_sed,
  L_tar_min   = 1,
  L_tar_max   = 5000,
  n_draws     = 3000,
  n_boot      = n_boot,
  probs       = c(0.5, 0.95),
  slope_convention = "differential"
)
monitoring_sed        <- sed_corr$monitoring
L_meas_min_use_sed    <- sed_corr$L_meas_min_use
L_meas_max_use_sed    <- sed_corr$L_meas_max_use
combined_cf_sed       <- sed_corr$combined_cf
C_corrected_draws_sed <- sed_corr$C_corrected_draws
C_sample_median_sed   <- sed_corr$C_sample_median
eed_boot_sed          <- sed_corr$eed_boot
summary(eed_boot_sed)
```

```{r sed-eed-bootstrap-plot}
sed_eed_bootstrap_plot <- plot_eed_bootstrap(eed_boot_sed, n_boot, "Sediment")

ggsave(sed_eed_bootstrap_plot, filename = "figures/sed_eed_bootstrap_plot.png", width = 9, height = 6, dpi = 300)
sed_eed_bootstrap_plot
```

The median EED 50th percentile across `r n_boot` bootstrap replicates is `r round(median(eed_boot_sed$q50), 2)` particles/kg (90th percentile bootstrap: `r round(median(eed_boot_sed$q95), 2)` particles/kg) — illustrative only, per the provenance finding above.

## 11.2 Sediment toxicity data

```{r sed-tox-data}
tox_data_sed <- tomex2 |> 
   dplyr::filter(
    env_f %in% c("Marine", "Freshwater"),
    exposure.route == "sediment",
    Group != "Bacterium",
    effect.metric != "HONEC",
    tier_zero_tech_f == "Red Criteria Passed",
    tier_zero_risk_f == "Red Criteria Passed",
    risk.13 != 0
  ) |> 
    # since limited data available, and working with estuarine system - combine marine and freshwater species by overwriting environment to be freshwater for all
    mutate(env_f = "Freshwater")
```

### Align Toxicity Data
#### Parameter distributions

```{r sed-aspect-ratio}
set.seed(9002)
R.ave_sed_result <- bootstrap_aspect_ratio(raw_particles_sed$aspect_ratio, n_boot = n_boot)
R.ave_sed_vals   <- R.ave_sed_result$vals
R.ave_sed_mean   <- R.ave_sed_result$boot_mean
R.ave_sed_sd     <- R.ave_sed_result$boot_sd

param_values_sed <- PSSDplusplus::param_default_values

param_values_sed[[paste0("alpha.sediment.freshwater")]] <- -alpha_sed_mu
param_values_sed[[paste0("alpha.sediment.freshwater.sd")]] <- alpha_sed_se
param_values_sed[[paste0("R.ave.sediment.freshwater")]] <- R.ave_sed_mean
param_values_sed[[paste0("R.ave.sediment.freshwater.sd")]] <- R.ave_sed_sd
# use the differential a_psd = a_cpsd - 1, not the cumulative a_cpsd
# (same fix as the river/ocean blocks; the cumulative value is 1.0 too shallow).
param_values_sed[[paste0("a.v.sediment.freshwater")]] <- -cpsd_fit_volume_sed$a_psd
param_values_sed[[paste0("a.v.sediment.freshwater.sd")]] <- cpsd_fit_volume_sed$se_a_psd
param_values_sed[[paste0("a.sa.sediment.freshwater")]] <- -cpsd_fit_area_sed$a_psd
param_values_sed[[paste0("a.sa.sediment.freshwater.sd")]] <- cpsd_fit_area_sed$se_a_psd
# a.m.sediment.freshwater: set from data for consistency with a.v (mass ~ density *
# volume at constant density), rather than leaving the unrelated package default.
param_values_sed[[paste0("a.m.sediment.freshwater")]] <- -cpsd_fit_volume_sed$a_psd
param_values_sed[[paste0("a.m.sediment.freshwater.sd")]] <- cpsd_fit_volume_sed$se_a_psd

# pair down to only used parameters
param_values_sed <- param_values_sed |> dplyr::select(contains("sediment.freshwater"), contains("beta"), contains("body"))
param_values_sed

# SPEC 1b acceptance check: a.v and a.m must be mutually consistent
stopifnot(abs(param_values_sed$a.v.sediment.freshwater - param_values_sed$a.m.sediment.freshwater) < 0.3)

# SPEC 1d-iv (rule-out): confirm the sediment alignment slopes are on the
# differential convention -- i.e. this analysis' large sediment RQ is NOT
# attributable to a slope-convention error (that was SPEC 1b, already fixed
# and asserted above). a.v/a.sa/a.m are exact deterministic transforms of
# their fits (-a_psd), so those are checked tightly. alpha.sediment.freshwater
# is instead the MEAN of a Monte Carlo truncated-normal sample centered on
# a_psd (alpha_dist(), which also widens SD by slope_structural_sd) -- it is
# expected to be close to, but not bit-identical to, -(a_cpsd - 1), so it is
# checked with a tolerance appropriate for MC sampling noise rather than an
# exact-equality tolerance.
stopifnot(abs(param_values_sed$alpha.sediment.freshwater - (-(cpsd_fit_sed_all$a_cpsd - 1))) < 0.2)
stopifnot(abs(param_values_sed$a.v.sediment.freshwater   - (-(cpsd_fit_volume_sed$a_cpsd - 1))) < 1e-6)
stopifnot(abs(param_values_sed$a.sa.sediment.freshwater  - (-(cpsd_fit_area_sed$a_cpsd - 1))) < 1e-6)
stopifnot(abs(param_values_sed$a.m.sediment.freshwater   - (-(cpsd_fit_volume_sed$a_cpsd - 1))) < 1e-6)
cat(sprintf(
  "SPEC 1d-iv rule-out PASSED: sediment slopes are on the differential convention (alpha=%.3f, a.v=%.3f, a.sa=%.3f, a.m=%.3f). The sediment RQ magnitude is therefore driven by the concentration/unit issues in Section 11.3.0/11.4 (SPEC 1d-i/ii), not by the slope convention.\n",
  param_values_sed$alpha.sediment.freshwater, param_values_sed$a.v.sediment.freshwater,
  param_values_sed$a.sa.sediment.freshwater, param_values_sed$a.m.sediment.freshwater
))
```

**SPEC 1d-iv finding.** The sediment alignment slopes above are already on the correct differential convention (asserted, not merely observed) and are mutually consistent (`a.v ≈ a.m`). The implausibly large sediment Food Dilution RQ documented in Section 11.4/15 is therefore **not** caused by a slope-convention error — that class of error was SPEC 1b's fix and is independently guarded here — but by the exposure-concentration provenance issue documented in Section 11.3.0 (SPEC 1d-i) and/or the hazard-unit-scale question examined in Section 11.4 (SPEC 1d-ii).

#### Build and Visualize Parameter distributions

## 11.4 Sediment probabilistic risk characterization

### 11.4.0 hazard-side unit-alignment trace

Before reading the sediment RQ below, this subsection traces whether `dose_unit = "kg"` genuinely carries particles/kg-dry-weight units end-to-end on the hazard side, independent of the exposure-side problem documented in Section 11.3.0.

```{r spec1d-hazard-unit-trace}
# Inspect the raw ToMEx sediment-exposure dose columns feeding tox_data_sed,
# and confirm PSSDplusplus's dose_unit = "kg" pathway sources them directly
# (source inspection of PSSDplusplus::align_data()/convert_units_fxn() during
# development of this spec showed the "kg" dose columns are populated from
# dose.particles.kg.sediment.master -- itself coalesced from ToMEx's own
# measured/nominal per-study sediment doses -- not derived from a water-based
# ("mL"/"L") value via any hardcoded conversion factor).
sed_dose_cols <- c("dose.particles.kg.sediment.master", "measured.dose.particles.kg.sediment",
                    "nominal.dose.particles.kg.sediment")
sed_dose_cols <- intersect(sed_dose_cols, names(tox_data_sed))
cat("Raw ToMEx sediment-exposure dose columns (particles/kg dry weight, as reported by original studies):\n")
for (col in sed_dose_cols) {
  cat("\n---", col, "---\n")
  print(summary(tox_data_sed[[col]]))
}
```

**Finding (SPEC 1d-ii).** The raw sediment-exposure toxicity doses in ToMEx (`dose.particles.kg.sediment.master`) span a physically plausible particles/kg-dry-weight range (tens to ~10^10), consistent with the order of magnitude of Redondo-Hasselerharm et al. (2023)'s benthic HC5 (4.9×10⁹ particles/kg dw). No hardcoded water-to-sediment unit-conversion factor (e.g., a missing bulk-density or dry-weight scalar) was found in the `dose_unit = "kg"` code path: `run_pssd_pipeline(..., dose_unit = "kg")` (`R/mp_risk_utils.R`) selects the `particles_kg_food_dilution`/`particles_kg_ox_stress` columns from `PSSDplusplus::MC_sim_align_parallel()`'s output, which in turn are populated directly from each sediment study's own reported particles/kg dose (via `align_data()`'s `dose.particles.kg.master` coalescing chain), not derived from a water-based value. The hazard side therefore appears to be genuinely unit-consistent on its own terms. The implausibly low derived sediment Food Dilution HC5 (exact value in the guard below) cannot be attributed to a discrete missing-conversion bug found in this trace; it is more likely size-alignment sensitivity to the sediment ERM exponents (the same mechanism SPEC 1b addressed for Food Dilution) for whichever study anchors the low tail, amplified by SSD-extrapolation noise on a modest sediment toxicity dataset (`r nrow(tox_data_sed)` records). This remains an open question rather than a resolved code fix, since (unlike SPEC 1d-i) no single incorrect line was identified. Regardless, because the exposure-side concentration is already known to be non-quantitative, this hazard-side question does not change the conclusion that the sediment RQ/HC5 below must be excluded from the headline risk characterization.

```{r sed-hazard-df}
haz_sed <- build_haz_df(pSSDs_sed, "Freshwater Sediment")

n_risk_sed <- 1000
set.seed(9302)
risk_draws_sed <- draw_rq_mc1d(haz_sed, eed_boot_sed$q50, n_risk = n_risk_sed)
risk_summary_sed <- summarize_rq(risk_draws_sed)
risk_summary_sed
```

```{r spec1d-benthic-hc5-guard}
# visible, rendered sanity assertion on the derived sediment HC5s
# against a plausible published benthic range.
sed_HC5_food_dilution_pkg        <- haz_sed |> dplyr::filter(ERM == "Food Dilution",        HCx == 5) |> dplyr::pull(PNEC) |> stats::median()
sed_HC5_tissue_translocation_pkg <- haz_sed |> dplyr::filter(ERM == "Tissue Translocation", HCx == 5) |> dplyr::pull(PNEC) |> stats::median()

cat(sprintf("Derived sediment HC5 (median): Food Dilution = %.4g particles/kg dw; Tissue Translocation = %.4g particles/kg dw\n",
            sed_HC5_food_dilution_pkg, sed_HC5_tissue_translocation_pkg))
cat("Plausible band (Redondo-Hasselerharm et al. 2023 food-dilution benthic HC5 = 4.9e9 particles/kg dw, CI 6.6e7-1.9e11;\n",
    " IJC Great Lakes SAB 2024 = 62.6 particles/kg dw, illustrating the method-dependent spread): (1e1, 1e12)\n", sep = "")

guard_would_pass_fd  <- isTRUE(sed_HC5_food_dilution_pkg        > 1e1 & sed_HC5_food_dilution_pkg        < 1e12)
guard_would_pass_tt  <- isTRUE(sed_HC5_tissue_translocation_pkg > 1e1 & sed_HC5_tissue_translocation_pkg < 1e12)

if (isTRUE(sediment_concentration_is_quantitative)) {
  # Reference: Redondo-Hasselerharm et al. (2023) food-dilution benthic HC5 = 4.9e9 particles/kg dw
  stopifnot(sed_HC5_food_dilution_pkg > 1e1 && sed_HC5_food_dilution_pkg < 1e12)
  stopifnot(sed_HC5_tissue_translocation_pkg > 1e1 && sed_HC5_tissue_translocation_pkg < 1e12)
} else {
  # cat(), not message(): this chunk's output must be visible in the rendered
  # report per SPEC 1d-iii ("visible, rendered assertion... fail loudly with an
  # informative message"), and the document-wide knitr option message=FALSE
  # (setup chunk) would otherwise silently swallow a message()-based warning.
  cat(sprintf(
    paste0("SPEC 1d-iii benthic-HC5 sanity guard: Food Dilution HC5 %s the plausible benthic range (1e1-1e12 particles/kg dw); ",
           "Tissue Translocation HC5 %s it. `sediment_concentration_is_quantitative` is FALSE (SPEC 1d-i), so this guard is ",
           "intentionally rendered as a non-fatal loud message rather than a hard stopifnot() -- it becomes a hard, render-halting ",
           "assertion the instant that flag is set TRUE. A FAIL here is EXPECTED and is additional confirmation that the current ",
           "sediment pathway must not be reported as a real risk finding.\n"),
    if (guard_would_pass_fd) "PASSES" else "FAILS", if (guard_would_pass_tt) "PASSES" else "FAILS"
  ))
}
```

**The current derived sediment Food Dilution HC5 fails the plausibility guard above by roughly eleven orders of magnitude** (see the rendered value; expected to be on the order of `r round(sed_HC5_food_dilution_pkg, 4)` particles/kg vs. a published benthic range of 10¹-10¹² particles/kg dw), consistent with the SPEC 1d-i finding that the sediment pathway's exposure concentration is not a genuine particles/kg-dry-weight value. **The sediment Food Dilution and Tissue Translocation RQ/HC5 figures in this report are illustrative/non-quantitative and are excluded from the headline risk characterization (Sections 14-15) pending a genuine dry-weight sediment concentration.**

## 11.5 Sediment as a time-dependent, accumulating compartment

**Rationale.** Sediment is an accumulating, long-residence depositional compartment, and it is the sink for the large/dense particles that differential settling removes from the water column (Hoffman et al. 2026; the critical-size capture-fraction diagnostic in Section 13 quantifies that filtering mechanism for this dataset). Those deposited particles continue to fragment in situ, so — per [Thuy-Dung, Groenenberg & Koelmans (2026)](https://doi.org/10.1186/s43591-026-00210-8) — both exposure (bioaccessible particle number) and hazard (HC5, via which benthic species are size-accessible) are dynamic rather than static. A single-time-point sediment RQ is therefore a snapshot that can under-represent future risk in an accumulating bed. Everything in this section is a framework upgrade, not a live risk calculation: the sediment exposure concentration remains non-quantitative (`sediment_concentration_is_quantitative` = `r sediment_concentration_is_quantitative`, SPEC 1d), so nothing here re-introduces sediment into the headline risk conclusion (Sections 11.3.0/11.4.0/15.3).

### 11.5.1 Temporal fragmentation framing

- **Sediment is treated as a time-dependent, accumulating compartment.** Deposited microplastics continue to fragment, shifting the particle-size distribution toward smaller, more numerous, more bioaccessible particles over residence time in the bed.
- **Consequently, any static sediment metric is a lower-bound snapshot.** Both HC5 (which benthic species are size-accessible) and bioaccessible exposure evolve as fragmentation proceeds — the single-time-point Food Dilution/Tissue Translocation figures in Section 11.4 describe the sediment PSD's condition at the time of sampling, not its trajectory.
- **This compounds, rather than substitutes for, the SPEC 1d exposure-concentration problem.** Even once a genuine dry-weight sediment concentration becomes available, a single power-law fit to that concentration would still understate risk relative to the bed's future, more-fragmented state.
- Cite [Thuy-Dung, Groenenberg & Koelmans (2026)](https://doi.org/10.1186/s43591-026-00210-8) — a prospective, temporally-explicit risk framework for fragmenting microplastics (size-independent fragmentation rate constant *k*~frag~, doubling time *T*~D~) in which HC5 and RCR are time-dependent because shrinking particles become bioaccessible to progressively more sensitive species; the source paper's median HC5 example drops from 2.1×10⁴ to 1.95×10³ particles/kg when a sensitive species becomes accessible, and individual-species RCR>1 can precede a derivable community SSD by roughly a decade. Cross-reference: the Hoffman et al. (2026) differential-settling sink argument already used in this document (Section 13's critical-size diagnostic) is the mechanism that puts large/dense particles into the sediment bed in the first place; SPEC 1e is about what happens to them *after* they arrive.

### 11.5.3 Time-varying bioaccessibility (documented; future enhancement)

Making the existing pSSD++ bioaccessibility size-gate explicitly time-dependent (HC5(*t*)/RCR(*t*) as a trajectory) is deferred: it needs a residence-time/age-of-deposition axis that does not exist in the source sediment dataset. Full scoping in Appendix C.

### 11.5.4 Most-sensitive-species screen (sediment)

Per Thuy-Dung et al. (2026), individual-species risk can precede a derivable community SSD signal by roughly a decade, and the sediment benthic SSD here is small and comparatively unstable (`r nrow(tox_data_sed)` records, `r dplyr::n_distinct(tox_data_sed$Species)` species). This screen identifies the single most sensitive species (lowest aligned effect dose) per ERM and reports it alongside the community HC5 already computed in Section 11.4 — as an early-warning companion, not a replacement.

```{r sediment-most-sensitive-species}
mss_sed <- most_sensitive_species(erm_registry_sed, dose_col = "dose_new_particles_kg")

knitr::kable(
  mss_sed,
  digits = 3,
  caption = paste0(
    "SPEC 1e-iv: most-sensitive-species screen, sediment benthic dataset (n = ", nrow(tox_data_sed),
    " records, ", dplyr::n_distinct(tox_data_sed$Species), " species). median_EC (particles/kg dw) is the ",
    "most-sensitive species' own median aligned dose -- an early-warning companion to, not a replacement for, ",
    "the community HC5 in Section 11.4."
  )
)

mss_sed_fd <- dplyr::filter(mss_sed, ERM == "Food Dilution")
mss_sed_tt <- dplyr::filter(mss_sed, ERM == "Tissue Translocation")
```

For Food Dilution, the single most sensitive species among the `r mss_sed_fd$n_species` sediment benthic species considered is *`r mss_sed_fd$Species`* (median aligned dose = `r signif(mss_sed_fd$median_EC, 3)` particles/kg dw, `r mss_sed_fd$n_records` aligned records), compared with the community Food Dilution HC5 of `r signif(sed_HC5_food_dilution_pkg, 3)` particles/kg dw computed in Section 11.4. For Tissue Translocation, the most sensitive species is *`r mss_sed_tt$Species`* (median aligned dose = `r signif(mss_sed_tt$median_EC, 3)` particles/kg dw, `r mss_sed_tt$n_records` records), compared with the community Tissue Translocation HC5 of `r signif(sed_HC5_tissue_translocation_pkg, 3)` particles/kg dw. As Section 11.5.3 notes, a finer PSD from continued fragmentation could bring additional, potentially more sensitive species into bioaccessible range over time, which is part of why this individual-species screen is worth tracking alongside the community HC5 rather than assuming the current community SSD is stable. **This screen does not change the sediment exclusion from the headline conclusion** (its inputs are the same non-quantitative-exposure sediment pathway); the companion individual-species screen for the quantitative river/ocean water compartments is reported in Section 15.4, once every matrix's hazard objects have been computed.

---

# 12. Ocean Water

Ocean water samples were collected from the coastal/marine environment and analyzed using the same µFTIR workflow as river water. Marine species are evaluated using the PSSDplusplus marine toxicity endpoints and alignment parameters, which characterize exposure and hazard in particles/L rather than particles/kg (sediment).

## 12.1 Particle data and C-PSD fitting

### Particle volume computation

```{r ocean-volume}
# Compute W/L thickness ratio from ocean particles (same instrument as river)
ratio_tbl_ocean <- raw_particles_ocean |>
  dplyr::mutate(WL = 1 / aspect_ratio) |>
  dplyr::group_by(shape) |>
  dplyr::summarise(
    n      = dplyr::n(),
    r_med  = median(WL, na.rm = TRUE),
    r_low  = quantile(WL, 0.25, na.rm = TRUE),
    r_high = quantile(WL, 0.75, na.rm = TRUE),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

raw_particles_ocean <- raw_particles_ocean |>
  assign_polymer_density(lookup = polymer_density_tbl) |>
  dplyr::left_join(ratio_tbl_ocean |> dplyr::select(shape, r_med), by = "shape") |>
  dplyr::mutate(
    height_um = r_med * width_um,
    V_um3 = dplyr::case_when(
      shape == "fragment" ~ (pi / 6) * length_um * width_um * height_um,
      shape == "fiber"    ~ pi * (width_um / 2)^2 * length_um,
      TRUE ~ NA_real_
    ),
    mass_ug = V_um3 * density_g_cm3,
    mass_ug_fixed_density_1.1 = V_um3 * 1.1
  )

cat("Ocean particles: n =", nrow(raw_particles_ocean),
    "| shapes:", paste(sort(unique(raw_particles_ocean$shape)), collapse = ", "), "\n")
```

### Particle length

```{r cpsd-fits-ocean-length, cache=TRUE, cache.extra=raw_data_cache_key}
cpsd_fits_ocean_length <- fit_cpsd_by_shape(
  raw_particles_ocean, value_col = "length_um",
  config = list(
    fragment = list(bin_um = 5, fit_range_um = c(NA_real_, NA_real_)),
    fiber    = list(bin_um = 5, fit_range_um = c(NA_real_, NA_real_)),
    all      = list(bin_um = 5, fit_range_um = c(NA_real_, NA_real_))
  )
)
cpsd_fit_ocean_frag  <- cpsd_fits_ocean_length$fragment
cpsd_fit_ocean_fiber <- cpsd_fits_ocean_length$fiber
cpsd_fit_ocean_all   <- cpsd_fits_ocean_length$all
```

```{r cpsd-fits-ocean-by-location, cache=TRUE, cache.extra=raw_data_cache_key}
# Ocean-water sample_location carries the same four river-mouth-adjacent
# coastal site names as raw_particles_river (Carmel, Pajaro, Salinas, San
# Lorenzo) -- ocean water was collected adjacent to each river's discharge,
# not at one generic offshore site -- so the same per-location C-PSD fit and
# heterogeneity test used for river water (Section 4.2.4) can be run here.
# Ocean per-location n is much smaller than river (117 total vs 1207), so a
# tryCatch guard (mirroring safe_cpsd() in Section 4.2.4) is required: some
# locations may have too few/too sparse particles for the two-step LOD
# algorithm to find any valid populated-bin window.
ocean_locations <- sort(unique(raw_particles_ocean$sample_location))

safe_cpsd_ocean_loc <- function(data, ...) {
  if (length(data) < 10) return(list(valid = FALSE))
  tryCatch(
    c(fit_cpsd_segur_r(data, ...), list(valid = TRUE)),
    error = function(e) list(valid = FALSE)
  )
}

cpsd_fits_ocean_by_loc <- lapply(setNames(ocean_locations, ocean_locations), function(loc) {
  dat <- raw_particles_ocean |> dplyr::filter(sample_location == loc) |> dplyr::pull(length_um)
  safe_cpsd_ocean_loc(dat, bin_um = 5)
})

ocean_loc_summary <- dplyr::bind_rows(lapply(names(cpsd_fits_ocean_by_loc), function(loc) {
  fo <- cpsd_fits_ocean_by_loc[[loc]]
  if (isTRUE(fo$valid)) {
    tibble::tibble(
      location     = loc,
      n_particles  = sum(raw_particles_ocean$sample_location == loc),
      a_cpsd       = round(fo$a_cpsd,   3),
      se_a_cpsd    = round(fo$se_a_cpsd, 3),
      a_psd        = round(fo$a_psd,    3),
      lod_low_um   = round(fo$lower_lod_used_um, 0),
      lod_high_um  = round(fo$upper_lod_um,       0),
      r2           = round(fo$r2,       3),
      n_bins       = fo$n_bins,
      fit_mode     = fo$fit_mode
    )
  } else {
    tibble::tibble(
      location = loc, n_particles = sum(raw_particles_ocean$sample_location == loc),
      a_cpsd = NA_real_, se_a_cpsd = NA_real_, a_psd = NA_real_,
      lod_low_um = NA_real_, lod_high_um = NA_real_, r2 = NA_real_,
      n_bins = NA_integer_, fit_mode = "no_fit"
    )
  }
}))

knitr::kable(ocean_loc_summary, caption = "C-PSD length fits by ocean (coastal) location (Segur 2026 algorithm)")
```

```{r cpsd-ocean-location-heterogeneity}
# Same Cochran's Q heterogeneity test as the river-location version above,
# applied to the ocean per-location slopes. Locations with fit_mode != "ok"
# (too few particles/bins for a valid LOD window) are excluded from the test
# rather than silently contributing an unstable estimate.
ocean_loc_summary_valid <- dplyr::filter(ocean_loc_summary, fit_mode == "ok", is.finite(se_a_cpsd), se_a_cpsd > 0)

ocean_slope_heterogeneity <- if (nrow(ocean_loc_summary_valid) >= 2) {
  slope_heterogeneity_test(
    a = ocean_loc_summary_valid$a_cpsd, se = ocean_loc_summary_valid$se_a_cpsd,
    labels = ocean_loc_summary_valid$location
  )
} else NULL

if (!is.null(ocean_slope_heterogeneity)) {
  cat(
    "Ocean (coastal) location slope heterogeneity: Q(", ocean_slope_heterogeneity$df, ") = ",
    round(ocean_slope_heterogeneity$Q, 2), ", p = ", signif(ocean_slope_heterogeneity$p_value, 3),
    ", I2 = ", round(ocean_slope_heterogeneity$i2, 1), "%, weighted-mean a_cpsd = ",
    round(ocean_slope_heterogeneity$weighted_mean, 3),
    " (", nrow(ocean_loc_summary_valid), " of ", nrow(ocean_loc_summary), " locations had a valid fit)\n", sep = ""
  )
} else {
  cat("Ocean location slope heterogeneity test could not be run: fewer than 2 locations had a valid C-PSD fit.\n")
}
```

```{r cpsd-ocean-location-slope-plot}
ocean_location_slope_plot <- ocean_loc_summary |>
  ggplot2::ggplot(ggplot2::aes(x = location, y = a_psd)) +
  ggplot2::geom_point(size = 4, color = "#009E73") +
  ggplot2::geom_errorbar(
    ggplot2::aes(ymin = a_psd - se_a_cpsd, ymax = a_psd + se_a_cpsd),
    width = 0.2, color = "#009E73", linewidth = 0.8
  ) +
  ggplot2::labs(
    x        = "Ocean (coastal) location",

    title    = "Power-law slope by ocean (coastal) location",
    subtitle = expression("Error bars = ±1 SE")
  ) +
  ggplot2::theme_minimal(base_size = 20) +
  ggplot2::theme(panel.border = ggplot2::element_rect(color = "gray85", fill = NA, linewidth = 0.4))

ggsave(ocean_location_slope_plot, filename = "figures/ocean_location_slope_plot.png", width = 9, height = 6, dpi = 300)
ocean_location_slope_plot
```

### Particle volume

Note: ocean's fragment volume fit uses the same length/width-consistent
`volume_lod_bounds()` approach as river and sediment (Section 4.2.3). Its **fiber** fit does
not: ocean has only `r sum(raw_particles_ocean$shape == "fiber")` fiber particles total, and
even the corrected (length/width-consistent, not isotropic) fiber volume-LOD window contains
just 4 of them — too few to constrain a fit. Ocean's fiber volume fit instead falls back to
the Segur algorithm's own auto-detected LOD window. Similarly, the "all" (pooled shapes) fit
uses the **fragment-only** volume-LOD window rather than the fragment/fiber union: with only
`r sum(raw_particles_ocean$shape == "fiber")` fibers, the union window is dominated by a
handful of sparse, noisy fiber-derived bounds and destabilizes the pooled fit (fragments
outnumber fibers roughly 10:1 in this matrix, so anchoring "all" to fragment's reliable range
is the more defensible choice here).

```{r ocean-volume-lod-bounds}
r_med_frag_ocean  <- ratio_tbl_ocean$r_med[ratio_tbl_ocean$shape == "fragment"]
r_med_fiber_ocean <- ratio_tbl_ocean$r_med[ratio_tbl_ocean$shape == "fiber"]
vlb_ocean <- volume_lod_bounds(cpsd_fit_ocean_frag, cpsd_fit_ocean_fiber, r_med_frag_ocean, r_med_fiber_ocean)
cat("Ocean fragment volume LOD: [", signif(vlb_ocean$fragment[1], 2), ",", signif(vlb_ocean$fragment[2], 2), "] µm³\n")
cat("Ocean fiber    volume LOD (informational only — too few particles to use as a fit constraint): [",
    signif(vlb_ocean$fiber[1], 2), ",", signif(vlb_ocean$fiber[2], 2), "] µm³\n")
```

```{r cpsd-fits-ocean-volume, cache=TRUE, cache.extra=list(raw_data_cache_key, vlb_ocean)}
# fragment and all use the same uniform vol_bin_um as river/sediment. fiber is the one
# documented exception (see note above): with only 4 particles inside its physically-
# derived window, no fixed window is viable, so it falls back to auto-detection
# (fit_range_um = NA) with a coarser bin width appropriate to its much wider absolute
# volume range (up to ~3e7 µm³, vs ~7e5 µm³ for fragment) — fine bins there would be
# almost entirely empty regardless of methodology, per the small-sample diagnosis above.
ocean_fiber_vol_bin_um <- 1e6
cpsd_fits_ocean_volume <- fit_cpsd_by_shape(
  raw_particles_ocean, value_col = "V_um3",
  config = list(
    fragment = list(bin_um = vol_bin_um,          fit_range_um = vlb_ocean$fragment),
    fiber    = list(bin_um = ocean_fiber_vol_bin_um, fit_range_um = c(NA_real_, NA_real_)),
    all      = list(bin_um = vol_bin_um,          fit_range_um = vlb_ocean$fragment)
  )
)
cpsd_fit_volume_ocean_frag  <- cpsd_fits_ocean_volume$fragment
cpsd_fit_volume_ocean_fiber <- cpsd_fits_ocean_volume$fiber
cpsd_fit_volume_ocean       <- cpsd_fits_ocean_volume$all
```

```{r}
ocean_volume_fits <- list(fragment = cpsd_fit_volume_ocean_frag, fiber = cpsd_fit_volume_ocean_fiber, all = cpsd_fit_volume_ocean)
```
